That subtitle and the book's frankness provoked controversy, though it also sold well. It has since been adapted for film, television, opera and the stage.
the-age-of-innocence: The Age of Innocence is set among the wealthy old families of New York in the 1870s, a world governed by unwritten rules about manners, money and reputation. Newland Archer, a young lawyer from a respectable family, is engaged to May Welland, a beautiful and seemingly perfect product of that society. Then May's cousin, the Countess Ellen Olenska, returns from Europe after leaving an unhappy marriage to a Polish nobleman. Her independence and disregard for convention scandalise New York, and Newland, asked to help the family manage her situation, finds himself increasingly drawn to her.

Wharton writes with elegant irony about a society that punishes anyone who steps out of line, often without a word being spoken. The novel examines duty and desire, the costs of conformity, and the quiet power that apparently innocent people can exercise. Its attention to clothes, dinners, opera boxes and drawing rooms is almost anthropological, but it is also a deeply felt story of longing and choice.

Wharton drew on memories of the New York of her own childhood. The novel was serialised in Pictorial Review in 1920 and published as a book that year. In 1921 it won the Pulitzer Prize for the Novel, making Wharton the first woman to win that award. It has been adapted for the stage, film and television, and remains her most widely admired work.
macbeth: Macbeth is a tragedy set in medieval Scotland. Returning from a victorious battle, the generals Macbeth and Banquo meet three witches who greet Macbeth with titles he does not yet hold, including future king, and tell Banquo that his descendants will reign. When part of the prophecy quickly comes true, Macbeth begins to think about murder. Urged on by his determined wife, Lady Macbeth, he kills King Duncan while the king is a guest in his castle and seizes the crown. But one crime leads to another, and suspicion, fear and guilt begin to unravel both husband and wife.

The shortest of Shakespeare's tragedies, Macbeth is fast, dark and intense. It explores ambition, fate and free will, the nature of power, and the psychological toll of violence, through some of Shakespeare's most haunting poetry and imagery of blood, sleep and darkness. Lady Macbeth is one of the great dramatic roles, and the play's portrait of a mind consumed by its own deeds still grips audiences.

The play was probably written around 1606, early in the reign of James I, and draws on Holinshed's Chronicles for its history. It was first printed in the First Folio of 1623. Among actors it carries a famous superstition, leading many to call it the Scottish play. It has been adapted into opera, notably by Verdi, and into many films.
the-idiot: The Idiot follows Prince Lev Nikolayevich Myshkin, a young man of noble family who returns to Russia after years of treatment for epilepsy at a sanatorium in Switzerland. Penniless, trusting and utterly sincere, he arrives in St Petersburg and quickly becomes entangled with the household of General Yepanchin and his three daughters, and with a group of ambitious, scheming and passionate people. Two women in particular claim his attention: Nastasya Filippovna, a beautiful and wounded woman whose past has made her the subject of gossip, and Aglaya Yepanchina, proud and spirited. A dark rival, the merchant's son Rogozhin, adds a dangerous intensity to everything that follows.

Dostoevsky set himself the task of portraying a truly good man and asked what would happen to such a person in a society driven by money, vanity and desire. Myshkin's kindness and honesty unsettle everyone around him, and some call him an idiot for it. The novel is full of feverish scenes, long confessional conversations and debates on faith, death and compassion.

Dostoevsky wrote the book while living abroad, and it was serialised in The Russian Messenger in 1868 and 1869. Reception was mixed at first, but it is now considered one of his major novels, alongside Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov. It has been adapted for stage, film and television in Russia and elsewhere.
the-red-and-the-black: The Red and the Black follows Julien Sorel, the clever, sensitive son of a carpenter in the small town of Verrières in eastern France. Julien worships Napoleon, but in Restoration France, after the emperor's fall, the path to glory through the army seems closed, and the Church offers a more practical route to advancement. Hired as tutor to the children of the town's mayor, Monsieur de Rênal, he begins an affair with the mayor's gentle wife. His career then carries him to a seminary in Besançon and on to Paris, into the household of the powerful Marquis de La Mole and his proud daughter Mathilde.

Stendhal examines ambition, hypocrisy and class in a society where talent alone cannot open doors. Julien is fascinating because he is so divided: calculating yet passionate, contemptuous of the aristocracy yet desperate to be accepted by it. Stendhal's close attention to his characters' shifting thoughts and motives makes the novel an early landmark of psychological realism, and its ironic voice still feels modern.

Published in 1830 and subtitled Chronicle of 1830, the novel was partly inspired by a real criminal case reported in the newspapers. It found only a limited readership at first, but its reputation grew greatly in later decades, and it is now regarded as one of the great French novels of the nineteenth century, adapted for film, television and the stage.
the-arabian-nights: The Arabian Nights, also known as One Thousand and One Nights, is a vast collection of stories gathered over centuries from Persian, Indian, Arabic and other traditions. It is held together by a frame story. King Shahryar, embittered by his wife's betrayal, resolves to marry a new bride each day and have her executed the next morning. Scheherazade, the clever daughter of his vizier, volunteers to marry him and each night tells him a story, breaking off at a moment of suspense so that he must spare her to hear what happens next. Her tales contain further tales, nested one within another.

The stories range from fables and love stories to crime, comedy, adventure and the supernatural, filled with genies, merchants, thieves, caliphs and talking animals. Many are set in a richly imagined Baghdad, Cairo or Basra. Beyond their entertainment value, they reflect on fate, cunning, justice and the power of storytelling itself, which, in the frame tale, literally saves lives.

The collection developed in Arabic over many centuries, drawing on an earlier Persian book. It reached European readers through Antoine Galland's French translation, published from 1704, which added tales such as Aladdin and Ali Baba that are not found in the older Arabic manuscripts; Galland heard some from a Syrian storyteller, Hanna Diyab. Later English translations followed, and the Nights have influenced writers, composers and filmmakers around the world.
crime-and-punishment: Crime and Punishment is set in the cramped rooms, taverns and stifling summer streets of St Petersburg. Rodion Raskolnikov, a proud and impoverished former law student, has convinced himself that certain extraordinary people have the right to step over moral rules for a higher purpose. Acting on this theory, he kills an elderly pawnbroker. The novel then follows him through feverish days of guilt, illness and suspicion, as he crosses paths with the drunken clerk Marmeladov and his daughter Sonya, his loyal friend Razumikhin, his devoted sister Dunya, and the patient, probing investigator Porfiry Petrovich.

This is less a mystery about who committed the crime than a deep psychological study of why, and of what it does to the person who commits it. Dostoevsky explores poverty, pride, faith, suffering and the danger of ideas cut loose from human feeling. Readers today still find in Raskolnikov a disturbingly modern figure: isolated, clever and trapped inside his own reasoning.

The novel was first published in instalments in the Russian Messenger during 1866. It confirmed Dostoevsky's standing as a major writer and remains one of the most widely read works of Russian literature. Its influence reaches crime fiction, existentialist philosophy and psychological drama, and it has been adapted many times for stage, cinema and television.
dracula: Dracula opens with Jonathan Harker, a young English solicitor, travelling to Transylvania to help a mysterious nobleman, Count Dracula, complete the purchase of a house near London. What begins as a business trip turns into an unsettling stay in a remote castle where Harker slowly realises he is more prisoner than guest. The danger then moves to England, touching his fiancée Mina Murray and her friend Lucy Westenra, and drawing in a small group of allies led by the Dutch professor Abraham Van Helsing, who understands the nature of the threat they face.

Stoker tells the story entirely through documents: diaries, letters, newspaper cuttings, a ship's log and phonograph records. This patchwork gives the novel a gripping sense of immediacy, as each character knows only part of the truth. Beneath the Gothic thrills lie anxieties about modern technology, sexuality, foreign influence and the fragility of reason.

Dracula was published in London in 1897. Stoker, an Irish writer who also worked as manager of the Lyceum Theatre, did not invent the vampire, but his Count became the definitive version of the figure. The novel has shaped horror fiction ever since and has been adapted countless times for the stage, film, television, radio and comics, making its villain one of the most recognisable characters in popular culture.
moby-dick: Moby-Dick begins with a young man who asks to be called Ishmael heading to sea to escape his restlessness. In New Bedford he befriends Queequeg, a harpooner from the South Seas, and the two sign on to the Nantucket whaling ship Pequod. Only once the voyage is under way does the ship's captain, Ahab, appear on deck and reveal his true purpose: to hunt down the great white whale that took his leg on an earlier voyage. The crew, including the cautious first mate Starbuck, is drawn into his quest across the world's oceans.

Melville mixes adventure with an astonishing range of other forms: sermons, stage-like scenes, soliloquies, and detailed chapters on whales, whaling and the work of the ship. The book asks large questions about obsession, fate, the limits of knowledge and humanity's place in nature, while also offering humour, warmth and friendship across cultures. Readers who accept its digressions find one of the most ambitious and original novels ever written.

The novel appeared in 1851, first in London under the title The Whale and shortly afterwards in New York as Moby-Dick. It sold poorly and puzzled many reviewers, and Melville died in relative obscurity. In the early twentieth century critics rediscovered it, and it is now widely considered one of the great American novels. It has inspired films, stage works, artworks and countless references in popular culture.
the-odyssey: The Odyssey follows Odysseus, king of the island of Ithaca, as he struggles to return home after the fall of Troy. The poem opens years after the war: his wife Penelope is besieged by suitors competing for her hand and his property, and his young son Telemachus sets out to seek news of his father. Meanwhile Odysseus is held on the island of the nymph Calypso. When he finally reaches the court of the Phaeacians, he recounts his earlier adventures, including encounters with the Cyclops Polyphemus, the enchantress Circe, the Sirens, and a journey to the land of the dead, all while pursued by the anger of the sea god Poseidon and aided by the goddess Athena.

The poem explores homecoming, loyalty, hospitality, cleverness and the bond between parents and children. Odysseus is a hero of wit as much as strength, and the story's structure, beginning in the middle and moving through tales within tales, feels surprisingly modern.

Composed in Greek hexameter verse and divided into twenty-four books, the Odyssey is traditionally attributed to Homer, though who he was and how the poems took shape remain debated. It has been studied and retold for nearly three thousand years and has inspired countless works, from ancient drama to James Joyce's novel Ulysses, as well as many translations, films and stage versions.
meditations: Meditations is a collection of private notes written by Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor from 161 to 180 AD. He wrote them in Greek, apparently for himself alone, and much of the work dates from the years he spent on military campaigns along the Danube frontier. Organised into twelve books, it is not a systematic treatise but a series of reflections, reminders and short exercises in which the emperor tries to train his own mind to live well.

The central ideas come from Stoic philosophy, which Marcus learned in part from the teachings of Epictetus. He reminds himself that we control our own judgements but not external events, that life is short and change is constant, that other people's faults should be met with patience, and that we are all parts of a single rational whole. Book One is a moving list of what he learned from family, teachers and friends. The writing is direct, honest and often self-critical, which is why so many readers today, from students to leaders, turn to it for practical guidance on anxiety, anger, duty and mortality.

The text survived through medieval manuscripts and was first printed in the sixteenth century. Since then it has been translated into many languages and has remained continuously in print, playing a central part in the modern revival of interest in Stoicism.
the-communist-manifesto: The Communist Manifesto was written by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels as a programme for the Communist League, a small organisation of radical workers and intellectuals. It sets out a view of history as a series of struggles between social classes and argues that modern industrial society has simplified this conflict into one between the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat, who must sell their labour to survive. The text describes how capitalism has transformed the world with astonishing speed, then argues that its recurring crises and its treatment of workers will lead to its overthrow.

Its sections move from this historical analysis to the aims of the communists, a critique of rival socialist movements, and a short list of practical demands such as a progressive income tax and free public education for children. The style is vivid and forceful, more like a speech than an academic study. Whether one agrees with it or not, it remains essential reading for understanding modern political history, debates about inequality and globalisation, and the movements it inspired.

The pamphlet was first published in London in February 1848, in German, just as revolutions were breaking out across Europe. It attracted little attention at first, but later editions and translations spread it worldwide, and it became one of the most influential political documents ever written.
heart-of-darkness: Heart of Darkness is framed as a story told at dusk aboard a small boat anchored on the Thames. The sailor Marlow recalls how he once took a job captaining a river steamer for a Belgian trading company in Africa. As he travels inland, he witnesses the cruelty, waste and absurdity of the colonial ivory trade, and he hears more and more about Kurtz, a gifted company agent stationed deep in the interior whose reputation seems to grow stranger with every report. Marlow's journey upriver to find him becomes the spine of the narrative.

Conrad's prose is dense, atmospheric and deliberately uncertain, often suggesting more than it states. The novella examines imperial greed, the hypocrisy of the so-called civilising mission, and the fragility of moral restraint. It is also a powerful study of storytelling itself. Its portrayal of Africans has been strongly criticised, most famously by the Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe, and reading it today means engaging with both its insight and its blind spots.

Conrad drew on his own journey up the Congo River in 1890. The story was first serialised in Blackwood's Magazine in 1899 and published in book form in 1902. It remains one of the most studied works of modern fiction and has inspired many adaptations and reimaginings, including the film Apocalypse Now, which moves the story to the Vietnam War.
the-autobiography-of-benjamin-franklin: Benjamin Franklin began writing his memoirs in 1771, addressing the first part to his son William, and returned to them several times in later life. He describes his childhood in Boston as one of many children of a candle and soap maker, his apprenticeship to his older brother James, a printer, and his decision as a teenager to run away to Philadelphia. From there he traces his slow rise as a printer and publisher, his founding of a discussion club called the Junto, and his involvement in civic projects such as a lending library, and he looks ahead to his scientific and public work.

The book is famous for its practical spirit. Franklin describes his plan to achieve moral perfection through thirteen virtues, including temperance, order, frugality and industry while cheerfully admitting his failures. The tone is lively, self-deprecating and full of shrewd advice on work, reputation and getting along with others. It offers a vivid portrait of colonial American life and of the ideal of the self-made man.

Franklin never finished the work, and the account breaks off well before the American Revolution. It was first published in a French translation in 1791, the year after his death, and English versions followed soon after. A reliable complete text appeared only in the nineteenth century. It has since become a classic of American autobiography and is widely read in schools.
the-wonderful-wizard-of-oz: Dorothy lives with her Aunt Em and Uncle Henry on a grey Kansas prairie until a cyclone lifts their house, with Dorothy and her little dog Toto inside, and sets it down in the colourful land of Oz. Told that only the great Wizard in the Emerald City can send her home, she sets off along the road of yellow brick. On the way she is joined by a Scarecrow who wants brains, a Tin Woodman who longs for a heart, and a Cowardly Lion in search of courage, and together they face wild creatures, a field of poppies and the hostility of the Wicked Witch of the West.

Baum set out to write a modern fairy tale for American children, with wonder and adventure but without heavy moralising. The story is simple, funny and quietly wise, especially in the way the companions show the very qualities they believe they lack. Its themes of friendship, self-belief and the meaning of home make it a pleasure to read aloud and to revisit as an adult.

The book was published in Chicago in 1900 with colour illustrations by W. W. Denslow and quickly became popular. Baum went on to write many more Oz books. The 1939 MGM film made it world-famous, and Oz has since inspired many other films, musicals and retellings.
the-war-of-the-worlds: The War of the Worlds is narrated by an unnamed writer living in Woking, Surrey, near London. Late one night a strange cylinder falls onto Horsell Common, and curious crowds gather to watch it unscrew. From it emerge Martians, who soon assemble towering three-legged fighting machines armed with a devastating Heat-Ray and a poisonous black smoke. As more cylinders arrive, the narrator flees across the countryside, separated from his wife, while his brother's account shows the panic of London's population as the invaders advance.

Wells uses the invasion to turn the tables on his readers. The British, who had built a vast empire by conquering others, find themselves helpless before a technologically superior power, and the novel invites reflection on imperialism, evolution and human arrogance. Its realistic descriptions of real places, refugees and the collapse of order give it a documentary feel that still makes it gripping, and it is one of the foundational works of science fiction.

The novel was first serialised in Pearson's Magazine in 1897 and published as a book in 1898. It established the template for the alien-invasion story. Its most famous adaptation is Orson Welles's 1938 American radio broadcast, presented as a series of news bulletins, and it has also been adapted for film, television, comics and a well-known musical album.
the-adventures-of-pinocchio: In a small Tuscan village, a poor old woodcarver named Geppetto carves a puppet from a piece of talking wood and names him Pinocchio. The puppet is barely finished before he runs off and starts getting into trouble. Impulsive, lazy and easily tempted, Pinocchio repeatedly promises to be good and go to school, only to be led astray by a cunning Fox and Cat, a fearsome puppet master, and the lure of a land where children never have to study. Along the way he meets the Talking Cricket and a kind Fairy with turquoise hair, and his nose grows whenever he tells a lie.

Collodi's story is much stranger and darker than many readers expect. It is a lively mix of comedy, fairy tale and moral lesson, full of sudden dangers, transformations and absurd humour. Beneath the adventures lie themes of responsibility, honesty, poverty and the love between a parent and child, and the book offers a vivid picture of nineteenth-century Italian life seen through a child's misadventures.

The story first appeared in instalments in a Roman children's magazine from 1881 and was published as a book in 1883. It became one of the most translated works of Italian literature and a classic of children's fiction worldwide. It has inspired many adaptations for film, animation, theatre and television, most famously Walt Disney's 1940 animated feature.
the-republic: The Republic is a dialogue in which Socrates, visiting the port of Piraeus near Athens, is drawn into a conversation about the meaning of justice. After he challenges the claim of the sophist Thrasymachus that justice is simply the advantage of the stronger, Plato's brothers Glaucon and Adeimantus press him to prove that a just life is better than an unjust one, even if no one rewards it. To answer, Socrates imagines building an ideal city, reasoning that justice may be easier to see on a larger scale.

Across ten books the dialogue covers an extraordinary range of ideas: a city divided into rulers, guardians and producers, mirrored by a soul divided into reason, spirit and appetite; the rule of philosopher-kings; the education of the guardians; the censorship of poetry; the theory of Forms; and the famous allegory of the cave, which pictures human beings mistaking shadows for reality. Some proposals, such as communal living for the guardians, are startling or troubling, and part of the value of reading the work is arguing with it. It remains a lively introduction to questions of ethics, politics, knowledge and education.

Written in the fourth century BC, the Republic has been studied continuously since antiquity. It has shaped Western philosophy, political theory and utopian writing more deeply than almost any other text, and it remains central to university courses around the world.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer: Tom Sawyer lives with his Aunt Polly, his half-brother Sid and his cousin Mary in St. Petersburg, a sleepy town on the Mississippi River. Clever, restless and allergic to school and Sunday sermons, Tom spends his days in schemes and games, famously persuading other boys to pay him for the privilege of whitewashing a fence. He falls for newcomer Becky Thatcher and roams the woods with his friend Huckleberry Finn, the town's carefree outcast. One night in the graveyard the two boys secretly witness a murder, and the knowledge of who really committed it hangs over them as the summer goes on.

Twain blends humour, nostalgia and genuine suspense. The book captures the imaginative world of childhood, full of pirates, robbers and buried treasure, while gently satirising adult hypocrisy, rigid schooling and small-town respectability. It is warm and funny, though modern readers will also notice its dated and stereotyped portrayal of some characters, which is worth discussing alongside its charms.

Twain drew on memories of his own boyhood in Hannibal, Missouri. The novel was published in 1876 and became one of his best-loved works. Huckleberry Finn, introduced here, went on to narrate his own celebrated novel. Tom's adventures have been adapted many times for film, television, stage and animation, and the whitewashed fence remains an iconic image of American childhood.
the-pilgrim-s-progress: The Pilgrim's Progress is presented as a dream. The narrator sees a man named Christian, weighed down by a heavy burden on his back, who learns that his home, the City of Destruction, is doomed. Guided by a figure called Evangelist, he leaves his family and sets out for the Celestial City. His road leads through places such as the Slough of Despond, the Valley of the Shadow of Death and the town of Vanity Fair, and he meets characters whose names reveal their nature, from Obstinate and Pliable to Faithful, Hopeful and the monstrous Giant Despair.

The work is a Christian allegory of the soul's journey towards salvation, but it also reads as a vivid adventure story full of fights, imprisonments, temptations and friendships. Bunyan's plain, rhythmic English, shaped by the King James Bible, keeps it accessible to readers of any faith. Its picture of life as a difficult journey, full of doubt and perseverance, continues to resonate.

Bunyan, a Puritan preacher from Bedfordshire, began the book while imprisoned for preaching without a licence. The first part was published in 1678, and a second part following Christian's wife Christiana appeared in 1684. It became one of the most widely read books in English and was translated into a great many languages. It has been adapted for stage, radio, opera and screen.
a-christmas-carol: Ebenezer Scrooge is a cold, tight-fisted London businessman who scorns Christmas, refuses charity and pays his clerk, Bob Cratchit, as little as possible. On Christmas Eve he is visited by the ghost of his former partner, Jacob Marley, who drags the chains he forged through a selfish life and warns Scrooge that he will be visited by three more spirits. The Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Yet to Come take him through scenes from his own childhood, the humble but loving Cratchit household with its frail son Tiny Tim, and a future that Scrooge is forced to confront.

Short enough to read in an evening, the story combines ghostly atmosphere, humour, sentiment and sharp social criticism. Dickens wrote it in part to draw attention to the hardship of the poor in industrial Britain, and its central question, whether a person can change and what we owe one another, remains as pressing as ever. Its memorable characters and lively language make it ideal for reading aloud.

Dickens published the novella in December 1843, with illustrations by John Leech. It was an immediate success, and Dickens later gave many public readings of it. The book helped popularise the idea of Christmas as a season of family, generosity and goodwill. It has been adapted countless times for stage, film, television, radio and animation, and the name Scrooge has entered everyday English.
middlemarch: Middlemarch, subtitled A Study of Provincial Life, is set in a fictional Midlands town in the years around 1830, a time of political reform, new railways and changing medicine. At its heart is Dorothea Brooke, an idealistic young woman who longs to do something meaningful with her life and chooses to marry the much older scholar Edward Casaubon. Alongside her story runs that of Tertius Lydgate, an ambitious young doctor eager to modernise medicine, who is drawn to the charming Rosamond Vincy. Around them a whole community comes to life, including Rosamond's easygoing brother Fred, the sensible Mary Garth, the young artist Will Ladislaw and the pious banker Bulstrode.

Eliot follows how hopes, money, gossip and marriage shape these lives, showing how small choices can have large consequences. Her narrator is wise, ironic and deeply compassionate, inviting readers to understand rather than judge. The novel's insight into ambition, compromise and the limits placed on women still feels remarkably fresh.

George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans. Middlemarch was first issued in eight parts in 1871 and 1872 and was well received. Its reputation has grown steadily, and many writers and critics regard it as one of the finest novels in English. It has been adapted for television and radio and is widely studied.
the-scarlet-pimpernel: The Scarlet Pimpernel is set in 1792, during the bloodiest years of the French Revolution. Aristocrats are being sent to the guillotine in Paris, but a mysterious Englishman known only as the Scarlet Pimpernel, after the small red flower he uses as his signature, keeps smuggling them out of France with a band of loyal followers. In London society, the beautiful French actress Marguerite is married to Sir Percy Blakeney, a wealthy baronet who seems to care only for fashion and foolish jokes. When the French agent Chauvelin puts pressure on Marguerite to help unmask the Pimpernel, she is caught between loyalties.

The novel is a fast-paced romantic adventure, full of disguises, chases and narrow escapes. Its great invention is the hero who hides his daring behind a mask of idleness, a device that later writers of masked heroes would borrow again and again. Modern readers may notice its strongly pro-aristocratic view of the Revolution, but its suspense, wit and romance remain very entertaining.

Baroness Orczy, born in Hungary and living in England, first developed the story as a play, written with her husband, which became a hit on the London stage. The novel was published in 1905 and was followed by many sequels. The story has been adapted repeatedly for film, television, radio and musical theatre.
othello: Othello begins in Venice, where Othello, a respected Moorish general in the service of the Venetian state, has secretly married Desdemona, the daughter of the senator Brabantio. His ensign Iago, resentful that Michael Cassio has been promoted over him, sets out to destroy Othello's happiness. When the action moves to Cyprus, where Othello commands the island's defence, Iago works through hints, half-truths and a carefully placed handkerchief to persuade him that Desdemona has been unfaithful.

The play is a tightly focused tragedy of jealousy, trust and manipulation. Iago is one of Shakespeare's most chilling creations, confiding in the audience while remaining hidden from everyone on stage, and his motives are still debated. The play also raises enduring questions about race, outsiders and the position of women, through characters such as Desdemona and Iago's wife Emilia. Its poetry, especially Othello's own speeches, is among Shakespeare's finest.

Shakespeare based the plot on an Italian story by Giovanni Battista Giraldi, known as Cinthio. The play was written in the early 1600s and is recorded as performed at court in 1604; it was first printed in 1622 and included in the First Folio of 1623. It has remained a stage favourite, inspired Verdi's opera Otello, and has been adapted many times for film and television, while the casting of the title role has become an important part of its modern history.
notes-from-underground: Notes from Underground is narrated by a nameless former civil servant living in a shabby room in St Petersburg, who calls himself a sick and spiteful man. The book has two parts. In the first, he delivers a rambling, combative monologue against the idea that human beings are rational creatures who will naturally act in their own best interests, arguing that people value their freedom of choice even more than their happiness. In the second, he recalls episodes from his younger life, including a humiliating dinner with former schoolmates and an encounter with a young woman named Liza.

The narrator is contradictory, self-pitying and often unpleasant, yet painfully honest about his vanity and isolation. Through him Dostoevsky attacks the confident belief that science and reason could design a perfect society, a view associated with radical writers of his day. The book is short but intense, darkly funny and unsettlingly familiar.

The work was first published in 1864 in Epoch, a journal run by Dostoevsky and his brother Mikhail. Its first part responds in particular to Nikolai Chernyshevsky's novel What Is to Be Done? Later readers saw in it an early statement of themes taken up by existentialist philosophers and modern novelists, and it is now widely regarded as a key text in the history of modern thought.
father-goriot: Father Goriot opens in 1819 at the Maison Vauquer, a dingy boarding house in a poor district of Paris. Among its lodgers are Goriot, a retired vermicelli maker who has given nearly all his fortune to his two married daughters, Anastasie and Delphine; Eugène de Rastignac, a young law student from a modest provincial family who dreams of success in high society; and Vautrin, a mysterious and worldly man who takes an interest in Eugène's ambitions. As Rastignac learns how the elegant salons of Paris really work, guided in part by his cousin Madame de Beauséant, his path becomes entangled with Goriot's devotion to his daughters.

Balzac paints a vivid, detailed picture of a society ruled by money and social rank, where love, family loyalty and honour are constantly tested by ambition. Its sharp observation of character makes it both a moving family drama and a lesson in how power and status operate, themes that still feel current.

The novel was serialised in 1834 and 1835 and published as a book in 1835. It is one of the central works of Balzac's vast cycle La Comédie humaine and the first in which he systematically brought back characters from other novels, a technique that linked his fictional world together. In French, Rastignac's name has come to mean an ambitious social climber. The book has been adapted for stage, film and television.
the-prophet: The Prophet is a book of poetic prose in which Almustafa, a wise man who has lived for twelve years in the city of Orphalese, sees the ship that will carry him back to the island of his birth. Before he leaves, the people of the city gather around him, and a seeress named Almitra and other townspeople ask him to speak about the great questions of life. In a series of short chapters he responds on subjects including love, marriage, children, giving, work, joy and sorrow, freedom, reason and passion, pain, friendship, time, prayer, beauty and death.

Gibran's style draws on the rhythms of scripture and on both Christian and Middle Eastern spiritual traditions. His answers are gentle, paradoxical and often surprising, suggesting for example that joy and sorrow are inseparable, or that children belong to life itself rather than to their parents. Its short sections make it easy to dip into for reflection or comfort.

Kahlil Gibran was born in Lebanon, then part of the Ottoman Empire, and emigrated as a child to the United States. He wrote The Prophet in English, and it was published in New York in 1923 with his own drawings. Though largely ignored by critics, it found a large, devoted readership, especially in the 1960s, and has been translated into many languages. Its passages are often read at weddings and funerals.
jane-eyre: Jane Eyre tells its story in her own voice, starting with a lonely childhood at Gateshead, where she is an orphan resented by her aunt, Mrs Reed. Sent away to Lowood, a harsh charity school, she finds hardship, illness and a precious friendship before growing into a capable young teacher. Wanting more of the world, she takes a post as governess at Thornfield Hall. There she meets the house's moody, sharp-tongued master, Edward Rochester, and an unlikely bond grows between them. Yet Thornfield is a house of strange noises and unexplained events, and its secret will put Jane's love and her principles to the hardest test.

The novel blends a coming-of-age story with romance and Gothic mystery. Its lasting power lies in Jane herself: plain, poor and outwardly quiet, yet insisting on her equal worth and her right to feel, think and choose for herself. Questions of conscience, independence, religion and the place of women run through the book, told in a direct first person that still feels modern.

Charlotte Brontë published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the pen name Currer Bell, and it was an immediate success, though some reviewers found its heroine improperly rebellious. It has never been out of print. Jean Rhys's 1966 novel Wide Sargasso Sea reimagined part of its story, and it has been adapted many times for screen, stage and radio.
the-strange-case-of-dr-jekyll-and-mr-hyd: The story unfolds mostly through the eyes of Mr Utterson, a reserved London lawyer. His distant kinsman Mr Enfield tells him of a sinister man named Edward Hyde who trampled a child in the street and then paid compensation with a cheque drawn on the account of a highly respected gentleman. Utterson is troubled, because his old friend Dr Henry Jekyll has made a will leaving everything to this same Hyde. As violence spreads through the foggy city and Jekyll grows ever more withdrawn, Utterson pieces together letters, testimonies and documents in an attempt to understand the bond between the cultivated doctor and the brutal stranger.

Stevenson's novella is short, tense and built like a detective puzzle. Beneath the mystery lies a searching study of the divided self: the gap between public respectability and private desire, the temptation to escape responsibility for one's own actions, and the fear that civilised manners are only a thin surface. Its compact structure and atmospheric London settings make it a rewarding read in a single sitting.

Published in January 1886, the book was a swift success in Britain and the United States and made Stevenson famous. The phrase "Jekyll and Hyde" entered everyday English as shorthand for a split personality. The story was adapted for the stage soon after publication and has since inspired countless films, plays, musicals, radio dramas and reworkings.
twenty-thousand-leagues-under-the-sea: In 1866 ships around the world report sightings of a huge, fast-moving creature that rams vessels at sea. Pierre Aronnax, a French professor of natural history, joins an American frigate sent to hunt it, accompanied by his loyal servant Conseil. Also aboard is Ned Land, a Canadian harpooner of great skill and short temper. When the chase ends in a collision, the three men find themselves prisoners aboard the Nautilus, an extraordinary electric submarine commanded by the mysterious Captain Nemo. Unable to leave, they travel with him through the oceans of the globe.

Verne mixes adventure with a great deal of real natural history, and his descriptions of marine life and undersea landscapes are a large part of the book's charm. At its heart, though, is Nemo himself: brilliant, bitter and drawn to freedom, a figure whose motives remain a puzzle. The novel also explores curiosity, captivity and the costs of turning one's back on humanity.

The novel first appeared as a serial in Pierre-Jules Hetzel's magazine between 1869 and 1870 and then in book form in 1870, as part of Verne's series of Extraordinary Voyages. The name Nautilus was later given to real submarines. The story has been adapted for film, television, animation, radio and comics.
the-iliad: The Iliad is set in the tenth year of the Greek siege of Troy, but it covers only a few weeks of the war. It opens with a bitter quarrel: Agamemnon, leader of the Greek army, takes from Achilles, the greatest of the Greek warriors, a captive woman awarded to him as a prize of honour. Furious and humiliated, Achilles withdraws from the fighting, and his mother, the sea goddess Thetis, persuades Zeus to let the Trojans gain the upper hand. As the battle turns, heroes on both sides, among them the Trojan prince Hector, fight, boast, grieve and die, while the gods of Olympus quarrel and intervene.

Although it is a poem of war, the Iliad is also deeply concerned with what war costs. Anger, pride, honour and grief drive its action, and it gives as much dignity to the Trojans as to the victors. Its portraits of friendship and loss remain moving and immediate.

Composed in Greek hexameter verse and traditionally attributed to Homer, the poem is usually dated to around the eighth century BC and was later divided into twenty-four books. It became a cornerstone of Greek education and has shaped Western literature ever since. It has been translated countless times, including a famous English verse version by Alexander Pope, and retold in novels, plays and films.
candide: Candide is a gentle, trusting young man raised in the castle of a German baron in Westphalia, where his tutor, the philosopher Pangloss, teaches that everything happens for the best in this best of all possible worlds. When he is caught kissing the baron's daughter, Cunégonde, Candide is thrown out of the castle, and the rest of the book follows his frantic travels across Europe and South America. War, shipwreck, earthquake, the Inquisition and swindlers all cross his path, and every catastrophe tests the cheerful doctrine he has been taught.

Voltaire's tale is short, fast and ferociously funny. Its targets include philosophical optimism of the kind associated with Leibniz, religious hypocrisy, colonial cruelty, war and the vanity of the powerful. The comedy comes from piling disasters on top of one another while the characters calmly explain why all is well. Beneath the laughter is a serious question that still matters: how should we live in a world full of suffering we cannot explain away?

Candide was published anonymously in 1759 and printed in several cities at once. It was quickly condemned and banned in places, yet it sold widely and became Voltaire's best-known work. The great Lisbon earthquake of 1755 helped shape its outlook. It has inspired stage versions, including an operetta by Leonard Bernstein, as well as many later satires.
on-the-principles-of-political-economy-a: David Ricardo's treatise asks how the produce of a nation is divided among its three great classes: landowners, who receive rent; capitalists, who receive profit; and workers, who receive wages. Building on Adam Smith, Ricardo develops a theory of value based on the labour needed to produce goods, a theory of rent arising from differences in the fertility of land, and an account of how profits tend to fall as more and poorer land is brought into cultivation. Later chapters examine taxes on rent, wages, profits and goods, as well as money, banking and foreign trade, with his famous example of English cloth and Portuguese wine.

The book is known for its abstract, step-by-step reasoning, and that method was itself an innovation. Its most enduring idea is comparative advantage: countries gain from specialising and trading even when one of them is more efficient at producing everything. Readers today will also find a clear window into debates over the Corn Laws, free trade and the conflict of interest between landowners and the rest of society.

First published in 1817, with revised editions in 1819 and 1821, the third adding a chapter on machinery, the Principles made Ricardo a leading figure of classical economics. It influenced John Stuart Mill and Karl Marx among many others, and the theory of comparative advantage remains a basic tool in the study of international trade.
the-federalist-papers: The Federalist Papers are a series of eighty-five essays written to persuade the people of New York to ratify the proposed United States Constitution. Under the shared pen name Publius, Alexander Hamilton wrote most of them, James Madison wrote many of the rest, and John Jay contributed a handful. The essays begin by explaining the weakness of the existing Articles of Confederation, then defend the Constitution section by section: the benefits of a strong union, the structure of Congress, the powers of the presidency and the role of an independent judiciary. Famous essays include Madison's discussion of faction and the large republic in No. 10 and his account of checks and balances in No. 51.

These are works of political persuasion, written quickly and under pressure, yet they offer some of the most thoughtful reflections on government ever produced in America. Their central themes, how to control power, protect liberty and balance majority rule with the rights of minorities, remain urgent.

The essays first appeared in New York newspapers from October 1787 and were collected in two volumes as The Federalist in 1788. Authorship of some essays was long disputed between Hamilton and Madison and has been studied by historians and statisticians. Today the papers are widely cited by courts, scholars and politicians as a guide to understanding the Constitution.
second-treatise-of-government: In the Second Treatise, John Locke asks where legitimate political power comes from and what its limits are. He begins with a state of nature in which people are free and equal, governed by a law of nature that forbids harming others in their life, health, liberty or possessions. He explains how property arises when people mix their labour with the common resources of the earth. Because the state of nature is insecure, people agree to form a political society, consenting to a government whose purpose is to protect their lives, liberties and estates. Locke then discusses the separation of legislative and executive power, the dangers of tyranny and the conditions under which a people may rightly resist and replace their rulers.

Locke builds his case step by step in a measured style. His ideas of natural rights, government by consent, limited power and the right of resistance became central to liberal political thought. Reading him today is a way to understand the origins of many assumptions modern democracies take for granted.

The Two Treatises of Government were published anonymously in 1689, after the Glorious Revolution; the First Treatise attacked Sir Robert Filmer's defence of the divine right of kings. Locke acknowledged authorship only near the end of his life. The Second Treatise deeply influenced the American revolutionaries, including Thomas Jefferson, and remains a foundational text of political philosophy.
the-jungle-book: The Jungle Book is a collection of stories and poems, most of them set in India. The best-known tales follow Mowgli, a small boy who wanders into the jungle as a baby and is adopted by a family of wolves of the Seeonee pack. Under the watchful eyes of Baloo, the sleepy brown bear who teaches him the Law of the Jungle, and Bagheera, the sleek black panther, Mowgli grows up among animals, while the lame tiger Shere Khan never forgets that he wanted the man-cub for himself. Other stories travel further afield: a white seal searches for a safe home for his people, and the brave mongoose Rikki-tikki-tavi defends a family's garden from cobras.

Kipling's tales are adventure stories with the form of fables. They explore belonging, loyalty, law, courage and the tension between the wild and the human world. His prose is vivid and rhythmic, and each story is paired with a poem, which gives the book a distinctive musical quality. Some attitudes reflect the imperial era in which Kipling lived, which invites discussion today.

Kipling, born in Bombay, wrote the stories while living in Vermont, and the collection was published in 1894, followed by The Second Jungle Book in 1895. The Mowgli stories were used by Robert Baden-Powell for the Wolf Cub movement within Scouting. The book has inspired many animated and live-action films, stage versions and retellings.
the-invisible-man: One wintry day a stranger arrives at the Coach and Horses inn in the Sussex village of Iping, his face hidden by bandages and goggles. He demands to be left alone with his crates of chemicals and bottles, and the villagers grow suspicious. Their gossip turns to alarm when strange thefts occur and the truth about the man, a scientist named Griffin, begins to emerge. As his secret is exposed, he flees, and the story widens into a desperate struggle as Griffin seeks help, shelter and power.

Wells uses a single fantastic idea to explore very human questions. Invisibility, which sounds like a gift of perfect freedom, turns out to bring cold, hunger, isolation and frustration, and the novel asks what happens to a person's morality when he can no longer be seen or held accountable. The early chapters have a comic, small-town flavour that gives way to tension and darkness, a contrast that makes the book still enjoyable and thought-provoking.

The Invisible Man was serialised in Pearson's Weekly and published as a book in 1897, during the period in which Wells also wrote The Time Machine and The War of the Worlds. It helped establish the scientific romance and has been adapted many times for film, television, radio and comics.
the-betrothed: The Betrothed is set in Lombardy between 1628 and 1630, when the region was under Spanish rule. Renzo and Lucia, two young silk workers from a village near Lake Como, are about to be married when the local priest, Don Abbondio, refuses to perform the ceremony. Two armed thugs have warned him off on behalf of Don Rodrigo, a local lord who has set his sights on Lucia. Separated, the couple are swept into the wider currents of their age: Lucia seeks refuge in a convent at Monza, Renzo is caught up in bread riots in Milan, and both meet figures such as the courageous friar Cristoforo and a feared, powerful nobleman known only as the Unnamed.

Manzoni combines a love story with a vast portrait of society showing how ordinary people suffer under injustice, famine, war and plague. The novel is deeply concerned with conscience, faith and providence, but it is also full of irony and humour.

First published in 1827, the novel was revised by Manzoni over the following years and republished in 1840 to 1842 in language closer to the Italian spoken in Florence, making it a model for a national language. It is widely regarded as the most important Italian novel of the nineteenth century and is studied in Italian schools. Verdi composed his Requiem in Manzoni's memory, and the book has been adapted for film, television and stage.
nicomachean-ethics: The Nicomachean Ethics asks a simple but far-reaching question: what is the best life for a human being? Aristotle argues that everyone seeks happiness, or eudaimonia, which he understands not as a passing feeling but as living and acting well over a whole lifetime. Such a life depends on virtue. He distinguishes virtues of character, such as courage, temperance, generosity and justice, from intellectual virtues, especially practical wisdom. Virtues of character are formed by habit and usually lie in a mean between excess and deficiency. Across ten books he examines responsibility and voluntary action, justice, self-control and its failures, pleasure, and, at length, friendship, ending with the contemplative life.

Aristotle writes as a careful observer of ordinary life rather than a preacher. He takes common opinions seriously, tests them, and keeps his conclusions practical. His view that good character is built through practice, and that friendship and community are part of a flourishing life, still speaks directly to modern readers thinking about education, ethics and wellbeing.

The text appears to derive from Aristotle's lectures at his school in Athens, the Lyceum, and is traditionally associated with his son Nicomachus. It became one of the most influential works of moral philosophy, studied in the medieval Islamic world and by Christian thinkers such as Thomas Aquinas, and it lies behind the modern revival of virtue ethics.
the-wind-in-the-willows: One spring morning Mole abandons his cleaning, scrambles up from his underground home and wanders to the riverbank, where he meets the Water Rat. Rat introduces him to boating, picnics and the pleasures of the river, and the two become firm friends. Through Rat, Mole meets the wise, gruff Badger, who lives deep in the frightening Wild Wood, and the wealthy, boastful Mr Toad of Toad Hall, whose passing enthusiasms lead him into ever deeper trouble. While Toad's escapades provide comedy and excitement, quieter chapters follow the changing seasons and the friends' simple pleasures.

The book is part animal adventure and part celebration of the English countryside. Its themes include friendship, home, loyalty and the pull between adventure and contentment. Grahame's prose is often lyrical, especially in chapters such as "The Piper at the Gates of Dawn," while Toad's vanity and reckless schemes remain gloriously funny. It is a story adults can enjoy as much as children.

Grahame developed the tales from bedtime stories and letters for his young son, Alastair, and the book was published in 1908. Its early reviews were mixed, but its popularity grew steadily. Illustrated editions by artists including E. H. Shepard and Arthur Rackham became much loved, A. A. Milne adapted it for the stage as Toad of Toad Hall, and it has inspired many films, animations and theatre versions.
robinson-crusoe: Robinson Crusoe is the son of a respectable family in York who ignores his father's advice to live a quiet, middling life and runs away to sea. After a series of adventures, including a spell as a planter in Brazil, he joins a voyage that ends in shipwreck. As the only survivor, he is cast ashore on an uninhabited island near the coast of South America. The novel describes, in careful detail, how he salvages tools and supplies from the wreck, builds shelter, grows grain and keeps a journal. Years of solitude bring moments of despair and religious reflection, until the discovery of a footprint on the shore changes his life on the island.

Defoe's matter-of-fact style, full of lists, practical problems and solutions, made the story feel like a true account. The book explores self-reliance, providence, repentance, and humanity's relationship with nature. Modern readers also find in it revealing attitudes to colonialism, property and race, especially in Crusoe's relationship with the man he names Friday, which makes it rich material for discussion.

Published in April 1719 as if written by Crusoe himself, the novel was an instant success. It is often cited as one of the earliest English novels, and it may have drawn on the experiences of the marooned sailor Alexander Selkirk. It gave its name to a genre, the robinsonade, and has been endlessly retold and adapted.
david-copperfield: David Copperfield tells his own life story, beginning with his birth at Blunderstone in Suffolk. His early years with his gentle mother and their devoted servant Peggotty are happy, but when his mother marries the cold, harsh Mr Murdstone, David's childhood darkens. Sent to a cruel school and then to work as a boy in a London warehouse, he lodges with the cheerful, always-indebted Mr Micawber before fleeing to seek help from his formidable great-aunt, Betsey Trotwood. From there the novel follows him through school, love and work, while a large cast of friends and enemies, including the charming Steerforth and the scheming Uriah Heep, shape his path.

The novel is a classic story of growing up, concerned with memory, character, love, work and the lasting effects of childhood. Dickens balances comedy and pathos with great skill, and his characters, from Mr Micawber to Uriah Heep, have become part of the language of literature. Its warmth and its sharp eye for injustice make it as engaging today as in Dickens's time.

The novel was first issued in monthly parts from 1849 to 1850 and published as a book in 1850. Dickens drew on his own painful experience of working in a factory as a child, and he later described it as his favourite among his books. It has been adapted many times for film, television, radio and the stage.
vanity-fair: Vanity Fair follows two young women who leave Miss Pinkerton's academy for girls on the same day. Amelia Sedley is the gentle, sheltered daughter of a prosperous London merchant; Becky Sharp is a penniless orphan, clever, witty and determined to rise in the world by any means. As Becky sets out to secure a husband and a place in society, and Amelia devotes herself to the dashing but shallow George Osborne, their lives intertwine with soldiers, aristocrats, servants and social climbers. The story moves from London drawing rooms to Brussels on the eve of the Battle of Waterloo.

Thackeray's subtitle, "A Novel without a Hero," signals his approach: almost nobody is simply good or bad, and the narrator comments with irony on the greed, snobbery and hypocrisy of the world he describes. Becky is one of the great antiheroines of English fiction, outrageous yet hard not to admire. The novel's satire of social ambition, money and status remains sharp and very readable.

The novel was first published in monthly parts in 1847 and 1848, illustrated by Thackeray himself, and appeared as a single volume in 1848. Its title comes from the town fair in John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress. It established Thackeray as a leading novelist of his day and has been adapted for film, television, radio and the stage.
kidnapped: Kidnapped is set in Scotland in the years after the Jacobite rising of 1745. When his father dies, seventeen-year-old David Balfour leaves his village with a letter that sends him to the House of Shaws, home of his miserly uncle Ebenezer. He soon realises that his uncle is hiding something about the family estate and wishes him harm. Tricked aboard the brig Covenant, David is carried off to be sold into service in the American colonies. At sea he meets Alan Breck Stewart, a proud and daring Jacobite, and the two are thrown together in an adventure that takes them across the Highlands, entangled in the aftermath of a real political murder.

Stevenson wrote a gripping adventure, but also a story about friendship between two very different people: the cautious Lowland Presbyterian loyal to King George and the fiery Highland supporter of the exiled Stuarts. Their arguments and loyalties reflect the divisions of Scotland itself. The vivid landscapes and the brisk first-person narration keep the novel fresh and lively.

Kidnapped was serialised in the magazine Young Folks and published as a book in 1886, the same year as Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. Stevenson drew on the Appin murder of 1752 and on the historical figure of Alan Breck Stewart. A sequel, Catriona, followed in 1893. The novel has been adapted for film, television, radio and comics.
king-lear: King Lear opens in ancient Britain, where the elderly king decides to divide his kingdom among his three daughters, giving the largest share to whichever declares she loves him most. Goneril and Regan respond with lavish flattery, but the youngest, Cordelia, refuses to compete in words, and Lear angrily disowns her. Having given away his power, Lear soon finds himself mistreated by the daughters he rewarded. A parallel plot follows the Earl of Gloucester, who is deceived by his illegitimate son Edmund into turning against his loyal son Edgar. As both old men suffer the consequences of misjudgment, Lear wanders onto a stormy heath, his mind beginning to break.

Often counted among Shakespeare's greatest tragedies, King Lear explores ageing, power, family loyalty, ingratitude, justice and the search for meaning in a seemingly indifferent universe. Its scenes of madness and the storm are among the most intense in drama, while the Fool's riddles bring bitter humour.

The play was written around 1605 to 1606 and performed at court in December 1606. It survives in two early texts, the 1608 Quarto and the 1623 Folio, which differ significantly. Shakespeare drew on legend, an earlier play about King Leir and, for the Gloucester plot, Philip Sidney's Arcadia. For a long period it was staged in Nahum Tate's softened rewrite before the original returned. It has inspired many films, operas and reinterpretations.
around-the-world-in-eighty-days: In October 1872, Phileas Fogg, a wealthy, precise and mysterious English gentleman who lives by an unvarying routine, astonishes his fellow members of the Reform Club in London by betting a fortune that he can travel around the world in eighty days. That same evening he sets off with his newly hired French valet, Passepartout, relying on steamships and railways. Their route runs through Suez, India, Hong Kong and the United States, and the journey is complicated by a Scotland Yard detective, Fix, who believes Fogg is a bank robber on the run and pursues him across the globe. Along the way Fogg rescues a young Indian woman, Aouda, who joins the travellers.

The novel is a race against time, full of obstacles, narrow escapes and comic misunderstandings. Fogg's cool calm contrasts with Passepartout's lively enthusiasm. It captures the excitement of an age when new railways and canals seemed to shrink the world, and it remains a brisk, entertaining adventure.

The story first appeared as a newspaper serial in 1872 and was published as a book shortly afterwards. It became one of Verne's most popular works, and Verne collaborated on a successful stage version. It inspired real attempts to beat Fogg's time, notably by the journalist Nellie Bly in 1889, and has been adapted many times for film, television, animation and theatre.
bel-ami: Georges Duroy, a former soldier, is drifting through Paris with little money and few prospects when he meets an old army comrade, Charles Forestier, now a successful journalist. Forestier helps him find work at the newspaper La Vie Française, though Duroy can barely write. What he lacks in talent he makes up for in good looks, charm and ambition, earning the nickname Bel-Ami. He soon learns that in this world, influence flows through the salons and bedrooms of influential women, and he begins to use his relationships with them to climb from the lowest rungs of journalism toward wealth and political influence.

Maupassant paints a cool, ironic portrait of Parisian society under the Third Republic, where journalism, finance, politics and love are entangled and corruption is taken for granted. Duroy is an antihero whose rise is fascinating precisely because he is so unscrupulous. The novel is sharp, economical and often darkly funny, and its picture of media power, opportunism and celebrity feels strikingly contemporary.

Bel-Ami was Maupassant's second novel, after A Woman's Life. It was serialised in the newspaper Gil Blas and published as a book in 1885. Some contemporaries took offence at its portrait of the press. It is regarded as one of the major French novels of the period and has been adapted for film, television and stage.
tao-te-ching: The Tao Te Ching is a short book of about five thousand Chinese characters, divided into eighty-one brief chapters. Its subject is the Tao, or Way, the nameless source and pattern of all things, and Te, the virtue or power that comes from living in harmony with it. The text teaches the value of simplicity, humility and stillness, and the strength of what seems weak: water, which yields yet wears away stone. It advises rulers to govern lightly, avoid force and display, and practise wu wei, often translated as non-action or effortless action, so that people can flourish naturally.

Its paradoxes and images invite slow reading and reflection rather than quick conclusions. It offers a counterweight to ambition, aggression and constant striving, and its ideas speak to those interested in philosophy, leadership, spirituality and the relationship between people and nature. Because the original is so terse, every translation is also an interpretation, and comparing versions is part of the pleasure.

Tradition credits the work to Laozi, said to have been an older contemporary of Confucius, though many scholars think the text took shape gradually and reached its familiar form around the fourth century BC. Early manuscripts discovered at Mawangdui and Guodian have shed new light on its history. It became the founding text of Taoism and is among the most translated works in the world.
anna-karenina: Anna Karenina opens in Moscow, where Anna, the elegant wife of the senior St Petersburg official Alexei Karenin, arrives to patch up her brother Stiva Oblonsky's troubled marriage. On her arrival she meets Count Vronsky, a handsome cavalry officer, and an attraction begins that will test everything her position in society depends on. Alongside her story runs another: Konstantin Levin, a thoughtful landowner, courts the young Kitty Shcherbatskaya and wrestles with questions of farming, faith and how to live honestly.

Tolstoy sets passion against duty, city against country, and public reputation against private conscience. He moves easily from ballrooms and racecourses to hay-mowing and childbirth, and gives even minor characters an inner life of their own. The double structure is the key: Anna's story and Levin's mirror each other, asking what makes a life meaningful and how far society judges men and women by different rules. Readers still return to it for its psychological precision and its sheer generosity of observation.

The novel first appeared in instalments in the journal The Russian Messenger between 1875 and 1877, and was published in book form in 1878. It was quickly recognised as a masterpiece, and writers from Dostoevsky onward praised it. Translated into many languages, it has been adapted many times for film, television, stage, ballet and opera, and remains one of the most widely read novels of the nineteenth century.
the-adventures-of-sherlock-holmes: This collection gathers twelve short stories featuring Sherlock Holmes, the consulting detective of 221B Baker Street, narrated by his friend and companion Dr John Watson. Clients arrive with puzzles large and small: a king fearing blackmail by the singer Irene Adler in "A Scandal in Bohemia", a pawnbroker hired for a strangely pointless job in "The Red-Headed League", a young woman afraid for her life in "The Speckled Band", and a missing husband in "The Man with the Twisted Lip". Each case begins with an odd detail and ends with Holmes explaining what everyone else overlooked.

The stories are short, brisk and built for pleasure. Doyle's great invention was a hero who solves crimes by close observation and logical reasoning, and a narrator who lets the reader share his amazement. The partnership between the cool, eccentric Holmes and the warm, practical Watson gives the tales their charm, while the gaslit London setting, with its fogs, cabs and lodging houses, remains vivid. They are an ideal introduction to detective fiction and still a model of how to plant clues fairly.

The stories first appeared in The Strand Magazine in 1891 and 1892, illustrated by Sidney Paget, whose drawings fixed the detective's image in the public mind. Their success turned Holmes into a sensation and the collection was published as a book in 1892. Holmes has since become one of the most frequently adapted characters in fiction, on stage, radio, film and television, and has inspired countless imitators and pastiches.
don-quixote: In a village of La Mancha lives a gentleman of modest means, Alonso Quijano, who has read so many books of chivalry that he decides to become a knight-errant himself. Renaming himself Don Quixote, he puts on old armour, mounts his bony horse Rocinante, chooses a peasant girl as his lady Dulcinea, and later persuades the farmer Sancho Panza to follow him as squire with the promise of an island to govern. Their adventures take them along the roads of Spain, where Quixote mistakes windmills for giants, inns for castles and flocks of sheep for armies.

The book is very funny, but it is also tender and deeply thoughtful. Cervantes explores the gap between imagination and reality, the power of reading to shape a life, and the friendship that grows between the idealistic knight and his earthy, proverb-loving squire. Its playful handling of narrators, stories within stories and characters who discuss their own book makes it feel surprisingly modern, and Quixote's stubborn idealism still moves readers.

Part One was published in Madrid in 1605 and became popular immediately. An unauthorised sequel by a writer calling himself Avellaneda appeared in 1614, and Cervantes answered it with his own Part Two in 1615. The novel has been translated into a great many languages and is often called the first modern novel. It has inspired paintings, ballets, operas, a celebrated stage musical, and numerous films.
the-divine-comedy: The Divine Comedy is a long narrative poem in three parts: Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso. It begins during Holy Week of the year 1300, when Dante, midway through life, finds himself lost in a dark wood. The Roman poet Virgil appears and leads him down through the circles of Hell, where sinners suffer punishments that fit their faults, and then up the mountain of Purgatory, where souls are cleansed. For the final ascent through the heavenly spheres, Dante is guided by Beatrice, the woman he had loved in his youth.

The poem is at once a personal story of spiritual recovery and a vast map of medieval thought, combining theology, philosophy, astronomy and politics. Dante fills it with real people, from popes and emperors to Florentine neighbours, which makes it sharp and often startlingly direct. Written in interlocking three-line stanzas known as terza rima, it moves from horror to hope to radiant light. Its images of the afterlife have shaped how Western culture imagines Hell and Heaven ever since.

Dante worked on the poem during his years of exile from Florence and completed it shortly before his death in 1321. He called it simply his Comedy; the adjective "Divine" was added later. Writing in the Tuscan vernacular rather than Latin, he helped establish the basis of the Italian literary language. The poem has inspired painters, sculptors, composers and writers for centuries, and has been translated into English many times.
the-prince: The Prince is a short treatise on how a ruler can win power and keep it. Machiavelli, a former official of the Florentine republic who lost his post when the Medici family returned to power in 1512, wrote it in 1513 and dedicated it to Lorenzo de' Medici. He begins by sorting principalities into types, hereditary and new, won by one's own arms or by those of others, and then turns to armies, the conduct of princes, and the condition of Italy in his own time.

What makes the book famous is its frankness. Machiavelli sets aside the traditional advice that rulers should simply be virtuous and asks instead what actually works, drawing on examples from ancient Rome and from recent figures such as Cesare Borgia. He discusses whether it is better to be loved or feared, how far a ruler should keep promises, and the struggle between a leader's skill, which he calls virtù, and the unpredictable force of fortune. Its clear, compact arguments still provoke debate about the relationship between ethics and politics.

The book circulated in manuscript during Machiavelli's lifetime and was printed only in 1532, five years after his death. It soon became notorious, and it was placed on the Catholic Church's Index of prohibited books in 1559. The word "Machiavellian" entered many languages as a byword for cunning, yet scholars have long read the book as a founding work of modern political science.
an-essay-on-the-principle-of-population: In this essay the English clergyman and scholar Thomas Malthus sets out a simple but unsettling argument. Human population, if unchecked, tends to grow in a geometrical ratio, doubling again and again, while the means of subsistence can at best increase in an arithmetical ratio. Because people cannot live without food, population must constantly be held down to what the land can support. Malthus describes the checks that do this: misery and vice in the form of famine, disease, war and poverty, as well as preventive checks such as delayed marriage.

The book was written partly as a reply to optimistic thinkers such as William Godwin and the Marquis de Condorcet, who believed that society could be steadily perfected. Malthus doubted that reform alone could abolish poverty, and he questioned the effects of the English Poor Laws. His tone is calm and logical, which makes his conclusions all the more striking. Reading it today helps make sense of continuing debates about resources, food security, the environment and the limits of growth.

The first edition appeared anonymously in 1798. Malthus expanded and revised it substantially in later editions, beginning in 1803, adding much evidence and giving more weight to moral restraint. The work provoked fierce criticism from many quarters, yet it deeply influenced economics, and both Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace credited it with helping them reach the idea of natural selection.
aesop-s-fables: Aesop's Fables is a collection of short tales, most featuring animals that speak and behave like people, each pointing towards a lesson about human conduct. Among the best known are the race between the slow, steady tortoise and the boastful hare, the shepherd boy who raises false alarms about a wolf, the ant who works through the summer while the grasshopper sings, the fox who decides the grapes he cannot reach must be sour, and the lion spared by a grateful mouse.

The fables are brief, often only a paragraph long, and their morals concern prudence, honesty, greed, vanity, gratitude and the dangers of flattery. Their power lies in simplicity: a single memorable situation sticks in the mind far longer than a lecture. Many phrases still used in everyday English, such as crying wolf and sour grapes, come from these stories. They work for children as first stories and for adults as compact reflections on how people really behave.

Ancient writers, including Herodotus, describe Aesop as a slave who lived in the sixth century BC and became famous as a storyteller, though little is known about him for certain and many fables credited to him were probably composed by others. The tales passed down orally and through later collections, notably the Latin verse of Phaedrus and the Greek verse of Babrius. They inspired later fabulists such as Jean de La Fontaine and have been retold, illustrated and adapted endlessly.
on-liberty: On Liberty is a philosophical essay about the proper limits of power that society can rightfully exercise over the individual. Mill argues that the only good reason for interfering with someone's freedom, whether by law or by social pressure, is to prevent harm to others. A person's own good, physical or moral, is not a sufficient reason. From this starting point he defends freedom of thought and discussion, the freedom to live according to one's own tastes and plans, and the freedom to associate with others.

Mill was especially concerned that in democratic societies the danger came not only from governments but from the tyranny of the majority, the quiet pressure of custom and opinion that discourages people from thinking or living differently. He insists that even false opinions deserve to be heard, because truth is strengthened by being challenged, and that individuality and experimentation are essential to human progress. His prose is clear and closely reasoned, and his arguments remain central to modern debates about free speech, censorship and personal choice.

The essay was published in 1859, shortly after the death of Mill's wife, Harriet Taylor Mill, whom he credited as a close collaborator and to whose memory he dedicated it. It became one of the founding texts of liberal political thought and is still widely studied in philosophy, politics and law.
little-women: Little Women follows the four March sisters as they grow up in a small New England town while their father is away serving with the Union army in the American Civil War. Sensible Meg longs for pretty things, tomboyish Jo dreams of becoming a writer, gentle Beth loves music and home, and youngest Amy has artistic ambitions and a taste for elegance. Guided by their wise mother, whom they call Marmee, the girls face money worries, quarrels and small adventures, and befriend Laurie, the lively boy who lives next door with his grandfather.

The novel is warm, funny and honest about the ordinary struggles of growing up: vanity, temper, shyness, envy and the difficulty of choosing one's own path. Jo, impatient with the expectations placed on girls, remains one of literature's most beloved heroines. Alcott writes about family affection, work, poverty and women's independence with a directness that still feels fresh, and many readers find in the sisters a reflection of their own families.

Alcott drew on her own childhood with her three sisters in Massachusetts. The first part was published in 1868 and was so successful that a second part followed in 1869; in Britain it was long issued separately as Good Wives. Alcott continued the family's story in Little Men and Jo's Boys. The book has been adapted many times for film, television, stage and opera.
the-island-of-doctor-moreau: Edward Prendick, an English gentleman with some training in science, survives the wreck of his ship and is picked up by a vessel carrying a strange cargo of animals. He is put ashore on a remote Pacific island, home to Montgomery, a drinking man with medical knowledge, and to Doctor Moreau, a once-respected physiologist driven out of London after scandalous reports about his experiments. Prendick soon notices the island's other inhabitants, oddly shaped beings who seem neither quite animal nor quite human, and who live by a strange set of rules.

Wells uses this nightmarish setting to ask unsettling questions about cruelty, scientific ambition without ethics, and the thin line between humanity and animality. Written in a period of intense debate over vivisection and over the implications of Darwin's theory of evolution, the novel works both as a gripping adventure and as a dark fable about what makes us human. Its themes speak directly to modern arguments about genetic engineering and the responsibilities of science.

The novel was published in 1896, the year after The Time Machine had made Wells's name. Many early reviewers found it shocking and distasteful, but it has since come to be regarded as a key early work of science fiction. It has been adapted for film several times and has influenced a long line of stories about creatures made by human hands.
heart: Heart, known in Italian as Cuore, takes the form of a diary kept through a school year by Enrico, a boy in the third grade of an elementary school in Turin. He records life in the classroom, his kind teacher, and his very different classmates: the big-hearted Garrone, the brilliant Derossi, poorer boys whose fathers are labourers, and the troublemaker Franti. Enrico's entries are interspersed with letters from his parents and sister, and each month the teacher reads aloud a short story about a boy who shows courage, loyalty or self-sacrifice.
