The book celebrates kindness, respect for parents and teachers, friendship across social classes and love of one's country, values De Amicis believed would help build the newly united Italy. Its monthly tales, such as "From the Apennines to the Andes", in which a young boy travels to South America in search of his mother, are among the most famous children's stories in Italian. Today it is also a vivid portrait of everyday life, poverty and schooling in a nineteenth-century Italian city, and its emotional sincerity still moves readers.

The book was published in Milan in October 1886 and became immensely popular, shaping the childhood reading of generations of Italians. It was widely translated, and its stories have been adapted for film, television and animation in Italy and abroad.
the-descent-of-man: In On the Origin of Species, published in 1859, Darwin had largely avoided the question of human origins. In The Descent of Man he takes it on directly. He gathers evidence from anatomy, embryology and behaviour to argue that human beings descended, like all other species, from earlier forms of life, and that our mental powers, emotions and even our moral sense differ from those of other animals in degree rather than in kind. He suggests that morality grew out of social instincts shared with other animals.

A large part of the book is devoted to sexual selection, the idea that many traits, from the peacock's tail to birdsong, evolved because they helped individuals win mates rather than survive. Darwin applies this idea to humans as well. The book is wide-ranging, patient and packed with observations, and it shows a great scientist reasoning carefully from evidence. Modern readers will also find views on race and on the differences between the sexes that reflect Victorian assumptions and have since been challenged, which makes it valuable for understanding the history of science as well as its achievements.

The work was published in two volumes in 1871, under the full title The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex, with a revised edition in 1874. It caused wide debate, and its arguments about human evolution and sexual selection remain foundational in biology.
peter-pan: In a London nursery, Wendy, John and Michael Darling are looked after by their devoted parents and by Nana, a dog who serves as their nurse. One night a boy named Peter Pan, who refuses to grow up, flies in through the window with the fairy Tinker Bell. He teaches the children to fly and takes them away to the Neverland, an island of mermaids, fairies and the Lost Boys, where Wendy is invited to be a mother to Peter's band. Their great enemy is the pirate Captain Hook, who is himself pursued by a crocodile that once swallowed a clock.

The story is full of adventure and comedy, but Barrie's narrator also writes with a wry, bittersweet awareness of childhood, memory, and the cost of growing up. Peter is charming, brave and forgetful, both enviable and a little sad. Modern readers will notice attitudes of its time, especially in the depiction of the island's native people, but the book's imaginative energy and its reflections on parents and children remain striking.

Peter Pan first appeared in Barrie's 1902 novel The Little White Bird and then in his hugely successful stage play of 1904. Barrie turned the play into this novel, published in 1911 as Peter and Wendy. In 1929 he gave the rights to Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children in London. The story has been adapted countless times on stage and screen.
gulliver-s-travels: Lemuel Gulliver, a ship's surgeon with a taste for travel, tells the story of four extraordinary voyages. Shipwrecked first in Lilliput, he finds himself a giant among people only a few inches tall, caught up in their petty quarrels and wars. In Brobdingnag the situation is reversed and he becomes a tiny curiosity among giants. His third journey takes him to the flying island of Laputa and neighbouring lands full of impractical scientists and projectors, and his fourth to a country ruled by the Houyhnhnms, rational horses, who share their land with brutish humanlike creatures called Yahoos.

On the surface the book is a lively adventure parodying the travel writing popular in Swift's day, which is why it has long been enjoyed by children in shortened forms. Underneath it is a sharp satire of politics, religious disputes, science, war and human pride. Changes of scale let Swift show human behaviour from new and unflattering angles. Its plain, deadpan style makes the absurdities funnier and the criticism harder to escape, and its questions about reason and human nature remain unsettling.

Swift, an Anglo-Irish clergyman who was Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin, published the book anonymously in London in 1726. It was an immediate success. A revised edition appeared in Dublin in 1735. Words such as Lilliputian entered the language, and the book has been adapted many times for film, television and the stage.
emma: Emma Woodhouse is handsome, clever and rich, and lives with her anxious, valetudinarian father in the village of Highbury. When her governess and friend Miss Taylor marries, Emma credits herself with making the match and decides to try again. She takes up Harriet Smith, a sweet but naive young woman of uncertain parentage, and sets about finding her a suitable husband, discouraging a proposal from a respectable farmer along the way. Their neighbour Mr Knightley, an old family friend, watches her schemes with growing disapproval, while the arrival of newcomers such as Frank Churchill and Jane Fairfax complicates village life.

Austen described Emma as a heroine whom no one but herself would much like, yet readers have long found her irresistible. The comedy comes from the gap between what Emma believes and what is really happening, and Austen's subtle narration lets us share her misjudgements. The novel is about self-knowledge, class, kindness and the small dramas of a closely watched community. Its gallery of characters, from the talkative Miss Bates to the self-important Mrs Elton, is among Austen's richest.

Emma was published by John Murray in December 1815, though the title page is dated 1816, and was dedicated to the Prince Regent. It was the last novel published in Austen's lifetime. Often considered her most technically accomplished work, it has inspired many adaptations for film, television and stage, including modern-day reworkings.
ulysses: Ulysses follows several Dubliners through a single day, 16 June 1904. Leopold Bloom, an advertising canvasser of Hungarian Jewish descent, goes about his errands: making breakfast for his wife Molly, attending a friend's funeral, visiting a newspaper office, eating lunch, and wandering through the city's pubs, libraries and streets. Meanwhile Stephen Dedalus, a young teacher and aspiring writer familiar from Joyce's earlier A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, drifts through his own day of debts, arguments and grief for his mother. Their paths cross and recross as the hours pass.

The novel's eighteen episodes loosely parallel Homer's Odyssey, with Bloom as a modern, ordinary Ulysses. Joyce changes style from chapter to chapter, using stream of consciousness, newspaper headlines, a play script, parodies of English prose through the ages, and much more. The result is demanding but richly rewarding: funny, earthy, learned and deeply humane, it shows how much life is contained in one unremarkable day and in the inner thoughts of ordinary people.

Parts of the novel were serialised in the American magazine The Little Review from 1918 until an obscenity prosecution halted it. The complete book was published in Paris by Sylvia Beach's Shakespeare and Company on 2 February 1922. It was banned for years in the United States and Britain. It is now regarded as a cornerstone of modernism, and 16 June is celebrated around the world as Bloomsday.
paradise-lost: Paradise Lost is an epic poem retelling the biblical story of the Fall. It begins after Satan and his rebel angels have been cast out of Heaven into a burning lake in Hell. Rousing his followers, Satan resolves to strike back at God by corrupting his newest creation, mankind. He journeys through Chaos towards the newly made world, where Adam and Eve live in innocence in the Garden of Eden. The poem moves between Hell, Heaven and Eden, and includes the angel Raphael's account of the war in Heaven and of the Creation.

Milton's stated aim was to justify God's ways to humankind, yet the poem's most memorable figure is arguably Satan, whose proud and eloquent speeches have fascinated readers for centuries. The poem explores free will, obedience, temptation, love between man and woman, and the meaning of loss. Written in grand, rolling blank verse full of classical and biblical learning, it can be challenging, but read aloud it has extraordinary music and power.

Milton, blind by then, composed the poem by dictation. It was first published in 1667 in ten books, and a second edition of 1674 rearranged it into twelve. He later wrote a shorter sequel, Paradise Regained. The poem profoundly influenced later writers, including the Romantic poets, and has inspired painters and illustrators, notably William Blake.
a-midsummer-night-s-dream: As Duke Theseus of Athens prepares to marry Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, a young woman named Hermia is ordered by her father to marry Demetrius, though she loves Lysander. The two lovers flee into the forest, followed by Demetrius and by Helena, who loves him. In the same wood, Oberon and Titania, king and queen of the fairies, are quarrelling, and Oberon's mischievous servant Puck is armed with a magic flower whose juice makes the sleeper fall in love with the first creature seen on waking. Also in the forest is a group of Athenian craftsmen, among them the irrepressible weaver Nick Bottom, rehearsing a play for the Duke's wedding.

The comedy weaves its several plots together with great lightness. It plays with the madness of love, the power of imagination and the strange logic of dreams, and its scenes of the craftsmen's earnest, clumsy theatre are among the funniest Shakespeare wrote. The poetry ranges from courtly verse to fairy songs to deliberate doggerel, and the play remains a favourite for first-time readers and audiences of all ages.

The play is generally dated to around 1595 or 1596 and was first printed in 1600. It has been performed constantly and has inspired music, including Felix Mendelssohn's famous incidental score, as well as ballets, an opera by Benjamin Britten, and many films.
journey-to-the-centre-of-the-earth: In Hamburg, the brilliant and impatient Professor Otto Lidenbrock discovers a coded message hidden in an old Icelandic manuscript. Deciphered with the help of his nephew Axel, it reveals that a sixteenth-century alchemist, Arne Saknussemm, claimed to have reached the centre of the earth by descending through the crater of the Icelandic volcano Snæfellsjökull. The professor sets off at once, dragging the reluctant Axel along. In Iceland they hire Hans, a calm and resourceful guide, and begin their descent into tunnels, caverns and an astonishing subterranean world.

Verne mixes science lesson and adventure story. The characters debate geology, palaeontology and the theory of the earth's internal heat as they travel, and the underground landscapes grow ever more wondrous. Narrated by Axel, whose fears contrast comically with his uncle's boundless enthusiasm, the story is full of suspense, humour and spectacle. It remains a perfect example of the pleasure of exploration and of the nineteenth century's faith in scientific curiosity.

The novel was published in 1864 by Pierre-Jules Hetzel as part of the series of Verne's adventure stories later known as the Voyages extraordinaires; an expanded edition appeared in 1867. It was widely translated and helped establish Verne as a pioneer of science fiction. The story has been adapted many times for film, television, radio and comics.
the-metamorphosis: Gregor Samsa, a travelling salesman who has long supported his parents and younger sister Grete, wakes one morning to find himself transformed into a huge insect-like creature. His first worries are strangely ordinary: he has missed his train and fears losing his job. But as his family and his employer's chief clerk discover what has happened, Gregor finds himself shut away in his room, unable to communicate, while the household around him begins to change in response to his condition.

Kafka tells this impossible event in calm, precise, almost matter-of-fact prose, and that contrast is the source of the story's eerie power. The novella has been read as a parable of alienation, of the way people are valued for their usefulness, of illness and dependence, and of family tensions and guilt. It is also, at moments, darkly comic. Short enough to read in a sitting, it raises questions that linger far longer, and it is often the first work through which readers meet Kafka.

Kafka wrote the story in 1912. It was first published in 1915, in the literary magazine Die weißen Blätter and then as a book by Kurt Wolff, one of the few works he saw in print during his lifetime. Kafka asked that the insect itself not be drawn on the cover. The novella is now one of the most influential works of twentieth-century fiction and has been adapted for stage, film and comics.
the-rubaiyat-of-omar-khayyam: The Rubaiyat is a sequence of quatrains, four-line poems in the Persian form called the rubai, attributed to Omar Khayyam, a scholar of Nishapur in Persia who was famous in his own time as a mathematician and astronomer. In Edward FitzGerald's English version, the poems are arranged into a loosely connected sequence that moves from dawn to nightfall. The speaker reflects on the brevity of life, the uncertainty of what lies beyond death, the limits of human knowledge, and the consolations of wine, friendship and love.

The poems combine sensual delight with philosophical doubt. They question the confident answers of both religion and learning, and urge the reader to seize the present moment before it passes. FitzGerald's rendering is free rather than literal, and is valued as an English poem in its own right, with memorable rhythms and imagery. Its blend of melancholy and pleasure continues to speak to readers who wonder about time, mortality and meaning.

FitzGerald published the first edition anonymously in London in 1859, working from Persian manuscripts introduced to him by his friend Edward Byles Cowell. It attracted little notice at first, but after being discovered by Dante Gabriel Rossetti and his circle it became enormously popular, and FitzGerald revised it through several later editions. Scholars still debate how many of the quatrains Omar actually wrote. The poem has inspired many illustrated editions, musical settings and other translations.
northanger-abbey: Catherine Morland, the daughter of a country clergyman, is seventeen and has read a great many novels when she is invited to spend the winter season in Bath with her family's wealthy neighbours, the Allens. In the assembly rooms and pump rooms of the fashionable city she meets the witty and kind Henry Tilney and his sister Eleanor, and becomes the close friend of the lively Isabella Thorpe, who shares her passion for 'horrid' Gothic novels, while Isabella's boastful brother John sets his sights on Catherine.

When Henry's stern father, General Tilney, invites her to stay at Northanger Abbey, the family's home, Catherine expects secret passages, hidden manuscripts and dark crimes like those in Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho, and her imagination soon leads her into embarrassing mistakes. Jane Austen's lightest and most openly comic novel is a parody of the Gothic romance and a warm defence of novel reading, but also a story about learning to judge people truly, with sharp observation of vanity, money and social ambition.

Austen wrote the novel in the late 1790s and sold it in 1803, under the title Susan, to the London publisher Crosby & Co. for 10 pounds, but it was never printed. Her brother Henry bought it back in 1816 for the same price. It was finally published after her death, in December 1817 (with 1818 on the title page), together with Persuasion. It has been adapted for television several times, notably by ITV in 2007 with Felicity Jones as Catherine.
twenty-years-after: In 1648 Cardinal Richelieu is dead and France is ruled by the regent Anne of Austria and her unpopular minister, Cardinal Mazarin, while the revolt of the Fronde stirs Paris. D'Artagnan, still a lieutenant of musketeers after twenty years, is sent by Mazarin to find his old companions. But Athos, now raising his ward Raoul, and Aramis, now an abbé, have chosen the other side, and only Porthos, rich and bored, agrees to join him. Across the Channel, King Charles I is fighting for his throne, and a dangerous young man named Mordaunt seeks revenge for the past.

Dumas mixes swordplay, escapes, disguises and humour with real history, from the barricades of Paris to the English Civil War, and shows the four friends older, wiser and tested by divided loyalties. Friendship ultimately proves stronger than politics.

Twenty Years After was published in instalments in the newspaper Le Siècle from January to August 1845, as the sequel to The Three Musketeers, written with the collaboration of Auguste Maquet. This edition offers the original French text and an English translation by an unnamed translator.
white-fang: White Fang is born in a cave in the frozen Yukon wilderness, the only survivor of a litter fathered by a wolf and born to Kiche, a she-wolf with dog's blood in her veins. His first lessons are those of the wild: eat or be eaten. When he and his mother wander into a Native American camp, he passes into the hands of Grey Beaver and learns a new law, the power of the gods who make fire, but also the hostility of the other dogs, who turn him into a lonely and ferocious fighter.

The novel follows White Fang from master to master: the stern but fair Grey Beaver, the cruel Beauty Smith who makes him a fighting dog for money, and finally Weedon Scott, a mining engineer who rescues him and slowly wins his trust with patience and kindness. Jack London tells the story largely from the animal's point of view, with vivid, physical writing about cold, hunger and combat, and a clear belief that character is shaped by environment as much as by instinct.

London published White Fang in 1906, first as a serial in The Outing Magazine, as a deliberate companion to The Call of the Wild (1903): where Buck goes from civilisation to the wild, White Fang travels the opposite road, from the wild to a home in California. Drawing on London's own time in the Klondike gold rush, it became one of his most popular books and has been adapted several times for film and animation.
a-study-in-scarlet: Dr John Watson, an army surgeon invalided home after the Second Afghan War, is looking for cheap lodgings in London when a friend introduces him to a strange young man who is also looking to share rooms. The man is Sherlock Holmes, and the two settle at 221B Baker Street. Watson soon discovers that his companion is a consulting detective, and is drawn into his first case: an American found dead in an empty house off the Brixton Road, with no visible wound and the German word RACHE, revenge, written in blood on the wall.

The book is in two parts. The first follows Holmes's method of observation and deduction as he outpaces the official police detectives Gregson and Lestrade. The second leaps back in time to the American West and the early Mormon settlement in Utah to tell the story behind the crime, a section that reflects the sensational and hostile view of Mormons common in Victorian fiction. Together they introduce nearly everything readers love about Holmes: his eccentric habits, his violin, his scorn for guesswork and his friendship with the loyal Watson.

Arthur Conan Doyle was a young doctor in Southsea when he wrote the novel. After several rejections it appeared in Beeton's Christmas Annual for 1887 and as a book in 1888. It drew modest attention at first, but its sequel, The Sign of the Four, and the short stories that followed in The Strand Magazine turned Holmes into the most famous detective in literature.
the-sign-of-the-four: Miss Mary Morstan, a young governess, comes to Baker Street with a puzzle. Her father, an officer in India, vanished on his return to London ten years earlier, and for the last six years she has received a single fine pearl by post on the same day each year. Now a letter invites her to a mysterious meeting. Holmes and Watson go with her, and the trail leads to the Sholto brothers, a dead man in a locked room at Pondicherry Lodge, and the great Agra treasure taken during the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

The second Holmes novel is faster and more atmospheric than the first, with night journeys through foggy London, a tracking dog called Toby and a famous steam-launch pursuit on the Thames. It also shows Holmes at his most complex, opening with his use of cocaine to escape boredom, while Watson falls in love with Mary Morstan. Like many adventure stories of its time, it reflects the imperial attitudes of Victorian Britain, especially in its portrayal of the Andaman Islander Tonga.

The novel was commissioned by the American magazine Lippincott's Monthly at a dinner in London in 1889, the same evening on which Oscar Wilde was asked for The Picture of Dorian Gray. It appeared in February 1890 and as a book later that year. Its success, followed by the short stories in The Strand Magazine from 1891, made Sherlock Holmes a household name.
the-mysteries-of-udolpho: In 1584, Emily St. Aubert lives happily with her parents in their château on the banks of the Garonne in Gascony. After her mother's death she travels with her father through the Pyrenees, where she meets the young and sensitive Valancourt. When her father dies too, Emily is left in the care of her vain aunt, Madame Cheron, who marries the dark and scheming Italian nobleman Montoni. He takes them to Venice and then to Udolpho, his remote and crumbling castle in the Apennines.

At Udolpho, Emily is surrounded by armed men, locked doors, mysterious music, a portrait hidden behind a black veil and rumours of a vanished lady of the castle. Montoni wants her property and will stop at little to get it. Ann Radcliffe builds suspense through landscape and atmosphere, with long descriptions of mountains, storms and moonlit ruins, and she is famous for her 'explained supernatural': the terrors that seem ghostly are finally given rational explanations.

Published in four volumes in 1794, the novel was a huge success and earned Radcliffe the large sum of 500 pounds. It became the model of the Gothic romance and influenced writers from Walter Scott and Lord Byron to Edgar Allan Poe. Jane Austen affectionately mocked its fans in Northanger Abbey, whose heroine Catherine Morland cannot stop talking about Udolpho.
the-moonstone: The Moonstone is a great yellow diamond, taken from a Hindu shrine and seized by a British officer, John Herncastle, during the storming of Seringapatam in 1799. Years later, Herncastle leaves it in his will to his niece, Rachel Verinder, and it is presented to her on her eighteenth birthday at her family's country house in Yorkshire. That same night the diamond disappears from her room. Three mysterious Indian men are seen near the house, the famous Sergeant Cuff arrives from London, and suspicion falls on the servants, the guests and even the family.

Instead of a single narrator, Wilkie Collins lets several characters tell the story in turn: the loyal old steward Gabriel Betteredge, who consults Robinson Crusoe in every crisis; the comically pious Miss Clack; a family lawyer; and others, including the young Franklin Blake. Each sees only part of the truth, which makes the novel both a clever puzzle and a lively comedy of character. It also introduces many elements later used by detective fiction, from a country-house theft and a skilled detective to false suspects and a reconstruction of the crime.

The novel was serialised in 1868 in All the Year Round, the magazine edited by Charles Dickens, and was a great popular success. T. S. Eliot later called it the first, the longest and the best of modern English detective novels. It is also notable for its sympathetic treatment of outsiders and for questioning the plunder of India by the British Empire.
ivanhoe: In 1194, King Richard the Lionheart has not yet returned from the Crusade and his brother Prince John rules England with the support of ambitious Norman barons. The proud Saxon Cedric has disinherited his son Wilfred of Ivanhoe for following the Norman king to the Holy Land and for loving Rowena, Cedric's ward, whom he hopes to marry to Athelstane, a descendant of the old Saxon kings. Ivanhoe comes home in disguise and enters the great tournament at Ashby as 'the Disinherited Knight', while a mysterious Black Knight, the outlaw archer Locksley, the Jewish moneylender Isaac of York and his daughter Rebecca are drawn into the struggle, which leads to the siege of the Norman castle of Torquilstone.

The novel is built around the conflict between conquered Saxons and conquering Normans, and the hope that they will one day become one people. Scott celebrates the colour and courage of chivalry while also showing its cruelty and pride, notably in the Templar Brian de Bois-Guilbert. Rebecca, wise, brave and generous, is one of his most admired heroines; through her and her father the book depicts the harsh persecution of Jews in medieval England, with sympathy for her but also with some of the stereotypes of its time in the portrait of Isaac.

Ivanhoe was published anonymously in three volumes in December 1819 (dated 1820), as a work 'by the author of Waverley'. It was Scott's first novel set in England rather than Scotland and was an immediate and lasting success, inspiring a wave of interest in the Middle Ages and shaping the modern image of Robin Hood and Richard the Lionheart. It has often been adapted, most famously in the 1952 Hollywood film starring Robert Taylor and Elizabeth Taylor.
twelfth-night: After a shipwreck off the coast of Illyria, the young Viola believes that her twin brother Sebastian has drowned. Disguised as a youth named Cesario, she enters the service of Duke Orsino, who is hopelessly in love with the Countess Olivia, a lady in mourning for her brother who refuses all suitors. Orsino sends Cesario to plead his cause, Olivia falls in love with the messenger, and Viola secretly falls in love with Orsino. Meanwhile, in Olivia's household, her riotous uncle Sir Toby Belch, the foolish Sir Andrew Aguecheek, the clever maid Maria and the jester Feste plot to humiliate the pompous steward Malvolio with a forged love letter.

The play, which opens with the famous line 'If music be the food of love, play on', is full of songs, wordplay and disguise, and it plays with the confusion of identity and gender to show how foolish and how powerful love can be. Its festive comedy also has a melancholy edge, carried by Feste's songs and by the harsh treatment of Malvolio, which many modern audiences find more troubling than funny. The title refers to the twelfth night after Christmas, a time of revelry and topsy-turvy celebration; the play's subtitle is What You Will.

Shakespeare probably wrote Twelfth Night around 1601–1602. Its first recorded performance took place on 2 February 1602 at Middle Temple Hall in London, as noted in the diary of the law student John Manningham. The plot draws on the Italian comedy Gl'ingannati and on a tale by Barnabe Rich, and the play was first printed in the First Folio of 1623. It remains one of his most performed comedies and was filmed by Trevor Nunn in 1996.
through-the-looking-glass: One winter evening, while playing with her black kitten, Alice wonders what lies on the other side of the drawing-room mirror, and finds that she can step right through it. In the Looking-Glass House everything is reversed: she has to hold a book up to the mirror to read the strange poem 'Jabberwocky', and walking away from a place is the best way to reach it. In a garden of talking flowers she meets the Red Queen, who shows her that the whole countryside is laid out like a huge chessboard. Alice joins the game as a pawn and sets out across the squares, hoping to reach the eighth and become a queen herself.

On her journey Alice meets some of Carroll's most famous creations: the quarrelling twins Tweedledum and Tweedledee, who recite 'The Walrus and the Carpenter'; the White Queen, who lives backwards in time; Humpty Dumpty, who explains the meaning of words as he pleases; and the kind, clumsy White Knight. More carefully structured than the first book, the story is a playful game of logic, language and mirror images, full of nonsense poems, puns and riddles, and illustrated, like Wonderland, by John Tenniel.

Published by Macmillan in December 1871 (with 1872 on the title page), the book was the sequel to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865). It sold 15,000 copies within weeks and was praised by critics as nearly equal to its predecessor. Its characters and phrases, and words invented in 'Jabberwocky' such as 'chortle' and 'galumph', passed into everyday English, and it has been adapted many times for the stage, radio, television and film, often combined with Wonderland.
thus-spake-zarathustra: At the age of thirty, Zarathustra leaves his home and goes to live in the mountains, where he enjoys his solitude for ten years with only an eagle and a serpent for company. Then, overflowing with wisdom, he decides to go down among men. In the marketplace of the first town he reaches, he proclaims that God is dead and that man is something to be overcome, announcing the coming of the Übermensch, the 'overman' or 'superman'; the crowd only laughs at him. Over the four parts of the book, Zarathustra gathers disciples, preaches to them, withdraws again to his cave, and struggles with the most difficult of his own thoughts.

Named after the ancient Persian prophet Zoroaster, Zarathustra is Nietzsche's spokesman for his central ideas: the death of God, the creation of new values beyond traditional Christian morality, the will to power and the eternal recurrence of all things. Rather than arguing like a treatise, the book speaks in parables, songs, dreams and short discourses that usually end with the refrain 'Thus spake Zarathustra'. Its lyrical, prophetic style deliberately echoes the language of Luther's Bible, and it is full of wordplay and images that have made it both widely quoted and much debated.

Nietzsche wrote the book between 1883 and 1885. The first three parts appeared separately in 1883 and 1884, while the fourth was printed at his own expense in 1885 in only forty copies for friends. The complete work in four parts was published in 1892, after his mental collapse. Thomas Common's English translation, used here, appeared in 1909. The book inspired Richard Strauss's tone poem Also sprach Zarathustra (1896), whose opening became world-famous through Stanley Kubrick's film 2001: A Space Odyssey.
mansfield-park: At the age of ten, Fanny Price is sent away from her large, struggling family to live at Mansfield Park, the grand house of her wealthy uncle and aunt, Sir Thomas and Lady Bertram. Timid and often overlooked, she finds a friend in her cousin Edmund. When Sir Thomas leaves to attend to his estate in Antigua, the lively Henry and Mary Crawford arrive in the neighbourhood, and the young people of the house throw themselves into flirtation and a scheme of amateur theatricals that Fanny watches with growing unease.

Austen sets charm against principle and asks what kind of upbringing makes a good person. Fanny is a quiet, steadfast heroine rather than a witty one, and the novel's irony falls on the vanity, idleness and selfishness around her. The family's wealth rests partly on a plantation in Antigua, worked by enslaved people in the period, a link the novel touches on only briefly but which modern readers have discussed at length.

Written at Chawton between 1812 and 1814, Mansfield Park was Austen's third published novel and appeared in 1814 from Thomas Egerton. It has long divided readers over its serious heroine, and it remains one of the most debated of her books. It has been adapted for film, including a 1999 version, and for television.
the-woman-in-white: Walking back to London late one night, the young drawing master Walter Hartright meets a strange woman dressed all in white who has escaped from an asylum. Soon afterwards he takes up a post at Limmeridge House in Cumberland, teaching the gentle Laura Fairlie and her clever, resolute half-sister Marian Halcombe. Walter is startled by Laura's likeness to the woman in white, and troubled to learn that Laura is engaged to the baronet Sir Percival Glyde.

Collins tells the story through a series of narrators, each giving evidence in turn as witnesses would in a court of law. The book mixes suspense, secrets and false identities with a pointed look at how little power the law gave a married woman over her own fortune. Marian Halcombe and the charming, sinister Count Fosco are among the most memorable characters in Victorian fiction.

The novel was serialised in Charles Dickens's weekly All the Year Round from 26 November 1859 to 25 August 1860 and published in book form in 1860. It made Collins famous and is generally regarded as the starting point of the sensation novel, as well as one of the first mystery novels in English. Collins adapted it for the stage in 1871.
north-and-south: Margaret Hale has grown up between her aunt's elegant house in Harley Street, London, and her father's country parsonage at Helstone in Hampshire. When her father leaves the Church of England for reasons of conscience, the family moves to Milton, a crowded manufacturing town in the north. There Margaret meets John Thornton, a proud, self-made cotton-mill owner, and the two take an instant dislike to each other just as tension grows between the mill owners and their workers.

Gaskell, who lived in Manchester, sets the values of the rural south against those of the industrial north and gives a voice to masters and workers alike. Strikes, poverty, illness and the question of what employers owe the people they employ are at the heart of the story, alongside a slowly developing relationship between two strong-willed people who must learn to understand each other.

The novel was serialised weekly in Household Words from 2 September 1854 to 27 January 1855 and published in two volumes in 1855. Gaskell wanted to call it Margaret Hale, but Charles Dickens, the magazine's editor, insisted on North and South. It is now counted among the finest Victorian novels about industrial England.
silas-marner: Silas Marner is a weaver and a devout member of a small chapel congregation at Lantern Yard, in a town in the north of England. Falsely accused of theft, betrayed by his closest friend and abandoned by his fiancée, he loses his faith and moves to the village of Raveloe. There he lives alone for fifteen years, working at his loom and finding comfort only in the gold coins he earns. Meanwhile, at the Red House, the squire's sons Godfrey and Dunstan Cass have secrets of their own.

Eliot tells a story close to a fable, about loss, trust and the way love and community can bring a broken life back into the world. She paints village life with warmth and humour, catching the talk of its inhabitants at the local inn, while showing how chance, conscience and choice shape people's fates.

Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe, Eliot's third novel, was published on 2 April 1861 by William Blackwood and Sons. Short and accessible, it became one of her most widely read works and has long been studied in schools. The Spanish translation offered here, by an unnamed translator, was published in Buenos Aires in 1919 by the Biblioteca de La Nación.
far-from-the-madding-crowd: Gabriel Oak, a young shepherd, proposes to the spirited Bathsheba Everdene and is turned down. When misfortune ruins him, he finds work on the farm she has just inherited at Weatherbury, where she decides to manage everything herself. Soon her attention is sought by two very different men: William Boldwood, a serious and solitary gentleman farmer next door, and Sergeant Frank Troy, a charming and reckless soldier.

Hardy follows the farming year, from lambing and sheep-shearing to harvest and storms, and fills the story with the humour of the farm workers who comment on events. Through Bathsheba, a woman running her own business in a man's world, he explores love, pride, loyalty and the part that chance plays in people's lives.

The novel first appeared anonymously as a monthly serial in the Cornhill Magazine and was published in book form on 23 November 1874. It was Hardy's fourth published novel and his first major success, and it introduced the name Wessex for his fictional region of south-west England. The title comes from Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard. It has been filmed several times, including Thomas Vinterberg's 2015 version.
cranford: The little town of Cranford is mostly in the hands of unmarried women and widows, its "Amazons", who live on small incomes and keep up appearances through a careful code of visiting hours, polite fictions and quiet economies. The narrator, Mary Smith, a young woman who often stays in the town, follows the lives of her friends, above all the strict Miss Deborah Jenkyns and her gentle younger sister, Miss Matty, as news, newcomers and the occasional misfortune ripple through their world.

Gaskell writes with warm, affectionate humour about people living in genteel poverty, their rivalries, their fears of change and the railway, and their deep loyalty to one another. Beneath the gentle comedy runs a thread of real feeling about loss, ageing and kindness, and the book is told in loosely linked episodes rather than a single plot.

Cranford began as a single story in Charles Dickens's magazine Household Words in December 1851. Dickens encouraged Gaskell to continue, and further episodes followed until 1853, when the stories were collected in book form under the title Cranford. It has remained one of her most popular works.
the-mill-on-the-floss: Maggie Tulliver and her brother Tom grow up at Dorlcote Mill, on the river Floss near the town of St. Ogg's. Maggie is quick, imaginative and impulsive, and she adores Tom, who is steady, stubborn and hard to please. As their father's fortunes are drawn into a bitter legal quarrel, the children's world changes, and Maggie's friendship with Philip Wakem, the sensitive son of her father's enemy, puts her loyalty to her family to the test.

Eliot paints provincial family life, its aunts, uncles, pride and petty quarrels, with humour and great psychological depth. The novel asks how a gifted girl with strong feelings can find her place in a narrow world, and explores duty, desire, memory and the bond between brother and sister. It is often seen as Eliot's most personal book, drawing on her own childhood.

The Mill on the Floss was published in three volumes by William Blackwood and Sons in 1860. It is widely regarded as one of Eliot's most powerful novels, and Maggie Tulliver as one of the most memorable heroines in English fiction.
the-mayor-of-casterbridge: Walking the roads of Wessex in search of work, the young hay-trusser Michael Henchard gets drunk at a country fair and sells his wife, Susan, and their baby daughter, Elizabeth-Jane, to a passing sailor. Sober and ashamed, he swears to give up drink. Many years later he has become a wealthy corn-factor and the mayor of Casterbridge, when Susan returns to the town with a grown-up Elizabeth-Jane, and a young Scotsman, Donald Farfrae, arrives looking for his fortune.

Hardy builds the novel around one powerful, proud and impulsive man, and asks how far character shapes fate. Rivalry in business and in love, secrets from the past and the life of a market town and its farming year are woven together with the sense of chance and consequence typical of his fiction.

The novel was serialised in twenty weekly parts in The Graphic from 2 January to 15 May 1886 and published in book form the same year. Casterbridge is Hardy's fictional version of Dorchester in Dorset. The book is among his best-known novels and has been adapted for television, including a 2001 version.
bleak-house: For generations the case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce has dragged on in the Court of Chancery, swallowing a fortune in legal costs. Esther Summerson, a modest young woman raised as an orphan, goes to live at Bleak House with the kindly John Jarndyce and his young wards, Ada and Richard, both hoping something from the case. Meanwhile, in fashionable society, the cold and beautiful Lady Dedlock is shaken by the sight of a piece of handwriting, and a sinister lawyer, Mr. Tulkinghorn, sets out to learn why.

The story is told by two voices, Esther's own gentle first-person account and a sharp, satirical narrator in the present tense. Dickens attacks the delays and injustice of the law, neglect of the poor and self-important philanthropy, while weaving a mystery, an investigation by Inspector Bucket, and a vast gallery of memorable minor characters.

Bleak House was published by Bradbury and Evans in twenty monthly instalments between March 1852 and September 1853, with illustrations by Hablot K. Browne ("Phiz"). It is often considered one of Dickens's finest novels.
hard-times: In the industrial town of Coketown, the retired merchant Thomas Gradgrind believes in nothing but facts and figures, and brings up his children, Louisa and Tom, without fancy or wonder. When he takes in Sissy Jupe, the daughter of a circus performer, two very different views of life meet. As Louisa grows up, her father's friend Josiah Bounderby, a boastful banker and mill owner, takes an interest in her, while the honest weaver Stephen Blackpool struggles with hardship at the factory.

Dickens sets the cold arithmetic of utilitarian thinking against the need for imagination, kindness and play, and draws a harsh picture of industrial life and its effects on workers. Short and sharply drawn compared with his longer novels, the book mixes satire, sorrow and sympathy for ordinary people.

Hard Times was serialised weekly in Dickens's own magazine Household Words from April to August 1854 and published in book form the same year. Its serialisation more than doubled the magazine's circulation. This edition contains the novel only.
adam-bede: In the rural community of Hayslope in 1799, Adam Bede is a skilled and upright carpenter, respected by everyone. He loves Hetty Sorrel, the pretty and vain young niece of the farmer Martin Poyser, but Hetty dreams of a grander life and is flattered by the attentions of Arthur Donnithorne, the good-natured young heir to the local estate. Hetty's cousin Dinah Morris, a gentle Methodist preacher, watches over the village with quiet compassion.

Eliot portrays country life, its work, speech and humour, with close and affectionate detail, and gives as much dignity to farmers and craftsmen as to the gentry. The novel explores moral responsibility, the consequences of small choices, suffering and forgiveness, and it shows the realism and sympathy for ordinary people that mark all her fiction.

Adam Bede was George Eliot's first full-length novel, published in 1859 by John Blackwood. Its success established the reputation of the author, whose real name was Mary Ann Evans, and it remains one of her best-loved works.
jude-the-obscure: Jude Fawley, a poor orphan raised by his great-aunt in a Wessex village, longs to become a scholar at Christminster, the university city whose towers he can glimpse from afar. Teaching himself Latin and Greek while working as a stonemason, he is drawn into an early marriage with Arabella Donn, a lively country girl, and later meets his cousin Sue Bridehead, a bright, independent and unconventional young woman.

Hardy writes a bleak and searching novel about thwarted ambition, the barriers of class and education, and the rules that church and society placed on marriage. Jude and Sue question the conventions of their time, and Hardy follows their struggles with deep sympathy and without easy consolation.

The novel was first serialised in Harper's New Monthly Magazine from December 1894 to November 1895, in a cut version, and published in book form in 1895. Its frank treatment of sex, marriage and religion caused an outcry among many reviewers and readers. It was Hardy's last novel; Christminster is his fictional version of Oxford.
little-dorrit: Amy Dorrit, known as Little Dorrit, was born and raised in the Marshalsea, the debtors' prison in London where her father William Dorrit has lived for so long that he is called its Father. She works quietly to support her family. Arthur Clennam returns to London after twenty years abroad and, suspecting that his cold and severe mother owes some wrong to the Dorrits, sets out to help them, coming up against the bureaucracy of the Circumlocution Office.

Dickens builds the novel around the image of imprisonment, real and figurative: debt, pride, social ambition, guilt and the endless red tape of government. He satirises officialdom and financial speculation while drawing a moving portrait of goodness in Little Dorrit herself and a vast cast of comic and sinister characters.

Little Dorrit was published in monthly parts from December 1855 to June 1857, with illustrations by Hablot Knight Browne ("Phiz"). Dickens's own father had been imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea in 1824. The serial was a great success on first publication.
agnes-grey: Agnes Grey, the younger daughter of a poor clergyman, decides to earn her own living as a governess to help her family. Her first post, with the Bloomfield family, brings her unruly, spoiled children and parents who give her responsibility without authority. In her second place, with the wealthy Murrays, she must look after self-centred young ladies, and her only comforts are the countryside, her own faith and the company of the kind local curate, Mr Weston.

Told in Agnes's own calm and honest voice, the novel gives a clear-eyed picture of the isolation and humiliations a governess could face, and of how the rich treated those who worked for them. Anne Brontë writes plainly and with quiet irony, and the book is a story of integrity, patience and modest hope.

Agnes Grey was Anne Brontë's first novel, drawn closely on her own years as a governess. It was published in December 1847 by Thomas Cautley Newby under the pen name Acton Bell, in the same set of volumes as her sister Emily's Wuthering Heights.
rob-roy: Frank Osbaldistone, the son of a London merchant, refuses to join his father's business and is sent to stay with his uncle's rough, hunting family in Northumberland. There he meets the clever, spirited Diana Vernon and his scheming cousin Rashleigh. When Rashleigh makes off with documents vital to the honour and fortune of Frank's father, Frank follows him north into Scotland and the Highlands, where he meets the Glasgow merchant Bailie Nicol Jarvie and the legendary outlaw Rob Roy MacGregor.

Scott sets a story of adventure, rivalry and romance against the political and economic background of the Jacobite rising of 1715. He contrasts commercial Lowland Scotland with the old clan society of the Highlands, and mixes vivid landscapes, Scots dialogue and humour with a sympathetic portrait of a world about to disappear.

Rob Roy was published in 1817 as one of the Waverley novels, which Scott issued anonymously. It was hugely popular and was soon adapted for the stage. The French translation offered here is by Auguste-Jean-Baptiste Defauconpret, published in 1830.
the-tenant-of-wildfell-hall: A young woman calling herself Mrs Helen Graham settles with her small son at Wildfell Hall, a half-ruined old house in a quiet country parish. Her reserve and independence set the neighbours talking, while the young farmer Gilbert Markham, who tells the story in letters to a friend, is drawn to her despite the rumours. To answer his doubts, Helen gives him her diary, which tells the story of her past.

Anne Brontë writes with unusual frankness about alcoholism, cruelty and the near-total power a husband held over his wife and child under the law of the time. The novel defends a woman's right to protect herself and her son, and combines a realistic picture of a dissolute circle of gentlemen with Helen's firm moral courage.

The Tenant of Wildfell Hall was published by Thomas Cautley Newby in June 1848 under the pen name Acton Bell. It was very popular and controversial, and many reviewers attacked it as coarse and shocking. It was Anne Brontë's second and last novel, and is now often described as one of the first feminist novels.
villette: After a series of family misfortunes leaves her alone in the world, the quiet and observant Lucy Snowe travels from England to Villette, the capital of a small European kingdom, and finds work in a girls' boarding school run by the watchful Madame Beck. There, among strangers who speak another language and follow another faith, she meets the handsome English doctor John Graham Bretton and the fiery, irritable teacher Monsieur Paul Emanuel.

Narrated by Lucy herself, guarded and often unreliable about her own feelings, the novel is an intense study of loneliness, self-reliance, longing and faith. Brontë draws on her own time in Brussels, which Villette is modelled on, and blends sharp observation, Gothic touches and psychological depth.

Villette was published in three volumes by Smith, Elder and Co. on 27 January 1853, under the pen name Currer Bell. It was the third and last novel Charlotte Brontë published in her lifetime, and many critics consider it her finest work.
the-pickwick-papers: Mr Samuel Pickwick, the generous and innocent founder of the Pickwick Club, sets out with three friends, the romantic Tupman, the poetic Snodgrass and the would-be sportsman Winkle, to travel England and report on what they see. Coaching inns, elections, cricket matches, Christmas festivities and the schemes of the swindler Alfred Jingle fill their journeys, and Mr Pickwick soon gains a devoted servant in the cheerful Londoner Sam Weller.

Dickens's first novel is a loose series of comic episodes that grows into a warm story about friendship, good nature and the follies of the world. Its humour, lively dialogue and gallery of eccentrics, with Sam Weller and his father Tony at the centre, made it one of the most popular comic books ever written.

Published in monthly parts from April 1836 to November 1837 by Chapman and Hall, under the full title The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club, it was written when Dickens was only twenty-four. The original illustrator, Robert Seymour, died after the first instalments. The book became a runaway success and made Dickens famous.
waverley: Edward Waverley, a romantic young Englishman raised on old books, takes a commission in the army and goes to Scotland. Visiting the old Baron of Bradwardine and his gentle daughter Rose, he is drawn on into the Highlands, where he meets the clan chief Fergus Mac-Ivor and his proud, passionately Jacobite sister Flora, just as Prince Charles Edward Stuart prepares the rising of 1745.

Scott follows a hero caught between two worlds, Hanoverian England and the old clan society of the Highlands, and shows history through the lives of ordinary and extraordinary people. The novel mixes adventure, romance, humour and Scots dialogue with a sympathetic and clear-eyed view of a lost cause.

Waverley was published anonymously in 1814 and was Scott's first novel. Its great success gave its name to the long series of Waverley novels that followed, and it is often regarded as one of the first historical novels in the Western tradition.
the-castle-of-otranto: Manfred, Prince of Otranto, is anxious to see his sickly son Conrad married to the young Isabella, for an old prophecy hangs over his family's hold on the castle. On the wedding day Conrad is crushed beneath a gigantic helmet that falls mysteriously into the courtyard. Desperate to secure an heir, Manfred turns his attentions to Isabella herself, who flees through the castle's underground passages, while a young peasant named Theodore becomes entangled in the strange events.

Walpole set out to combine the marvels of old romances with the natural characters of modern fiction. Haunted portraits, secret passages, prophecies, persecuted heroines and hidden identities fill this short and fast-moving tale, and many of its devices became standard features of Gothic fiction.

The Castle of Otranto was first published on 24 December 1764 under a pretence: Walpole presented it as a translation of an old Italian manuscript. In the second edition he acknowledged his authorship and added the subtitle A Gothic Story. It is generally regarded as the first Gothic novel.
the-return-of-the-native: Egdon Heath, a vast and ancient stretch of moorland in Wessex, is home to a small scattered community. Eustacia Vye, beautiful, proud and bored, longs for passion and a life far from the heath. Thomasin Yeobright's attempt to marry the innkeeper Damon Wildeve has gone wrong, and the faithful reddleman Diggory Venn, who loves her, watches over her. Then news comes that Thomasin's cousin Clym Yeobright, a successful diamond merchant, is returning home from Paris, and Eustacia sets her heart on him.

Hardy makes the heath itself a powerful presence, indifferent and timeless, against which his characters' desires and mistakes play out. The novel explores ambition, restlessness, family loyalty and the conflict between dreams and circumstances, with the folk customs and talk of the heath-dwellers adding humour and colour.

The Return of the Native first appeared in twelve monthly instalments in the magazine Belgravia during 1878 and was published in book form the same year. It was Hardy's sixth published novel. He had some difficulty finding a publisher for it, but reviews, though mixed, were generally positive.
nicholas-nickleby: When his father dies leaving the family with nothing, nineteen-year-old Nicholas Nickleby, his mother and his sister Kate turn for help to his uncle Ralph, a cold and grasping moneylender in London. Ralph sends Nicholas to work as an assistant master at Dotheboys Hall, a Yorkshire boarding school run by the cruel Wackford Squeers, where neglected boys are starved and beaten. There Nicholas befriends Smike, a broken and mistreated youth, and soon finds himself at odds with his uncle.

Dickens wanted to expose the notorious cheap Yorkshire schools where unwanted children could be left for years. Around that serious purpose he builds a lively, sprawling story full of comedy, melodrama and generosity, with characters such as the travelling theatre manager Vincent Crummles and his company.

Nicholas Nickleby was Dickens's third novel, published in twenty monthly instalments under the name Boz between March 1838 and September 1839, and in book form in 1839. The character of Squeers was inspired by a real Yorkshire schoolmaster, William Shaw.
shirley: In the West Riding of Yorkshire in 1811 and 1812, trade is crippled by the Napoleonic Wars, and workers who fear for their jobs are breaking the new machines in the cloth mills. Robert Moore, a determined mill owner, refuses to give in to them. His quiet young cousin Caroline Helstone, who lives with her uncle the rector, loves him in secret, while the wealthy and independent heiress Shirley Keeldar, who owns the land his mill stands on, becomes Caroline's close friend.

Brontë sets a story of friendship and love against a time of social unrest, and gives a sharp account of the limited lives open to women without money or occupation. The novel contrasts its two heroines, the reserved Caroline and the bold Shirley, and mixes satire of local curates with serious reflection on work, class and independence.

Shirley was published by Smith, Elder and Co. in 1849 under the pen name Currer Bell, as Charlotte Brontë's second published novel after Jane Eyre. The attack on Robert Moore's mill draws on the real Luddite attack on Rawfolds Mill in Liversedge in 1812.
a-journal-of-the-plague-year: In 1665 bubonic plague breaks out in London. The narrator, known only by the initials H. F., is a saddler who decides to stay in the city rather than flee, and he records what he sees and hears as the epidemic grows: the weekly bills of mortality, houses shut up with their families inside, people fleeing to the country, quack doctors and prophets, mass graves, and acts of panic, cruelty and kindness.

Defoe combines lists, official regulations and statistics with vivid scenes and stories, so that the book reads at once like a historical record and a novel. It is a powerful study of how a city and its people behave in the face of a deadly epidemic, and of the choices between staying and fleeing, duty and survival.

First published in March 1722, the book appeared under the initials H. F. Defoe was only a small child in 1665, and the work is a reconstruction drawing on records and accounts of the time; it may have drawn on the memories of his uncle Henry Foe. It was published when people in England feared that an outbreak of plague in Marseilles might reach them.
the-vicar-of-wakefield: Dr Charles Primrose, a good-hearted and simple country vicar, lives contentedly with his wife Deborah and their six children until the merchant who holds his savings goes bankrupt. Forced to move to a smaller parish, the family finds itself under the eye of the young landowner Squire Thornhill, whose attentions flatter the vicar's daughters Olivia and Sophia, while a poor and eccentric gentleman, Mr Burchell, also becomes a friend of the family.

Told by the vicar himself, the story mixes gentle comedy, sentiment and moral reflection, poking fun at the family's vanities while celebrating patience, faith and kindness in misfortune. Its simple style, humour and warmth made it one of the most widely read novels of the eighteenth century.

Goldsmith wrote the novel in 1761–1762. According to a well-known story, Samuel Johnson sold the manuscript for sixty pounds in October 1762 to help his friend out of debt, but the publisher held it back until 1766, when it appeared in London.
evelina: Evelina Anville has been raised in rural seclusion by her kindly guardian, the Reverend Mr Villars, at Berry Hill. When she travels to London with the family of her friend Maria Mirvan, she is dazzled and bewildered by fashionable society, its balls, theatres and pleasure gardens, and by the handsome and courteous Lord Orville. Her blunders, her unwelcome suitors and the arrival of her vulgar French grandmother, Madame Duval, make her entrance into the world anything but smooth.

Told in letters, mostly from Evelina to Mr Villars, the novel is a sharp and funny social comedy about manners, class and the dangers a young woman faced in a world run by men. Burney's ear for dialogue and her gallery of comic characters, from the coarse Captain Mirvan to Evelina's pretentious cousins, made it one of the liveliest novels of its century.

Evelina was published anonymously in 1778 by Thomas Lowndes. Burney even disguised her handwriting, and her brother delivered the manuscript to the publisher in disguise. The book was a great success, and its authorship soon became known.
the-last-days-of-pompeii: In the luxurious city of Pompeii, the young Athenian Glaucus falls in love with the beautiful Ione, who is under the guardianship of Arbaces, a powerful and sinister Egyptian priest of Isis with designs of his own. Nydia, a blind flower girl whom Glaucus has rescued from cruel masters, secretly loves him. Around them move the pleasures of Roman society, gladiators, a small community of early Christians, and the quiet threat of the mountain above the town.

Bulwer-Lytton recreates the daily life of a Roman city in rich detail, its villas, baths, temples and amphitheatre, and contrasts its decadence with the old faiths of Egypt and Greece and the rising Christian religion. The story builds towards the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79, which destroyed the city.

The novel was published in 1834. Bulwer-Lytton was inspired by the painting The Last Day of Pompeii by the Russian artist Karl Bryullov, which he had seen in Milan. The book was very popular and has been adapted for the screen, including a 1959 film.
lorna-doone: John Ridd is a boy when his father, a farmer on Exmoor, is killed by the Doones, a clan of outlaws descended from disgraced gentry who live in a hidden valley and raid the countryside with near impunity. Exploring the valley, the young John meets a beautiful girl, Lorna, who is being raised among the Doones. As he grows into a strong and honest young man, his love for Lorna sets him against the clan and its fierce heir, Carver Doone.

Told by John Ridd in his old age, the novel mixes romance, adventure and the rhythms of farm life on Exmoor with real events of the late seventeenth century, including the Monmouth Rebellion. Blackmore's love of the landscape and its seasons fills the book, along with humour and local dialect.
Lorna Doone: A Romance of Exmoor was published in 1869. It became extremely popular, has never been out of print, and is by far Blackmore's best-known work.
the-warden: The Reverend Septimus Harding, a kind and modest clergyman who loves music, is the warden of Hiram's Hospital in the cathedral town of Barchester, a charity that houses twelve old men. The warden's comfortable income comes from the same medieval bequest. John Bold, a young reforming surgeon who is in love with Harding's daughter Eleanor, begins to ask whether the money is fairly divided, and the question soon reaches the lawyers and the newspapers.

Trollope turns a small local dispute into a gentle but pointed comedy about conscience, the Church of England, the power of the press and the difficulty of reform. Mr Harding's quiet integrity is set against the energy of his forceful son-in-law, Archdeacon Grantly, who is determined to defend the Church at all costs.
Published in 1855, The Warden was the first of Trollope's six Chronicles of Barsetshire, set in the imaginary county of Barsetshire. It was followed by Barchester Towers (1857).
the-turn-of-the-screw: On Christmas Eve, a man named Douglas reads his friends a manuscript written by a governess he once knew. As a young woman, she accepted a post at Bly, a remote country house, to care for two orphaned children, the charming Miles and Flora, on condition that she never trouble their uncle in London. Soon she begins to see a strange man and woman about the grounds, and the housekeeper, Mrs Grose, recognises them as two former servants, Peter Quint and Miss Jessel.

James tells the story through the governess's own account, and never settles whether the ghosts are real or the product of her imagination. The tension, the hints and silences, and the unsettling innocence of the children make it one of the most discussed ghost stories in English.

The Turn of the Screw was first serialised in Collier's Weekly from January to April 1898, then published in October 1898 in the volume The Two Magics. Early readers took it as a straightforward ghost story; from the 1930s some critics argued that the apparitions exist only in the governess's mind, and its ambiguity is now seen as central.
our-mutual-friend: Gaffer Hexam and his daughter Lizzie make a living from the river Thames, and one night they bring in a drowned man believed to be John Harmon, heir to a fortune made from dust heaps on condition that he marry Bella Wilfer, a young woman he has never met. With Harmon apparently dead, the money passes to the kindly, unlettered Mr and Mrs Boffin, who take the pretty and mercenary Bella into their home, while a mysterious young man appears in the Wilfer household and Lizzie attracts the attention of two very different men.

Dickens builds a vast panorama of London, from riverside poverty to the empty display of fashionable society, around one central question: what money can make of life. Satire, mystery, comedy and darkness mix in a large cast that includes the scheming ballad-seller Silas Wegg and the troubled schoolmaster Bradley Headstone.
Our Mutual Friend was published in monthly instalments from May 1864 to November 1865. It was the last novel Dickens completed; he died in 1870 leaving The Mystery of Edwin Drood unfinished.
barchester-towers: When the old bishop of Barchester dies, the new bishop, Dr Proudie, arrives with his domineering wife and his oily chaplain, Obadiah Slope. Archdeacon Grantly and the traditional clergy of the diocese prepare for battle. Meanwhile Eleanor Bold, the widowed daughter of the gentle Mr Harding, finds herself pursued by suitors, including Mr Slope himself, as the eccentric Stanhope family, among them the captivating Signora Neroni, returns from Italy and adds to the confusion.

Trollope turns church politics, ambition and courtship into one of the great comedies of English fiction. His narrator comments freely and wittily on the characters, and the struggle between Mrs Proudie and Mr Slope for control of the bishop is among his most famous creations.
Barchester Towers was published by Longmans in 1857, two years after The Warden, as the second of Trollope's six Chronicles of Barsetshire.
daniel-deronda: The novel opens at a roulette table in a German resort, where the beautiful and self-assured Gwendolen Harleth notices a young Englishman watching her: Daniel Deronda, the ward of the wealthy Sir Hugo Mallinger, who knows nothing of his own parents. When her family loses its money, Gwendolen considers marriage to the cold and calculating Henleigh Grandcourt. Deronda, meanwhile, saves a young Jewish singer, Mirah, from despair, and is drawn into London's Jewish community, where he meets the visionary scholar Mordecai.

Eliot weaves two stories together: a sharp portrait of English high society and of a woman who marries for money, and Deronda's search for his identity and purpose. The novel's sympathetic portrayal of Jewish life, culture and hopes for a national homeland was unusual and controversial at the time.

Daniel Deronda was published in eight instalments from February to September 1876. It was George Eliot's last completed novel and the only one set in the society of her own day. It was soon translated into German and Dutch and is said to have influenced early Zionist thinkers.
washington-square: Catherine Sloper lives with her father, the wealthy and respected Dr Austin Sloper, in a fine house on Washington Square in New York. She is gentle, dutiful and shy, and her father, who still mourns his brilliant wife, finds her a disappointment. When the handsome and charming Morris Townsend begins to court her, encouraged by her romantic and meddling aunt Mrs Penniman, Dr Sloper is convinced that the young man is after Catherine's fortune.

James tells a short, finely balanced story of a daughter caught between the will of her father and the attentions of her suitor. With quiet irony and deep psychological insight, he explores pride, money, love and the slow growth of Catherine's own strength of character.

Washington Square was serialised in 1880 in the Cornhill Magazine and in Harper's New Monthly Magazine, and published in book form the same year. It was adapted for the stage in 1947 and became the 1949 film The Heiress, directed by William Wyler.
the-house-of-mirth: Lily Bart is admired by everyone in New York society for her beauty and charm, but she has no money of her own and depends on a wealthy aunt. To keep her place among the rich, she knows she must marry well, yet each time an advantageous match is within reach, something in her holds back. Her friendship with Lawrence Selden, a lawyer of modest means who stands slightly apart from society, offers her another view of life.

Wharton gives an unsparing portrait of the wealthy New York of the 1890s, its rules, gossip, gambling debts and cruelty to those who fail. The novel explores how a woman raised only to be decorative is trapped by money, reputation and her own choices. Its portrayal of the Jewish financier Simon Rosedale reflects the antisemitic prejudices of the society, and of the time, it describes.

The House of Mirth was serialised in Scribner's Magazine from January 1905 and published as a book on 14 October 1905. It was an immediate bestseller and established Wharton as a major American novelist. Its title comes from Ecclesiastes: "the heart of fools is in the house of mirth."
the-old-curiosity-shop: Little Nell Trent lives with her grandfather among the dusty treasures of his old curiosity shop in London. Secretly, the old man has been borrowing money from the cruel and grotesque moneylender Daniel Quilp, gambling it away in the hope of securing Nell's future. When everything is lost, grandfather and granddaughter slip away and set out on foot through the English countryside, meeting travelling showmen, kindly strangers and rogues, while Quilp, the loyal shop boy Kit Nubbles and the easygoing clerk Dick Swiveller are drawn into their story.

Dickens contrasts innocence and greed, the city and the country, and mixes sentiment and pathos with some of his most vivid comic and villainous figures. Quilp and Dick Swiveller have long been among the favourite characters of his readers.

The novel was serialised from April 1840 to February 1841 in Master Humphrey's Clock, Dickens's own weekly, which the story soon took over completely, and it was published in book form in 1841. It was enormously popular, with weekly sales rising to around a hundred thousand copies.
ethan-frome: A visitor spending the winter in the snowbound Massachusetts village of Starkfield becomes curious about Ethan Frome, a silent, crippled man who seems older than his years. Piecing together his story, he imagines Ethan as a young farmer, tied to a failing farm and to his sickly, complaining wife Zeena, whose cheerful young cousin Mattie Silver has come to live with them and help in the house.

Wharton writes a short, stark and tightly constructed tale about duty, longing, poverty and isolation, in which the harsh winter landscape mirrors the characters' lives. Far from the elegant New York society of her other novels, it shows her mastery of tragedy on a small scale.

Ethan Frome was published by Scribner's on 6 November 1911. Wharton is thought to have drawn on a sledding accident she had heard about in Lenox, Massachusetts, in 1904. It is one of her most widely read works.
the-awakening: Edna Pontellier, the wife of a prosperous New Orleans businessman and mother of two small boys, spends the summer at the seaside resort of Grand Isle among Creole families. There, through her friendship with the charming young Robert Lebrun, the music of the independent pianist Mademoiselle Reisz and the experience of learning to swim, she begins to feel stirrings of independence. Back in New Orleans, she starts to break with the conventions of her marriage and her social world.

Chopin writes with sensuous, impressionistic prose about a woman's search for selfhood, freedom and passion at a time when wives were expected to devote themselves entirely to husband and children. The novel reflects the society of its time, including its servants of colour described in the racial terms of the period.

The Awakening was published in 1899 and was harshly received, with reviewers calling it vulgar and morbid. It soon went out of print and was largely forgotten until it was rediscovered in the 1960s and 1970s; it is now considered a classic of American literature. This edition also includes a selection of Chopin's short stories.
the-red-badge-of-courage: Henry Fleming, a young farm boy, has enlisted in the Union Army dreaming of heroic deeds. Waiting in camp with the other new recruits, among them a tall soldier and a loud young man, he wonders anxiously whether he will run when the fighting starts. When his regiment finally goes into battle, the reality of war is very different from anything he imagined.

Crane tells the story almost entirely from inside the mind of "the youth", following his fear, pride, guilt and self-deception from moment to moment. Its vivid, impressionistic images of battle and its refusal to glorify war made it one of the most influential war novels ever written, all the more remarkable because Crane had never seen combat when he wrote it.

A shortened version appeared in newspapers in 1894, and the novel was published in book form by D. Appleton and Company on 3 October 1895. It was an immediate success, going through ten editions in its first year.
my-antonia: After the death of his parents, ten-year-old Jim Burden travels from Virginia to live with his grandparents on the Nebraska prairie. On the same train comes the Shimerda family, immigrants from Bohemia, who must struggle to survive their first hard winter on the land. Jim becomes the friend and teacher of their lively elder daughter, Ántonia, and the novel follows their lives from the open prairie to the small town of Black Hawk and beyond.

Told as Jim's memoir many years later, the novel is a celebration of the land, the seasons and the immigrant women who helped settle the plains, and a meditation on memory and the past. Cather's clear, luminous prose gives dignity to hard work and ordinary lives. Some passages, such as the portrait of a Black pianist, reflect the racial attitudes of their time.

My Ántonia was published in 1918 by Houghton Mifflin in Boston. It is generally considered Willa Cather's best-known work and a classic of American literature about the frontier and the immigrant experience.
main-street: Carol Milford, a lively and idealistic young librarian in St. Paul, marries Will Kennicott, a solid, good-natured country doctor, and moves with him to Gopher Prairie, a small town on the Minnesota prairie. Full of plans to make the town more beautiful and cultured, with new buildings, theatre and literary clubs, she soon finds herself up against the narrow-mindedness, complacency and gossip of its leading citizens.

Lewis writes a sharp, often funny satire of small-town America and its conformity, materialism and fear of new ideas, while giving a sympathetic but unsentimental portrait of a restless woman searching for a fuller life. Gopher Prairie is based on Sauk Centre, Minnesota, where Lewis grew up.

Main Street was published in 1920 by Harcourt, Brace and Howe. It was a huge commercial success and established Lewis as a major American novelist; in 1930 he became the first American to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.
the-house-of-the-seven-gables: In the seventeenth century, Colonel Pyncheon seized the land of Matthew Maule, a poor man executed for witchcraft, and built a grand house with seven gables on it; Maule cursed him from the scaffold. Two centuries later, the house has decayed along with the family's fortunes. The proud, impoverished old spinster Hepzibah Pyncheon is forced to open a little cent-shop to support her brother Clifford, newly released after thirty years in prison, while their powerful cousin Judge Jaffrey Pyncheon watches them, and a young country cousin, Phoebe, and a mysterious lodger, Holgrave, bring new life to the house.

Hawthorne explores how the sins and greed of one generation weigh on the next, mixing Gothic mystery, gentle humour and moral reflection. The old house itself, with its shadows, portraits and secrets, becomes a central character.
The House of the Seven Gables was published in 1851 and is one of Hawthorne's most celebrated works. It is set in Salem, Massachusetts.
the-deerslayer: In the 1740s, the young woodsman Natty Bumppo, called Deerslayer by the Delaware people among whom he was raised, comes to the remote lake the settlers call the Glimmerglass with the boastful giant Hurry Harry. They join the old trapper Thomas Hutter, who lives on the lake with his daughters, the beautiful Judith and the simple, gentle Hetty. War has broken out, Iroquois allied with the French are in the forest, and Deerslayer has come to meet his friend Chingachgook and help rescue Chingachgook's betrothed, Hist.

Cooper's story of frontier adventure is also a portrait of a young man of simple, honest principles, and of a wilderness of great beauty on the edge of change. Like his other frontier novels, it portrays Native American peoples through the romantic and often stereotyped views of its time, contrasting "good" and "bad" nations.

Published in 1841, The Deerslayer was the last of Cooper's Leatherstocking Tales to be written but is the first in the order of Natty Bumppo's life. The Glimmerglass is Otsego Lake in New York State, also the setting of The Pioneers (1823).
little-men: Jo March of Little Women has married Professor Bhaer, and together they run Plumfield, a school and home in the country for a crowd of boys, and a few girls. The story opens with the arrival of Nat Blake, a poor street musician sent by their friend Laurie, and follows the children's games, quarrels, adventures and lessons, especially the struggles of the wild and troubled Dan.

Alcott writes warmly about childhood and about an education based on kindness, trust, play and useful work rather than harsh discipline. The episodic chapters mix humour and gentle moral lessons, and familiar characters from Little Women reappear.
Little Men was published in 1871 as the sequel to Little Women, and was followed in 1886 by Jo's Boys, which completes the story of the Plumfield children.
black-beauty: Black Beauty tells his own story, beginning with a happy childhood in a meadow and his training by a kind master at Birtwick Park, where he makes friends with the gentle pony Merrylegs and the spirited mare Ginger. As his fortunes change, he passes from owner to owner, from comfortable country stables to hard labour, and later works as a cab horse in the streets of London.

Through the eyes of a horse, Sewell shows the difference between kind and thoughtless treatment, exposing cruel practices of the time such as the bearing rein, a strap that held a horse's head painfully high. The simple, direct narration makes it a moving story for children and adults alike.

Black Beauty: The Autobiography of a Horse was published in 1877 by Jarrold and Sons of Norwich. Sewell's stated aim was to encourage kindness, sympathy and understanding in the treatment of horses, and the book is credited with helping to end the use of the bearing rein. It has become one of the best-known animal stories ever written.
o-pioneers: On the windswept prairie near the little town of Hanover, Nebraska, the Swedish immigrant John Bergson dies after years of struggle with the land, leaving his farm to the care of his capable eldest daughter, Alexandra. While her brothers and many neighbours lose heart and want to sell, Alexandra has faith in the soil and in the future. Her friendship with Carl Linstrum, a gentle neighbour who leaves for the city, and her love for her youngest brother Emil shape the years that follow.

Cather celebrates the courage and vision of the immigrant settlers of the Great Plains and the beauty of the prairie through the seasons.
