Alongside Alexandra's story runs a story of passion between Emil and a married neighbour, Marie Shabata, showing the price of desire in a close-knit farming community.

O Pioneers! was published in 1913 and is often seen as Willa Cather's first great novel. It is the first of her three novels of the Great Plains, sometimes called her Prairie Trilogy, together with The Song of the Lark and My Ántonia.
sister-carrie: In 1889, eighteen-year-old Caroline Meeber, known to her family as Sister Carrie, leaves her small Wisconsin town for Chicago with a few dollars and great hopes. Factory work is hard and poorly paid, and she soon accepts the help and attentions of Charles Drouet, a cheerful travelling salesman. Through him she meets George Hurstwood, the prosperous and respected manager of a fashionable saloon, and her life, and his, take unexpected turns that lead them to New York.

Dreiser describes the lure of the big city, money and fine things with great detail and without moral judgement, showing characters driven by desire, chance and circumstance. As Carrie rises, the novel follows another life heading the opposite way, in one of the most powerful portraits of decline in American fiction.

Sister Carrie was Dreiser's first novel, published by Doubleday, Page and Company on 8 November 1900. The publisher, uneasy about a heroine who lives outside marriage without being punished, printed only a small edition and did little to promote it. It is now regarded as a founding work of American naturalism.
typee: Tired of hard life and harsh treatment aboard a whaling ship, the young sailor known as Tom and his friend Toby jump ship at the island of Nukuheva in the Marquesas. Struggling across the mountains, they descend into the valley of the Typee, a people the sailors fear as cannibals. Instead they are welcomed, fed and cared for, and Tom, nursing an injured leg, lives among them, befriending the devoted Kory-Kory and the lovely Fayaway, while wondering whether he will ever be allowed to leave.

Melville mixes adventure, travel description and reflection, often comparing the life of the islanders favourably with that of so-called civilised Western society and criticising missionaries and colonial powers. At the same time the book views the Polynesian people through the exotic and stereotyped lens of nineteenth-century travel writing.

Typee, Melville's first book, was published in 1846 by John Murray in London and Wiley and Putnam in New York. It draws, with much invention, on his own experience of deserting the whaler Acushnet at Nuku Hiva in 1842 with a shipmate, Richard Tobias Greene. It was a sensational success and made Melville famous as the man who had lived among cannibals.
ben-hur: Judah Ben-Hur, a young Jewish nobleman of Jerusalem, is reunited with his childhood friend Messala, now an arrogant Roman officer. When a tile falls from Ben-Hur's roof onto the new Roman governor, Messala seizes the chance to ruin him: Judah is condemned to the galleys and his mother and sister disappear. Years later, after saving the life of the Roman commander Quintus Arrius, Judah returns to the East determined to find his family and confront Messala.

Wallace combines a grand adventure, with sea battles and the famous chariot race in Antioch, with the story of the coming of Christ, whose life crosses Judah's at key moments. The novel draws a broad picture of the Roman world and Judea and explores revenge, faith and forgiveness.

Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ was published by Harper and Brothers on 12 November 1880. It became the best-selling American novel of the nineteenth century, overtaking Uncle Tom's Cabin, and has been adapted for the stage and the screen, including a 1925 film.
pollyanna: After the death of her father, a poor missionary minister, eleven-year-old Pollyanna Whittier is sent to live with her wealthy and severe Aunt Polly in the town of Beldingsville. Aunt Polly takes her in out of duty, not love, and gives her a bare attic room. But Pollyanna has a secret her father taught her: the glad game, in which she looks for something to be glad about in every situation, however bad.

Pollyanna's cheerfulness gradually touches the lonely, the sick and the bitter around her, from the reclusive Mr Pendleton to a bedridden invalid and an orphan boy named Jimmy. The story is a gentle and warm-hearted tale about optimism, kindness and the power of seeing the good in life.

Pollyanna was published in 1913 and became a great success and a classic of children's literature. Porter wrote one sequel, Pollyanna Grows Up (1915); many later sequels were written by other authors.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co: Hank Morgan, a head superintendent at an arms factory in Hartford, Connecticut, is knocked unconscious in a fight and wakes up in England in the year 528, at the court of King Arthur. Captured and condemned to be burned, he remembers that a solar eclipse is due and passes himself off as a great magician, rivalling Merlin. Soon he is "The Boss", the king's chief minister, determined to bring the inventions and ideas of his own century to the age of chivalry.

Twain mixes slapstick comedy and fantasy with biting satire of monarchy, aristocracy, the established Church, slavery and superstition. As Hank travels the land with the talkative Sandy and the king himself in disguise, the book raises serious questions about progress, power and the dangers of technology.
A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court was published in 1889. It is often cited as one of the early classics of time-travel fiction.
babbitt: George F. Babbitt is a successful real-estate broker in Zenith, a growing Midwestern city. He believes in business, boosters' clubs, modern gadgets and doing what his neighbours do, and his days are filled with deals, dinners, speeches and worries about status. Only with his old friend Paul Riesling does he admit to a vague dissatisfaction, until events shake his comfortable routine and he tries, for a while, to rebel.

Lewis satirises the conformity, materialism and boosterism of American middle-class life after the First World War with a sharp ear for slang and speeches, while making Babbitt a recognisable and at times sympathetic figure. The word "Babbitt" came to mean a self-satisfied, conformist businessman.
Babbitt was published in 1922, two years after Main Street. In 1930 Lewis became the first American to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.
daisy-miller: At a grand hotel in Vevey, Switzerland, Frederick Winterbourne, a young American who has lived long in Europe, meets Daisy Miller, a pretty, chatty girl from Schenectady travelling with her mother and her little brother Randolph. Charmed but puzzled, he cannot decide whether she is innocent or improper. When they meet again in Rome, Daisy's outings with a young Italian, Mr Giovanelli, scandalise the American expatriate community.
In this short and subtle novella, James contrasts American innocence and spontaneity with European manners and snobbery, and leaves readers, like Winterbourne, uncertain how to judge its heroine.
Daisy Miller first appeared in the Cornhill Magazine in June and July 1878 and in book form the following year. It brought James his first widespread critical and commercial success.
herland: Three young American men, the sociologist Van, who tells the story, the romantic Jeff and the swaggering Terry, hear rumours of a land where only women live, hidden on a plateau in an unexplored region. Flying in, they find a peaceful and orderly country with no men at all, where for two thousand years children have been born to women alone. Captured and gently educated by their hosts, including Ellador, Celis and Alima, the men must explain, and defend, the world they come from.

Gilman's feminist utopia uses humour and dialogue to question ideas about gender, motherhood, education and economics taken for granted in her time. Some of its assumptions, notably about race and selective breeding, reflect the eugenic thinking common in the early twentieth century.

Herland was serialised in 1915 in The Forerunner, the monthly magazine that Gilman wrote and edited herself. It was first published as a complete book only in 1979, and has since become a classic of feminist fiction.
rebecca-of-sunnybrook-farm: Ten-year-old Rebecca Rowena Randall, one of seven children on the poor Sunnybrook Farm, is sent to live with her mother's older sisters in their brick house in Riverboro, Maine, so that she can be educated. Aunt Jane is gentle and kind, but Aunt Miranda is stern and quick to disapprove of Rebecca's chatter, daydreams and high spirits.

The novel follows Rebecca through school, friendships, small adventures and mishaps as she grows into a thoughtful and gifted young woman, helped along by a kind young businessman, Adam Ladd. It is a warm, humorous portrait of childhood and village life in New England.
Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm was published in 1903 and became a lasting classic of American children's literature. It was adapted for the screen, including a 1917 film.
kim: Kimball O'Hara, the orphaned son of an Irish soldier, runs wild in the streets of Lahore, passing easily for a local boy. When an elderly Tibetan lama arrives in search of the sacred River of the Arrow, Kim becomes his disciple and guide on the roads of India. At the same time, through the horse-dealer Mahbub Ali and Colonel Creighton, he is drawn into the Great Game, the secret rivalry between Britain and Russia in Central Asia.

Kipling paints a vivid and affectionate picture of the peoples, languages, religions and landscapes of India, and of the friendship between the streetwise boy and the gentle holy man. The novel is also a book of the British Empire, written from the point of view of its colonial order, and its view of India reflects the assumptions of its time.

Kim was serialised in McClure's Magazine from December 1900 to October 1901 and in Cassell's Magazine during 1901, and published in book form in October 1901. It is often ranked among the greatest novels in English.
king-solomon-s-mines: The seasoned elephant hunter Allan Quatermain agrees to help Sir Henry Curtis and his friend Captain John Good search for Sir Henry's brother, who vanished while looking for the fabled diamond mines of King Solomon. Guided by an old map and joined by a mysterious tall African named Umbopa, they cross a burning desert and icy mountains to reach the hidden land of the Kukuana, ruled by the cruel king Twala and his ancient witch-finder, Gagool.

Haggard's fast-paced, first-person adventure helped create the "lost world" genre, with its hidden kingdoms, ancient treasures and perilous journeys. Written from the viewpoint of a white colonial hunter, it reflects the imperial and racial attitudes of its time towards Africa and its peoples, even as some African characters are given dignity and heroism.

King Solomon's Mines was published by Cassell in September 1885. Haggard is said to have written it after betting his brother that he could write a story as good as Treasure Island. It was an immediate bestseller and has been filmed several times, including a 1937 version.
pygmalion: Sheltering from the rain in Covent Garden, the brilliant and ill-mannered phonetics expert Henry Higgins meets Eliza Doolittle, a Cockney flower seller, and boasts to his fellow linguist Colonel Pickering that he could teach her to speak so well that she might pass for a duchess. Eliza takes him at his word and arrives at his house to ask for lessons, and the experiment begins, complicated by her irrepressible father, the dustman Alfred Doolittle.

Shaw's comedy uses language and accent to expose the absurdities of the English class system, and asks what becomes of Eliza once she has been transformed. Witty dialogue and strong characters combine with serious questions about independence, education and dignity. This edition includes Shaw's preface and his prose sequel explaining what happens afterwards.

Pygmalion was first performed in German translation in Vienna on 16 October 1913, and in English at His Majesty's Theatre in London in April 1914, with Herbert Beerbohm Tree and Mrs Patrick Campbell. It became Shaw's most popular play and inspired the musical My Fair Lady (1956).
a-doll-s-house: It is Christmas in the comfortable home of Torvald Helmer, a lawyer about to become a bank manager, and his lively wife Nora, whom he treats as a charming pet. Nora has a secret: years ago, to save her husband's health, she borrowed money without his knowledge, by means she cannot admit. When Krogstad, an employee at Torvald's bank, threatens to reveal everything, Nora must face the truth about her marriage, with her old friend Mrs Linde and the family friend Dr Rank looking on.

Ibsen's realistic drama questions the roles assigned to husbands and wives and the idea of a woman's duty to herself. Its tight plot and everyday setting made it a turning point in modern theatre, and its ending is still much discussed.
A Doll's House was published on 4 December 1879 and first performed at the Royal Danish Theatre in Copenhagen on 21 December 1879. This English translation is by R. Farquharson Sharp.
five-children-and-it: Cyril, Anthea, Robert, Jane and their baby brother, known as the Lamb, are spending the summer in the country when, digging in a gravel pit, they discover an ancient, bad-tempered creature: the Psammead, a sand-fairy who can grant wishes. He agrees to grant them one wish a day, which lasts only until sunset. Wishing to be beautiful, rich or winged, the children soon learn that getting exactly what you ask for can lead to all kinds of trouble.

Nesbit writes with humour and a natural sense of how real children think, talk and squabble, and places magic in an everyday setting. Her mix of fantasy and realism made the book a landmark in children's literature.

The stories first appeared in the Strand Magazine from April to December 1902 and were published as a book the same year. It was followed by The Phoenix and the Carpet (1904) and The Story of the Amulet (1906), and has never been out of print.
the-lost-world: Edward Malone, a young journalist on the Daily Gazette, wants to do something brave to impress the woman he loves. He finds his chance with Professor George Edward Challenger, a hot-tempered zoologist who claims to have found living prehistoric animals in the Amazon basin and has been mocked by the scientific world. Malone sets out to prove or disprove him, together with the sceptical Professor Summerlee and the adventurer and big-game hunter Lord John Roxton.

Doyle combines scientific speculation, humour and thrilling adventure, with dinosaurs, dangerous ape-men and the explorers' constant bickering. Told in the first person by Malone, the story also reflects the colonial attitudes of its time in its portrayal of the region's indigenous peoples.

The Lost World was serialised in the Strand Magazine from April to November 1912, with illustrations by Harry Rountree, and published as a book the same year. It introduced Professor Challenger, who returned in later stories, and helped shape the "lost world" adventure story.
the-prisoner-of-zenda: Rudolf Rassendyll, a well-off and easygoing young Englishman, travels to the small Central European kingdom of Ruritania for the coronation of its new king, Rudolf V, a distant cousin who looks exactly like him. When the king is drugged on the eve of his coronation as part of a plot by his ambitious half-brother, Black Michael, the loyal Colonel Sapt persuades Rassendyll to take the king's place, and he soon finds himself in love with the king's betrothed, Princess Flavia.
Hope's swift and witty adventure of impersonation, sword fights, intrigue and doomed romance, with the dashing villain Rupert of Hentzau, created the imaginary kingdom of Ruritania.

The Prisoner of Zenda was published in 1894. It was followed by a sequel, Rupert of Hentzau (1898), and has been filmed several times. The Spanish translation offered here, by an unnamed translator, was published in Buenos Aires in 1909 by the Biblioteca de La Nación.
lord-jim: Jim, the son of an English parson, goes to sea dreaming of heroic deeds. As chief mate of the Patna, an old steamer carrying hundreds of Muslim pilgrims across the Indian Ocean, he joins the captain and officers in abandoning the ship when it seems about to sink, an act that brings public disgrace. The seaman Marlow, who attends the inquiry, becomes fascinated by Jim and follows his attempts to escape his past, until the merchant Stein offers him a new life in the remote settlement of Patusan.

Conrad tells the story through Marlow's long, searching narration, moving back and forth in time and gathering other witnesses' views. The novel explores honour, guilt, courage, self-knowledge and the gap between ideals and actions, against the background of European colonialism in Southeast Asia, which it portrays from the perspective of its time.

Lord Jim was serialised in Blackwood's Magazine from October 1899 to November 1900 and published in book form in 1900. The Patusan section was partly inspired by the life of James Brooke, the first White Rajah of Sarawak.
an-ideal-husband: Sir Robert Chiltern is a rising government minister, admired for his integrity and adored by his high-minded wife, Lady Chiltern. At a glittering party in their London home, the scheming Mrs Cheveley reveals that she knows the dishonest act on which his fortune was built, and threatens to expose him unless he supports a fraudulent scheme. Sir Robert turns to his friend Lord Goring, a witty and apparently idle dandy, for help.

Wilde mixes political drama, blackmail and moral questions about public and private virtue with dazzling epigrams and comedy. Beneath the wit, the play asks whether anyone can live up to an ideal, and how love should deal with human weakness.

An Ideal Husband was first performed at the Haymarket Theatre in London on 3 January 1895, shortly before Wilde's downfall later that year. It was published in book form in 1899, without the author's name.
just-so-stories: In a series of comic and inventive tales addressed to "O Best Beloved", Kipling tells how animals and people came to be as they are: how the Whale got his throat, how the Camel got his hump, how the Rhinoceros got his skin, how the Leopard got his spots, and how the curious Elephant's Child got his long trunk. Other stories tell how the first letter was written and how the alphabet was made.

Kipling's rhythmic, playful language, with its repetitions and invented words, is made to be read aloud, and each story is followed by a poem. Some passages, notably in the story of the Leopard, use racial language and stereotypes of their time that are offensive today.

Just So Stories for Little Children was published by Macmillan in 1902, with illustrations by Kipling himself. The first stories were told at bedtime to his daughter Josephine, who insisted they be told "just so"; she died in 1899, before the book appeared. It remains one of his best-known works.
eugenie-grandet: Félix Grandet, a former cooper turned wine merchant and landowner, is one of the richest men in Saumur, yet he lives like a pauper, measuring out the sugar and the candles while his wife, his daughter Eugénie and the faithful servant Nanon obey his every rule. Local families compete for Eugénie's hand and her future fortune. Then, one evening, her elegant cousin Charles arrives from Paris, carrying a letter that will change his life, and hers.

Balzac draws an unforgettable portrait of avarice and of its effect on a family, and a precise picture of the manners of the provincial middle class. Eugénie's quiet, steadfast love and the slow passing of years give the novel its deep emotional power.

Eugénie Grandet was first serialised in 1833 and published in book form in 1834. It belongs to the "Scenes of Provincial Life" in Balzac's vast cycle La Comédie humaine. This edition offers the original French text and the English translation by Katharine Prescott Wormeley.
notre-dame-de-paris: On 6 January 1482, Paris celebrates the Festival of Fools, and the hunchbacked bell-ringer of Notre-Dame, Quasimodo, is crowned Pope of Fools. Among the crowd dances Esmeralda, a beautiful young street performer with her goat Djali, who has captured the attention of the struggling poet Pierre Gringoire, the handsome captain Phoebus and the grave archdeacon Claude Frollo, Quasimodo's guardian, whose fascination with her turns into obsession.

Hugo brings medieval Paris to life in vast, colourful scenes and makes the cathedral itself the heart of the novel, with celebrated chapters defending Gothic architecture. Love, fate, cruelty and compassion meet in a story of outcasts and the powerful. Its portrayal of Esmeralda and the city's "gypsies" draws on the romantic and stereotyped images of Romani people common in its time.

Notre-Dame de Paris was published on 16 March 1831. It was a great success and helped awaken interest in the preservation of France's Gothic monuments. This edition offers the original French text and the English translation by Isabel F. Hapgood.
carmen: A French scholar travelling in Andalusia in search of an ancient battlefield shares his cigars and his food with a dangerous stranger in the hills, and later meets a striking young woman, Carmen, in Córdoba. When he finds the stranger again in a prison cell, awaiting execution, the man, Don José, tells him his story: how, as a soldier in Seville, he met Carmen and how his love for her drew him into smuggling and banditry.

Mérimée writes with precise, restrained prose, framing a tale of passion, jealousy and freedom within the cool account of a learned traveller. The novella's portrait of Carmen and of Romani life reflects the fascination and the stereotypes of nineteenth-century writers, which the narrator presents as scholarly observation.

The first three parts of Carmen appeared in the Revue des deux Mondes on 1 October 1845, and the fourth was added when it was published as a book in 1846. It inspired Georges Bizet's opera Carmen (1875). This English translation is by Lady Mary Loyd.
tartuffe: Orgon, a wealthy Parisian, has fallen completely under the spell of Tartuffe, a penniless man who poses as a model of piety. He has taken him into his home, admires everything he says, and now plans to marry him to his daughter Mariane, who loves Valère. His wife Elmire, his brother-in-law Cléante, his son Damis and above all the outspoken maid Dorine see through the impostor, but Orgon will not listen.
Molière's comedy is a sharp satire of religious hypocrisy and of the blindness of those who let themselves be deceived. Its comic scenes and lively characters have kept it on the stage ever since.

Tartuffe was first performed at Versailles in 1664 and was immediately banned after objections from church authorities. Molière rewrote it, and the final version was allowed to be performed publicly in 1669. This English verse translation is by Curtis Hidden Page.
fathers-and-sons: In 1859, Arkady Kirsanov returns home from university to his father's modest estate, bringing with him his friend Yevgeny Bazarov, a young doctor who declares himself a nihilist: he accepts no authority, tradition or principle that cannot be proved. Arkady's gentle father, Nikolai Petrovitch, and his elegant, proud uncle, Paul Petrovitch, are disturbed and provoked by Bazarov's ideas, while the young men's visit to the cool and intelligent widow Madame Odintsov tests Bazarov's own convictions.

Turgenev portrays the gap between the liberal generation of the 1840s and the radical young people of the 1860s with great fairness and subtlety. Bazarov became one of the most debated characters in Russian literature, and the novel explores love, friendship, family and the limits of ideas.

Fathers and Sons was first published in 1862 in the magazine The Russian Messenger, and provoked fierce controversy among both conservatives and radicals. This English translation is by C. J. Hogarth.
the-black-tulip: In August 1672, a furious crowd in The Hague turns on the brothers Johan and Cornelius de Witt, the former leaders of the Dutch Republic. Their quiet godson, Cornelius van Baerle, a wealthy young doctor, cares nothing for politics: his passion is tulips, and he hopes to win the great prize offered by the city of Haarlem for the first black tulip. His envious neighbour, Isaac Boxtel, spies on him day and night, and when Cornelius is thrown into prison, his only hope lies with Rosa, the jailer Gryphus's daughter.

Dumas combines a dramatic page of Dutch history with a tender love story and a tale of patience, rivalry and obsession. Shorter and more intimate than his great musketeer novels, it shows his gift for suspense and lively dialogue.

The Black Tulip was published in 1850, written with the collaboration of Auguste Maquet. It is set against the background of the Dutch passion for tulips. This edition offers the original French text and an English translation by an unnamed translator.
michael-strogoff: A Tartar rebellion led by Feofar Khan has cut Siberia off from Moscow, and the telegraph lines are down. The traitor Ivan Ogareff, a former colonel thirsting for revenge, plans to betray the city of Irkutsk, where the Tsar's brother is holding out. The Tsar sends Michael Strogoff, a courageous courier from Omsk, to carry a warning across thousands of miles of hostile land. On the way he meets Nadia, a young woman travelling to join her exiled father, and two rival war correspondents, Harry Blount and Alcide Jolivet.

Verne writes a breathless adventure across rivers, steppes and forests, full of danger, disguise and endurance, and paints a vast picture of nineteenth-century Russia and Siberia. Loyalty, courage and love are tested at every step.

Michael Strogoff was published by Pierre-Jules Hetzel in 1876 as one of Verne's Extraordinary Voyages. It has been adapted many times for the stage and screen. This edition offers the original French text, an English translation and a German translation, both by unnamed translators.
the-mystery-of-the-yellow-room: At the Château du Glandier, the scientist Professor Stangerson and his daughter Mathilde work on their research. One night, cries and shots are heard from the Yellow Room, where Mathilde sleeps. When the door, locked and bolted from the inside, is broken down, she is found gravely wounded, and the attacker has disappeared. The young journalist Joseph Rouletabille, eighteen years old and full of confidence, sets out to solve the case against the famous detective Frédéric Larsan, while Mathilde's fiancé, Robert Darzac, behaves strangely.

Leroux builds an ingenious puzzle around an apparently impossible crime, with plans of the château, clues and reasoning laid before the reader, and adds humour, suspense and a mysterious past. Rouletabille became one of the great detectives of French fiction.

The Mystery of the Yellow Room was first published in the magazine L'Illustration from September to November 1907 and as a book in 1908. It is one of the first and most famous locked-room mysteries. This edition offers the original French text and an English translation by an unnamed translator.
manon-lescaut: A man of quality meets a young nobleman, the Chevalier des Grieux, escorting a group of women condemned to be deported, and later hears his story. At seventeen, about to enter the Church, des Grieux met the beautiful Manon Lescaut at an inn in Amiens, where she was being sent to a convent, and ran away with her to Paris. Torn between his love for Manon, who cannot bear poverty, and the advice of his loyal friend Tiberge, he is drawn into gambling, deception and disgrace.

Told by des Grieux himself, the novel is a passionate and painfully honest account of a love that overturns every principle. Prévost portrays both lovers with sympathy, and Manon, at once loving and faithless, remains one of the most fascinating heroines in French fiction.

Manon Lescaut appeared in 1731 as the last volume of Prévost's Memoirs and Adventures of a Man of Quality. In 1733 copies were seized in Paris for their immoral content, which only increased its popularity. This edition offers the original French text, an English translation by an unnamed translator and a Spanish translation by Antonio de Hoyos y Vinent.
taras-bulba: The fierce old Cossack Taras Bulba welcomes home his sons Ostap and Andrii, back from their studies at the academy, and soon takes them to the Zaporozhian Sich, the camp of the free Cossacks on the Dnieper. When war breaks out against the Poles, father and sons ride out with the Cossack army and lay siege to the city of Dubno, where Andrii's feelings for a young Polish noblewoman set him against his own people.

Gogol's romantic, epic novella celebrates the wild freedom, comradeship and courage of the Cossacks while showing the violence and fanaticism of their wars. It also reflects the hostility of its time towards Poles and Jews, who are portrayed through harsh stereotypes.
Taras Bulba was first published in 1835 in the collection Mirgorod and revised in a longer version in 1842. This edition also contains other tales by Gogol, among them "The Cloak".
ninety-three: In 1793, at the height of the French Revolution, the royalist peasants of the Vendée and Brittany rise against the Republic. The Marquis de Lantenac, an old and ruthless nobleman, lands secretly from England to lead them. Against him the Republic sends a young officer, Gauvain, who is Lantenac's great-nephew, watched over by the stern former priest Cimourdain, Gauvain's old tutor. Caught between the two sides is a poor peasant woman, Michelle Fléchard, searching desperately for her three lost children.

Hugo's last novel is a vast and dramatic meditation on revolution, violence, loyalty and mercy. Its three parts, set at sea, in Paris and in the Breton forests, alternate between epic scenes, portraits of revolutionary leaders and moments of intimate humanity.
Ninety-Three was published in 1874, shortly after the bloodshed of the Paris Commune. This edition offers the original French text, Quatrevingt-treize, and the English translation by Aline Delano.
pierre-and-jean: The Roland family lives quietly in Le Havre: the father, a retired jeweller who loves fishing, the gentle mother, and two grown-up sons, Pierre, a doctor, and Jean, a lawyer. One day the family learns that Léon Maréchal, an old friend from their years in Paris, has left his entire fortune to Jean alone. While everyone rejoices, Pierre, jealous and restless, cannot stop wondering why.

In this short and intense novel, Maupassant follows the growth of suspicion and jealousy in a man's mind with great psychological precision, against the background of the harbour and the sea. The French edition includes the famous preface "Le Roman" ("The Novel"), in which Maupassant sets out his views on realism and the art of fiction.

Pierre et Jean, Maupassant's fourth novel, was written in the summer of 1887 and published by Paul Ollendorff on 9 January 1888. This edition offers the original French text and the English translation by Clara Bell.
the-devil-s-pool: Germain, a hard-working ploughman of the Berry region, has been a widower for two years and has three small children. His father-in-law urges him to remarry and suggests a well-off widow in a neighbouring village. Germain agrees to go and meet her, and on the way he is asked to take along Marie, a poor sixteen-year-old girl going to work as a shepherdess. Lost in the fog near a place called the Devil's Pool, they are forced to spend the night in the woods.

Sand celebrates the beauty of the countryside, the dignity of peasant life and simple, honest feelings in a gentle, idealised pastoral story. The book opens with reflections on art and labour and ends with a description of traditional country wedding customs.

La Mare au Diable was published in 1846 and is one of Sand's most popular "rustic" novels, set in the Berry region where she lived. This edition offers the original French text and the English translation by George Burnham Ives.
the-gambler: Alexei Ivanovich is tutor to the children of a Russian general who is living above his means in a German spa town, waiting for a rich old relative, the Grandmother, to die and leave him a fortune. Alexei is hopelessly in love with the general's proud stepdaughter Polina, who treats him with scorn and asks him to gamble for her. Around them gather a shady French marquis, the elegant Mademoiselle Blanche and a reserved Englishman, Mr Astley, while the roulette wheel turns at the casino.

Dostoevsky draws on his own compulsive gambling and stormy love affair to portray obsession, pride and humiliation, and satirises Russians, French, Germans and English abroad. Fast, feverish and often comic, the short novel captures the excitement and despair of the gaming tables.

The Gambler was published in 1866. Dostoevsky dictated it in just twenty-six days to meet a publisher's deadline, with the help of a young stenographer, Anna Snitkina, who later became his wife. This English translation is by C. J. Hogarth.
indiana: Indiana, a young woman born on the Île Bourbon, is married to Colonel Delmare, a gruff, jealous and much older retired officer, and lives with him in a lonely manor in Brie, watched over by her silent and devoted cousin, Sir Ralph Brown. When the elegant and seductive Raymon de Ramière enters her life, she believes she has at last found the love she has dreamed of, unaware that he is also courting her maid and foster-sister, Noun.

Sand's first novel is a passionate protest against marriages that make wives the property of their husbands, and a romantic exploration of love, illusion and freedom. It also reflects the colonial society of its time, from which its heroine comes.
Indiana was published in 1832 and made its author famous under the new pen name George Sand. This English translation is by George Burnham Ives.
the-mysterious-island: In March 1865, during the American Civil War, five Northern prisoners escape from Confederate Richmond in a balloon: the engineer Cyrus Harding, the journalist Gideon Spilett, the sailor Pencroft, the young Herbert and Harding's devoted servant Neb, together with his dog Top. Swept away by a hurricane, they come down on an unknown volcanic island in the Pacific, which they name Lincoln Island. With nothing but their knowledge and hard work, they set out to make it their home, while strange events suggest they are not alone.

Verne celebrates human ingenuity and cooperation as the castaways make fire, bricks, iron, glass and even electricity from what they find. The novel combines a detailed survival story with mystery and adventure, and links up with characters from his earlier novels Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas and In Search of the Castaways.

The Mysterious Island was serialised in Hetzel's Magasin d'éducation et de récréation and published in book form in 1875, as one of Verne's Extraordinary Voyages. This edition offers the original French text and an English translation; in it Cyrus Smith of the French original is called Cyrus Harding.
salammbo: After the First Punic War, Carthage cannot pay the mercenaries who fought for it. During a riotous feast in the gardens of the general Hamilcar Barca, the Libyan giant Matho sees Hamilcar's daughter Salammbô, a priestess of the moon goddess Tanith, and falls under her spell. Guided by the cunning former slave Spendius, Matho steals the goddess's sacred veil, and the mercenaries' revolt turns into a merciless war against the city.

Flaubert recreates the ancient world with dazzling, exotic and often brutal detail, from temples and palaces to battles and sieges. The novel is a sensuous and violent tale of passion, religion and war, drawn largely from the account of the Mercenary War by the Greek historian Polybius.

Salammbô was published in 1862 and was very popular. It is set in Carthage during the Mercenary War of 241–237 BC. This edition offers the original French text and an English translation by an unnamed translator.
colomba: Returning home to Corsica after serving in Napoleon's army, the young lieutenant Orso della Rebbia travels on the same ship as an English colonel, Sir Thomas Nevil, and his romantic daughter Lydia, who is fascinated by tales of bandits and vendettas. In his village, Orso is welcomed by his sister Colomba, a passionate young woman convinced that their father was murdered by the rival Barricini family, and determined that her brother will take revenge.

Mérimée paints the landscapes, customs and code of honour of Corsica with sharp, ironic precision, contrasting the civilised visitors with the fierce traditions of the island. Colomba herself, proud and implacable, is one of his most memorable heroines.

Colomba first appeared in the Revue des deux Mondes on 1 July 1840, after Mérimée had visited Corsica in 1839 as inspector of historical monuments. This edition offers the original French text and the English translation by Lady Mary Loyd.
the-government-inspector: The Mayor of a small Russian town gathers his officials with alarming news: a government inspector is on his way from St Petersburg, travelling incognito. Every one of them has something to hide. When two local gossips report that a mysterious young man has been staying at the inn for two weeks without paying, they decide he must be the inspector. The young man, Khlestakov, a frivolous minor clerk who has gambled away his money, is only too happy to accept their hospitality, their bribes and the attentions of the Mayor's wife and daughter.

Gogol's comedy is a merciless satire of bureaucracy, bribery, vanity and fear, in which every character is shown up by the misunderstanding. Its epigraph, "Don't blame the mirror if your face is crooked", sums up its intention.

The play was first performed at the Alexandrinsky Theatre in St Petersburg in 1836, with the support of Tsar Nicholas I, and it caused great controversy. Pushkin is said to have given Gogol the idea for its plot. This English translation, titled The Inspector-General, is by Thomas Seltzer.
swann-s-way: The narrator recalls the sleepless nights of his childhood and his anxious longing for his mother's goodnight kiss during summers in the little town of Combray. One winter day, the taste of a small cake, a madeleine, dipped in lime-blossom tea, suddenly brings that whole world back: his family, the old servant Françoise, the walks along Swann's way and the Guermantes way. The book then goes back in time to tell the story of Charles Swann, a refined man of society, and his jealous passion for Odette de Crécy, before returning to the narrator's own first love, Swann's daughter Gilberte.

Proust's long, flowing sentences explore memory, perception, desire, jealousy, art and the passing of time with extraordinary subtlety and humour. The section "Swann in Love" can be read almost as a self-contained novel.

Du côté de chez Swann was published in November 1913 by Grasset, at Proust's own expense, as the first volume of À la recherche du temps perdu. This edition offers the original French text and C. K. Scott Moncrieff's English translation, published in 1922 as the first volume of Remembrance of Things Past.
the-ladies-paradise: Denise Baudu arrives in Paris from the provincial town of Valognes with her two younger brothers, hoping for help from her uncle, a draper. But his old shop is dying, crushed by the huge department store across the street, the Ladies' Paradise, run by the ambitious and seductive Octave Mouret. Denise takes a job there as a saleswoman and discovers a world of dazzling displays, fierce rivalries and hard work, while Mouret's empire keeps growing at the expense of the neighbourhood's traders.

Zola describes the birth of modern mass retailing and consumer culture with extraordinary energy, from advertising and sales to the crowds of women shoppers. The novel weighs the excitement of progress against the human cost for the small shopkeepers, and follows a quiet, determined heroine who keeps her dignity.

Au Bonheur des Dames was published in 1883 as the eleventh novel of Zola's Rougon-Macquart cycle. The store was modelled largely on Le Bon Marché in Paris, which Zola visited while preparing the book. This edition offers the original French text and the English translation by Ernest A. Vizetelly.
the-princess-of-cleves: In the last years of the reign of Henri II, the beautiful and virtuous Mademoiselle de Chartres, carefully raised by her mother, appears at court and marries the Prince of Clèves, who loves her deeply but whom she does not love. Soon she meets the Duke of Nemours, the most handsome and admired man at court, and a passion grows between them that she fights with all her strength.

Set among the intrigues, rivalries and love affairs of the French court, the novel follows the heroine's inner struggle with remarkable psychological insight and restraint. Its famous scene in which she confides her feelings to her husband was much debated by its first readers.

La Princesse de Clèves was published anonymously in March 1678. It is often regarded as the first great French novel and a forerunner of the psychological novel. This edition offers the original French text and an English translation by an unnamed translator.
five-weeks-in-a-balloon: Dr Samuel Fergusson, a daring English explorer, announces to the Royal Geographical Society that he will cross Africa from east to west in a hydrogen balloon of his own design, the Victoria, linking up the discoveries of earlier explorers and looking for the source of the Nile. With his sceptical friend Dick Kennedy, a Scottish hunter, and his faithful servant Joe, he sets off from Zanzibar over deserts, lakes and forests.

Verne's first great adventure novel combines scientific explanation, geography and suspense, with storms, thirst, wild animals and dangerous encounters. Written from the point of view of European explorers of its time, it portrays the African peoples they meet through the stereotypes of the colonial era.

Five Weeks in a Balloon was published by Pierre-Jules Hetzel in 1863. It was Verne's first novel in what became his Extraordinary Voyages, and its success launched his career. This edition offers the original French text and an English translation published under the pseudonym "William Lackland".
atala: In eighteenth-century Louisiana, the aged and blind Chactas, of the Natchez people, tells a young Frenchman named René the story of his youth. Captured by an enemy tribe and condemned to death, he was freed by Atala, the Christian daughter of their chief, and the two fled together through forests and storms, in love, until they found refuge with an old missionary, Father Aubry. But Atala is bound by a secret that makes their love impossible.

Chateaubriand's short, lyrical tale is famous for its sweeping descriptions of American landscapes and its melancholy blend of passion, nature and religion. It presents Native Americans through the idealised, "noble savage" vision of European writers of its time.

Atala was published in 1801. In 1802 it was included in Chateaubriand's defence of Christianity, The Genius of Christianity, together with René. This English translation, by an unnamed translator, is illustrated by Gustave Doré.
the-sorrows-of-young-werther: Werther, a young man of artistic temperament, settles in the countryside near the village of Walheim and writes enthusiastic letters to his friend Wilhelm about nature, simple people and his own feelings. At a country ball he meets Charlotte, a warm and lively young woman who cares for her younger brothers and sisters, and falls in love with her at once, although she is promised to Albert, a calm and sensible man. As Werther's passion grows, his letters become ever more troubled.

Goethe's short novel, written almost entirely in Werther's letters, explores intense emotion, nature, art and despair with a new kind of inward, personal voice. It became a defining work of the German Sturm und Drang movement and influenced the Romantics.

The Sorrows of Young Werther was written in a few weeks in early 1774 and published by Weygand in Leipzig in the autumn of 1774, when Goethe was in his twenties. It was an immediate sensation across Europe and made him famous. This edition offers English and French translations; the French translation by Pierre Leroux is introduced by George Sand.
apology: In 399 BC the philosopher Socrates stands before a jury of Athenian citizens, accused by Meletus, Anytus and Lycon of failing to honour the city's gods, introducing new divinities and corrupting the young. In his defence he explains how the oracle at Delphi declared that no one was wiser than he, and how his attempts to understand this led him to question politicians, poets and craftsmen, revealing that they knew less than they believed.

Plato's account of the trial is both a moving portrait of his teacher and a powerful statement of the philosophical life: the duty to seek truth, to examine oneself and to act justly whatever the consequences. Socrates compares himself to a gadfly sent to keep the city awake.

The Apology is Plato's version of the speech Socrates gave at his trial in 399 BC, after which he was condemned to death. This edition offers the classic English translation by Benjamin Jowett, with his introduction.
symposium: To celebrate the poet Agathon's victory in a drama competition, a group of friends meet for an evening of conversation and wine, and agree that each will give a speech in praise of Eros, the god of love. Phaedrus, Pausanias, the doctor Eryximachus, the comic playwright Aristophanes and Agathon himself each give their view, and then Socrates recounts what he learned about love from a wise woman, Diotima. Late in the evening the drunken Alcibiades arrives and delivers a startling speech in praise of Socrates.

Mixing philosophy, comedy and drama, the dialogue explores love in all its forms, from physical desire to the love of wisdom and beauty itself. Aristophanes' myth of the divided humans searching for their other halves and Diotima's "ladder of love" are among its most famous passages.

The Symposium was written by Plato in the fourth century BC and is one of his most admired dialogues for both its ideas and its literary art. This edition offers the classic English translation by Benjamin Jowett, with his introduction.
hedda-gabler: Hedda, the beautiful and proud daughter of the late General Gabler, has just returned from a long wedding journey with her husband, George Tesman, a well-meaning but dull young scholar who hopes for a university post. Settled in their new villa, she is already bored. When her old schoolfellow Thea Elvsted arrives with news of Eilert Lovborg, a brilliant and once dissolute writer who was close to Hedda in the past and is now Tesman's rival, Hedda sees a chance to shape someone's destiny, while the worldly Judge Brack watches with interest.

Ibsen's drama creates a fascinating, enigmatic heroine, frustrated by the narrow role society allows her and by her own fears and pride. Tight, realistic dialogue and rising tension drive the play towards its climax.

Hedda Gabler was published in Copenhagen in December 1890 and first performed at the Residenztheater in Munich on 31 January 1891. This English translation is by Edmund Gosse and William Archer, with an introduction by Archer.
the-school-for-scandal: Lady Sneerwell presides over a society of scandalmongers, including the aptly named Sir Benjamin Backbite and Crabtree, who delight in ruining reputations. Old Sir Peter Teazle quarrels constantly with his young and extravagant wife. Meanwhile, Sir Oliver Surface returns from India and decides to test his two nephews: Joseph, who is admired for his fine moral sentiments, and his younger brother Charles, a cheerful spendthrift with a reputation for dissipation.
Sheridan's comedy of manners is a sparkling satire of gossip, hypocrisy and appearances, full of witty dialogue and brilliantly constructed comic scenes, culminating in the famous "screen scene".
The School for Scandal was first performed at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, in London on 8 May 1777. It was an immediate success.
barnaby-rudge: In 1775, at the Maypole inn near Epping Forest, regulars recall an unsolved murder committed twenty-two years before at the Warren, the house of the Haredale family. Barnaby Rudge, an innocent and good-hearted young man of simple mind, wanders the countryside with his mother and his talking raven, Grip. Around them move the honest locksmith Gabriel Varden and his pretty daughter Dolly, the scheming Sir John Chester and his son, and the rough ostler Hugh. Five years later, in 1780, the anti-Catholic Gordon Riots break out in London, and all their lives are caught up in the violence.

Dickens combines a family mystery, romance and comedy with powerful scenes of mob violence, burning houses and the storming of Newgate prison. The novel explores fanaticism, the manipulation of crowds and the bonds between parents and children.

Barnaby Rudge: A Tale of the Riots of 'Eighty was serialised from February to November 1841 in Dickens's weekly Master Humphrey's Clock and published as a book the same year. It was the first of his two historical novels, the other being A Tale of Two Cities.
the-ambassadors: Lambert Strether, a cultivated but unadventurous man from Woollett, Massachusetts, is engaged to the wealthy widow Mrs Newsome. She sends him to Paris to rescue her son Chad, who has stayed in Europe too long, from an entanglement she assumes to be scandalous, and bring him home to run the family business. Guided by the perceptive Maria Gostrey and accompanied by his gloomy friend Waymarsh, Strether finds Chad wonderfully changed, meets the charming Madame de Vionnet, and begins to wonder what he himself has missed in life.

Told almost entirely through Strether's point of view, the novel is a subtle comedy of perception and misunderstanding, contrasting American moral certainty with the beauty and complexity of European life. Its famous advice, "Live all you can", sums up Strether's awakening.
The Ambassadors was serialised in the North American Review throughout 1903 and published in book form the same year. Henry James considered it his best novel.
the-sea-wolf: Humphrey Van Weyden, a gentleman scholar and literary critic from San Francisco, is thrown into the sea when his ferry sinks in the fog. He is picked up by the Ghost, a schooner bound for the seal-hunting grounds of the North Pacific, whose captain, Wolf Larsen, refuses to set him ashore and makes him a cabin boy. Larsen is physically powerful, well read and utterly ruthless, and he delights in debating philosophy with his reluctant passenger, until another survivor, the writer Maud Brewster, comes aboard.

London's novel is both a gripping sea adventure and a duel of ideas about strength, morality and the meaning of life. Life on the ship is harsh and violent, and Humphrey must learn to survive and to discover his own strength.
The Sea-Wolf was serialised in The Century Magazine from January to November 1904 and published as a book the same year. Its first print run sold out before publication.
the-thirty-nine-steps: In the months before the First World War, Richard Hannay, a mining engineer recently back from Africa, is bored with life in London. One evening a nervous neighbour, Franklin Scudder, tells him of a plot by a secret organisation, the Black Stone, to steal British military plans and provoke war. A few days later Hannay finds Scudder murdered in his flat. Suspected of the crime and pursued by the conspirators, he takes Scudder's coded notebook and flees to Scotland, across the moors of Galloway.

Buchan's short, fast-paced novel set the pattern for the modern spy thriller: an ordinary man on the run, disguises, chases, narrow escapes and a race against time. Hannay's resourcefulness and humour carry the reader through.

The Thirty-Nine Steps first appeared in Blackwood's Magazine in August and September 1915 and was published as a book in October 1915. It was the first of five novels featuring Richard Hannay, and was adapted into a famous 1935 film by Alfred Hitchcock.
the-princess-and-the-goblin: Eight-year-old Princess Irene lives in a large house on a mountainside, cared for by her nurse Lootie while her father the king travels his kingdom. Deep in the mines beneath the mountain live the goblins, who hate the people above and come out at night. Exploring the house one rainy day, Irene finds a hidden stair leading to a beautiful, ancient lady who says she is her great-great-grandmother. Meanwhile Curdie, a brave young miner, overhears the goblins plotting against the princess.

MacDonald's fairy tale mixes adventure, humour and gentle mystery with deeper themes of faith, courage and trust in what cannot be seen. Its imaginative world and spiritual depth made it a classic of children's fantasy.

The Princess and the Goblin was first serialised in the magazine Good Words for the Young from November 1870 and published as a book in 1872, with illustrations by Arthur Hughes. It was followed by The Princess and Curdie.
much-ado-about-nothing: Don Pedro, Prince of Aragon, and his soldiers return from war to the house of Leonato, governor of Messina. The young lord Claudio falls in love with Leonato's gentle daughter Hero, and a wedding is quickly arranged. Meanwhile Hero's cousin Beatrice and the soldier Benedick, who both mock love and marriage, carry on their "merry war" of wit, and their friends decide to trick them into falling in love. But Don Pedro's resentful brother, Don John, is plotting to wreck Claudio's happiness.

Shakespeare's comedy mixes sparkling verbal sparring with deception, slander and reconciliation. Beatrice and Benedick are among his most beloved characters, and the bumbling constable Dogberry adds broad comedy.

Much Ado About Nothing is thought to have been written in 1598–1599 and was first printed in quarto in 1600. This edition offers the English text (from the First Folio, in its original spelling) and the French translation by François Guizot.
the-merchant-of-venice: Bassanio, a young Venetian with no money, wants to court Portia, a rich and clever heiress of Belmont. His devoted friend Antonio, a merchant whose fortune is tied up in ships at sea, borrows three thousand ducats for him from the Jewish moneylender Shylock, whom he has often insulted. Shylock agrees to the loan on one condition: if it is not repaid on time, he may take a pound of Antonio's flesh.

The play mixes romantic comedy, with Portia's caskets and her disguise as a lawyer, and a dark drama of revenge, mercy and justice. Its portrayal of Shylock and the treatment he receives reflect the antisemitism of Shakespeare's time; Shylock's famous speech asking "Hath not a Jew eyes?" has long fuelled debate about how the play should be read and performed.

The Merchant of Venice is believed to have been written between 1596 and 1598 and was first printed in 1600. This edition offers the English text (from the First Folio, in its original spelling), the French translation by François Guizot and the German translation by August Wilhelm von Schlegel.
julius-caesar: Julius Caesar returns to Rome in triumph, and some senators fear he means to make himself king. The envious Cassius persuades the noble and idealistic Brutus, Caesar's friend, to join a conspiracy against him. Ignoring warnings and omens, Caesar goes to the Senate on the Ides of March. After the assassination, Mark Antony turns the people against the conspirators with a brilliant funeral speech, and war follows.

Shakespeare's Roman tragedy explores power, honour, friendship, persuasion and the unforeseen consequences of political violence. Although named after Caesar, the play centres largely on Brutus and his moral dilemma.

Julius Caesar was written in 1599 and was among the first plays performed at the new Globe Theatre; a Swiss traveller, Thomas Platter, saw it there in September 1599. Shakespeare drew mainly on Thomas North's translation of Plutarch's Lives. The play was first printed in the First Folio of 1623. This edition offers the English text (from the First Folio, in its original spelling), the French translation by François Guizot and the German translation by August Wilhelm von Schlegel.
as-you-like-it: Duke Frederick has usurped his brother's dukedom, and the old Duke lives in exile in the Forest of Arden with his loyal followers. When Frederick banishes his niece Rosalind as well, she escapes to the forest disguised as a young man, Ganymede, with her cousin Celia and the jester Touchstone. There she meets Orlando, a young man fleeing his cruel brother, who has fallen in love with her and is hanging poems on the trees.

This pastoral comedy plays with disguise, love and the contrast between court and country life. Rosalind is one of Shakespeare's wittiest heroines, and the melancholy Jaques speaks the famous lines beginning "All the world's a stage".

As You Like It was written around 1599 and first printed in the First Folio of 1623. This edition offers the English text (from the First Folio, in its original spelling), the French translation by François Guizot and the German translation by August Wilhelm von Schlegel.
the-taming-of-the-shrew: A drunken tinker, Christopher Sly, is tricked by a lord into believing he is a nobleman, and a play is performed for him. In Padua, the wealthy Baptista will not let his gentle younger daughter Bianca marry, despite her many suitors, until her elder sister Katherina, famous for her fierce temper, is married. Petruchio, a gentleman from Verona who has come "to wive it wealthily", decides to woo and tame her.

The play is full of farce, disguises and verbal sparring. Its central idea of a husband "taming" his wife reflects the attitudes of its time, and critics and audiences have long debated how seriously it is meant to be taken.
The Taming of the Shrew was written between 1590 and 1592 and first printed in the First Folio of 1623. This edition follows the First Folio text in its original spelling.
ghosts: Mrs Helen Alving, the widow of a respected captain and chamberlain, is about to open an orphanage built in her husband's memory. Pastor Manders, her old friend and adviser, arrives for the ceremony, and her beloved son Oswald, a painter, has come home from Paris. As the young maid Regina and her father, the carpenter Engstrand, pursue their own plans, Mrs Alving reveals to Manders the truth about her marriage, and the past returns to haunt them all.

Ibsen's drama attacks hypocrisy, empty duty and the dead ideas and conventions that weigh on the living, the "ghosts" of the title. Its frank treatment of subjects such as hereditary disease and the failures of marriage made it one of the most controversial plays of its century.

Ghosts was published in Copenhagen in December 1881 and caused a scandal; theatres in Scandinavia refused to stage it, and its first performance took place in Chicago in 1882, in a production for Scandinavian immigrants. This edition offers the English translation by William Archer and the German translation by Marie von Borch.
an-enemy-of-the-people: Dr Thomas Stockmann is medical officer of the baths that have brought new prosperity to his small coastal town. When he discovers that the water is contaminated and endangering visitors' health, he expects to be thanked for his discovery. Instead his brother Peter, the town's mayor, the local newspaper editor Hovstad and the printer Aslaksen, speaking for the respectable majority, turn against him to protect the town's finances.

Ibsen's play is a sharp drama about truth, public interest, the press and the tyranny of the majority. Dr Stockmann, idealistic, stubborn and sometimes comic, ends by declaring that the strongest man in the world is the one who stands most alone.
An Enemy of the People was written in 1882 and first performed at the Christiania Theatre in January 1883. This English translation is by R. Farquharson Sharp.
lady-windermere-s-fan: Lady Windermere, young, happily married and strict in her principles, is preparing for her birthday ball when she learns from the gossiping Duchess of Berwick that her husband has been visiting a woman of doubtful reputation, Mrs Erlynne, and giving her money. To her horror, Lord Windermere insists on inviting Mrs Erlynne to the ball. Hurt and angry, Lady Windermere is tempted by the declarations of the charming Lord Darlington.

Behind the glittering epigrams of high society, Wilde's first great comedy questions the hypocrisy of moral judgements and the idea that people can be simply divided into good and bad. Its subtitle is "A Play About a Good Woman".
Lady Windermere's Fan was first performed on 20 February 1892 at the St James's Theatre in London, produced by the actor-manager George Alexander, who had encouraged Wilde to write it.
arms-and-the-man: In 1885, during the war between Serbia and Bulgaria, Raina Petkoff, the daughter of a wealthy Bulgarian family, dreams of her fiancé Sergius, the dashing hero of a cavalry charge. That night a fugitive soldier fighting for the Serbs climbs into her bedroom: Captain Bluntschli, a practical Swiss mercenary who carries chocolates rather than ammunition. She hides him, and when the war ends he unexpectedly returns.
Shaw's comedy mocks romantic illusions about war, heroism and love, contrasting Sergius's empty gallantry with Bluntschli's common sense. Raina calls him her "chocolate cream soldier".
Arms and the Man was first performed on 21 April 1894 at the Avenue Theatre in London. This edition includes an introduction by an unnamed writer.
she-stoops-to-conquer: Young Charles Marlow travels to the country to meet Kate Hardcastle, the bride his father has chosen for him. Marlow is painfully shy with respectable women but bold with servants and barmaids. Thanks to a joke by Kate's mischievous stepbrother, Tony Lumpkin, Marlow and his friend Hastings take the Hardcastles' house for an inn and treat her father like a landlord. Kate seizes the chance to "stoop to conquer", pretending to be a barmaid to win his heart.

Goldsmith's comedy of mistakes, disguise and good humour mocks pretension and celebrates natural feeling. Its comic characters, from the bumbling Mr Hardcastle to Tony Lumpkin, keep the action lively through one long night.

She Stoops to Conquer; or, The Mistakes of a Night was first performed at Covent Garden Theatre in London on 15 March 1773 and was a great success. Goldsmith dedicated the published play to Samuel Johnson.
resurrection: Prince Dmitri Nekhludoff, a wealthy landowner, is called to serve on a jury in Moscow. Among the accused in a poisoning case he recognises Maslova, once known as Katusha, the young girl he seduced and abandoned years earlier at his aunts' estate, and whose fall into poverty and prostitution began with that betrayal. When a careless error by the court sends her to hard labour in Siberia, Nekhludoff resolves to win her release and to atone for what he has done.

Tolstoy's last novel follows its hero through courts, prisons and convict convoys, and is a severe criticism of the justice system, the official Church, private ownership of land and the indifference of the privileged classes. Its theme is moral awakening, the "resurrection" of the title, told in a plain and direct style.

Resurrection was published in serial form in the magazine Niva in 1899 and appeared as a book at the end of that year. Tolstoy gave the proceeds to help the Doukhobors, a persecuted religious community, emigrate to Canada. This English translation is by Louise Maude, who translated many of Tolstoy's works with her husband Aylmer Maude.
the-cossacks: Dmitri Olénin, a young Moscow nobleman weary of idle society life, leaves for the Caucasus as a cadet and is quartered in a Cossack village on the Terek River. He is drawn to the free, physical life of the Cossacks, goes hunting with the old hunter Uncle Eróshka, befriends the young warrior Lukáshka and falls in love with Maryánka, the girl Lukáshka hopes to marry.

The short novel contrasts the artificial life of the city with the natural world of the mountains and the Cossack community, and explores a young man's search for happiness and self-sacrifice. Tolstoy drew on his own years in the Caucasus in the early 1850s.
The Cossacks was published in 1863 in the journal The Russian Messenger. This English translation is by Louise and Aylmer Maude.
poor-folk: Makar Alexievitch Dievushkin, a middle-aged copying clerk in a St Petersburg government office, lives in a corner of a crowded lodging house. Across the courtyard lives Barbara (Varvara) Alexievna, a young woman who has lost her family and her home. The two write to each other almost every day, describing their poverty, their memories and their small joys, while Makar spends what little he has on gifts for her.

Dostoevsky's first novel is told entirely in letters. It shows the humiliation and dignity of the "little man" of the city, the power of money over human relations, and the tenderness that survives in hard conditions.

Poor Folk was published in January 1846 in the St Petersburg Collection, an almanac, and was praised by the critic Vissarion Belinsky, which launched Dostoevsky's literary career. This English translation is by C. J. Hogarth.
mother: Pelagueya Nilovna Vlasova, widow of a brutal and drunken factory worker, lives in a workers' settlement with her son Pavel. When Pavel gives up drink, starts reading forbidden books and gathers young workers and intellectuals in their home, she is at first afraid for him. Little by little she grows close to his comrades, learns to understand their ideas and begins to take part in their secret work.

Gorky's novel describes the hard life of factory workers and the growth of the socialist movement in Russia, and centres on a simple, religious woman's awakening to political consciousness. It is often regarded as a forerunner of Soviet socialist realism.

Gorky wrote Mother in 1906 while in the United States. It first appeared in English in Appleton's Magazine in 1906, before its Russian publication in 1907. The novel drew on real events, the workers' May Day demonstration of 1902 in Sormovo, near Nizhny Novgorod. This edition reproduces an anonymous English translation.
the-lady-with-the-dog-and-other-stories: In the title story, Dmitri Gurov, a Moscow banker unhappily married and used to brief affairs, notices a young woman walking her dog on the seafront at Yalta. She is Anna Sergeyevna, also married and holidaying alone. What begins as another passing adventure turns into a love that neither of them can escape when they return to their ordinary lives. The volume gathers this story with other tales by Chekhov.

Chekhov's stories observe ordinary people with sympathy and without moral judgement, and often leave their endings open. They are known for their economy, their quiet irony and their attention to small details of everyday life.
The Lady with the Dog was first published in December 1899 in the journal Russkaya Mysl. This collection belongs to the series of Chekhov's tales translated into English by Constance Garnett.
the-way-we-live-now: Augustus Melmotte, a financier of uncertain origins, arrives in London and quickly becomes the most talked-about man in the city, attracting investors and noble directors to a scheme for a great American railway. Around him circle Lady Carbury, a widow who writes books to support her spendthrift son Sir Felix; Felix himself, who courts Melmotte's daughter Marie for her fortune; Lady Carbury's daughter Hetta, torn between her cousin Roger Carbury and the young engineer Paul Montague; and Mrs Hurtle, an American woman from Paul's past.

Trollope's long novel is a broad satire of the greed and dishonesty he saw in English commercial, political and literary life, and of the new power of speculative finance. Its portraits of Melmotte and of the Jewish banker Brehgert reflect the antisemitic attitudes of its time.
The novel was inspired by the financial scandals of the early 1870s. It was first published in twenty monthly parts from February 1874 to September 1875, and in book form by Chapman and Hall in 1875.
mcteague: McTeague, a huge and simple former miner, runs a dental parlour on Polk Street in San Francisco. His friend Marcus Schouler brings his cousin Trina Sieppe to him for treatment, and McTeague falls in love with her. Soon after their engagement Trina wins five thousand dollars in a lottery. As the couple settle into married life among neighbours such as old Mr Grannis, who keeps a small dog hospital, the shy Miss Baker, the junk dealer Zerkow and the servant Maria Macapa, money, jealousy and resentment begin to take hold.

McTeague is a classic of American naturalism: Norris sought to show how heredity, environment and greed shape and degrade human lives. The novel's portrait of Zerkow draws on antisemitic stereotypes of its time.
McTeague was published in 1899. It was adapted for the cinema as McTeague (1916) and as Erich von Stroheim's Greed (1924).
the-legend-of-sleepy-hollow: Around 1790, in the quiet glen of Sleepy Hollow near the Dutch settlement of Tarry Town on the Hudson, the people love ghost stories, above all the tale of a Headless Horseman. The bookish and superstitious schoolmaster Ichabod Crane hopes to win the hand of Katrina Van Tassel, the daughter of a wealthy farmer, but he has a rival in the strong and mischievous Brom Bones. One autumn night, after a party at the Van Tassels', Ichabod rides home alone.

Irving's tale mixes humour, local folklore and the supernatural, and offers an affectionate, ironic picture of the old Dutch communities of New York. The story is presented as found among the papers of the fictional historian Diedrich Knickerbocker.

The Legend of Sleepy Hollow appeared in 1820 in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent., a collection of essays and stories that Irving published in instalments in 1819 and 1820 under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon. He wrote it while living in Birmingham, England.
life-on-the-mississippi: Twain begins with the history of the Mississippi and his boyhood dream of working on the river. He then tells how, as a young man before the Civil War, he persuaded the experienced pilot Horace Bixby to take him on as a "cub" and learned to read the ever-changing river. In the second part he describes a journey made many years later by steamboat from St Louis to New Orleans and later on the upper river, observing how the towns and the river trade have changed.
Part memoir and part travel book, it mixes humour, tall tales, history and description. Some passages use the racial language and attitudes of its time towards Black and Native Americans.
The chapters on Twain's apprenticeship first appeared as "Old Times on the Mississippi" in The Atlantic Monthly. The complete book was published in 1883.
little-lord-fauntleroy: Cedric Errol lives modestly in New York with his widowed mother, whom he calls "Dearest", and his friends include Mr Hobbs the grocer and Dick the bootblack. One day a lawyer, Mr Havisham, arrives with news from England: Cedric's grandfather, the Earl of Dorincourt, who had disowned his son for marrying an American, has lost all his sons, and Cedric is now Lord Fauntleroy, heir to the title and a great estate. He travels to England to live with the old earl, a proud and bitter man.
Burnett's story contrasts the boy's open, generous nature with the selfishness of the aristocratic grandfather, and shows the power of kindness to change those around it.

Little Lord Fauntleroy was published as a serial in St. Nicholas Magazine from November 1885 to October 1886, then as a book by Scribner's in New York in 1886, with illustrations by Reginald Birch. In these illustrations and in the stage play that followed, Cedric wears long curls, velvet knee breeches and a lace collar, later known as a "Lord Fauntleroy collar".
captains-courageous: Harvey Cheyne, a boy of about fifteen and the son of a wealthy California railroad magnate, is travelling to Europe on a transatlantic liner when he falls overboard off the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. He is rescued by the crew of the fishing schooner We're Here, from Gloucester, Massachusetts. Its captain, Disko Troop, does not believe his stories of wealth and will not cut short the fishing season, so he offers Harvey a place in the crew alongside his son Dan, Long Jack, Manuel, Salters, Penn and the others.

Kipling's novel follows Harvey's transformation through hard work, danger and comradeship at sea, and gives a detailed picture of the life of the cod fishermen of the North Atlantic. Its portrait of the ship's Black cook and some of the dialogue use the racial language of its time.
Captains Courageous was serialised in McClure's Magazine from November 1896 and published as a book in 1897.
martin-eden: Martin Eden, a rough young sailor from a working-class background, rescues Arthur Morse from a fight and is invited to dinner with his wealthy family in Oakland. There he meets Arthur's sister Ruth, a university student, and falls in love with her and with the world of books she represents. Determined to become worthy of her, he throws himself into self-education and resolves to earn his living as a writer, struggling against poverty and rejection, and finding a friend in the poet Brissenden.

Often described as London's most autobiographical novel, Martin Eden draws on his own struggle for education and literary success. It explores class, ambition, love and the nature of success, and London himself presented the book as an attack on individualism. Some passages reflect the racial ideas and language of its time.

Martin Eden was serialised in The Pacific Monthly from September 1908 to September 1909 and published as a book by Macmillan in 1909. Ruth Morse is said to have been modelled on Mabel Applegarth, London's first love, and Brissenden on his friend the poet George Sterling. This edition also offers the Italian translation by Gian Dàuli.
the-memoirs-of-sherlock-holmes: In these stories Dr Watson recounts more cases of his friend Sherlock Holmes, the consulting detective of Baker Street. Holmes investigates the disappearance of the racehorse Silver Blaze and the murder of its trainer, a gruesome parcel received by a quiet lady in Croydon, and other mysteries. Watson also learns about Holmes's early life, including his first case and his brother Mycroft. The collection ends with Holmes's confrontation with Professor Moriarty, the criminal mastermind.
Conan Doyle's stories combine logical deduction, vivid characters and atmosphere, and helped to define the modern detective story.

The twelve stories first appeared in The Strand Magazine from December 1892 to December 1893 and were collected in book form at the end of 1893. The first British edition left out "The Adventure of the Cardboard Box", which the first American edition included; this edition includes it.
the-first-men-in-the-moon: Bedford, a businessman in financial difficulty, retires to the Kent coast to write a play and meets Cavor, an absent-minded scientist who has invented Cavorite, a substance that blocks gravity. Seeing a fortune to be made, Bedford joins Cavor in building a sphere coated with it, and the two men travel to the Moon. There they discover a strange landscape and the Selenites, insect-like creatures who live in vast caverns beneath the surface and are ruled by the Grand Lunar.

Told by Bedford, the novel combines scientific adventure, humour and social satire, contrasting Bedford's greed with Cavor's pure curiosity and using the society of the Selenites to comment on human civilisation.
The First Men in the Moon was serialised in The Strand Magazine from December 1900 to August 1901, with illustrations by Claude Shepperson, and published as a book in 1901.
at-the-back-of-the-north-wind: Diamond is the son of a coachman and sleeps in a loft above the coach-house, close to the horse old Diamond, whose name he shares. One night the North Wind, who appears to him as a beautiful and sometimes frightening lady, speaks to him through a hole in the wall and begins to carry him on journeys over London and beyond. Back in the everyday world, Diamond's family faces hard times, and the gentle boy helps those around him, among them the crossing-sweeper Nanny, her friend Jim and the kind Mr Raymond.

MacDonald's book mixes fantasy and realistic scenes of poverty in Victorian London, and is full of songs, dreams and stories within the story. It reflects on goodness, suffering and death through the eyes of a child.
At the Back of the North Wind was serialised in the children's magazine Good Words for the Young from 1868 and published as a book in 1871.
she: Ludwig Horace Holly, a Cambridge scholar, becomes guardian of the young Leo Vincey, whose dying father leaves him a mysterious iron box to be opened on his twenty-fifth birthday. Its contents, including an ancient inscribed potsherd, tell of a distant ancestor and a woman in Africa. Holly, Leo and their servant Job set out for the east coast of Africa, survive a shipwreck, and are taken by the Amahagger people, guided by the old man Billali, to the ruins of Kôr and their queen Ayesha, "She-who-must-be-obeyed".

Haggard's romance combines adventure, the supernatural and meditations on love, power, immortality and death. Its picture of Africa and of the Amahagger relies on the colonial and racial stereotypes of its time.
She was serialised in The Graphic in London and Harper's Weekly in New York from October 1886 to January 1887, with illustrations by E. K. Johnson, and then published as a book in 1887.
the-master-of-ballantrae: In 1745, when Prince Charles Edward Stuart lands in Scotland, the Durie family of Durrisdeer decides to keep a foot in each camp: one son will join the Jacobite rising, the other will stay loyal to King George. The elder, James, the brilliant and charming Master of Ballantrae, rides out with the rebels, while his quiet younger brother Henry stays at home, inherits his place and marries Alison Graeme, the heiress whom James had been expected to marry. The story is told by Ephraim Mackellar, the family's loyal steward.

Stevenson's novel is a dark study of rivalry, jealousy and moral ambiguity between two brothers, told by a narrator whose judgement is not always reliable. Its action moves from Scotland to India, the Americas and the wilderness of New York. The Indian servant Secundra Dass and the Native American characters are depicted through the stereotypes of the period.

The Master of Ballantrae was serialised in Scribner's Magazine from November 1888 to October 1889. Stevenson finished it in 1889 during his travels in the Pacific, and it was published in book form by Cassell in London the same year.
nostromo: In the imaginary South American republic of Costaguana, the port of Sulaco depends on the San Tomé silver mine, which Charles Gould, an Englishman born in the country, has revived with the backing of American capital. When a new revolution breaks out under General Montero, the silver must be kept out of the rebels' hands. The task falls to Nostromo, the admired Italian foreman of the dock workers, who is seen as incorruptible, together with the sceptical journalist Martin Decoud. Around them are Mrs Emilia Gould, the embittered Dr Monygham, the old Garibaldino Giorgio Viola and Antonia Avellanos.
