Conrad's complex novel moves back and forth in time and between many characters. It examines material interests, colonial and foreign investment, political violence and corruption, and the way public reputation and private integrity can diverge.
Nostromo was serialised in T.P.'s Weekly from January to October 1904 and published as a book the same year.
greenmantle: In November 1915, Richard Hannay, recovering from a wound received at the battle of Loos, is called to the Foreign Office and asked to investigate a German plan to raise a religious uprising across the Muslim world in support of the Ottoman Empire, centred on a mysterious prophet known as Greenmantle. With his friend Sandy Arbuthnot, the American John Blenkiron and the old South African scout Peter Pienaar, he travels in disguise through wartime Germany to Constantinople, facing the brutal Colonel Stumm and the mysterious Hilda von Einem.

Buchan's second Hannay novel is a fast-paced spy story set during the First World War, ending at the battle of Erzerum in eastern Anatolia in 1916. It reflects the wartime British outlook of its time, and its descriptions of Muslims, Turks, Germans and other peoples rely on period stereotypes.
Greenmantle was published by Hodder & Stoughton in London in 1916. It is the second of the five novels featuring Richard Hannay, after The Thirty-Nine Steps (1915) and before Mr Standfast (1919).
the-story-of-the-treasure-seekers: After their mother's death and the failure of their father's business, the six Bastable children, Dora, Oswald, Dicky, Alice, Noel and Horace Octavius, known as H. O., live in a modest house on the Lewisham Road in London. Determined to restore the family fortunes, they try one plan after another: digging for treasure, becoming detectives, writing poetry for the newspapers, selling sherry and looking for a princess to rescue, often with the help, or hindrance, of Albert-next-door.

The story is told by one of the children, who claims not to reveal which one, but whose identity soon becomes obvious. Nesbit's humour and her realistic, unsentimental portrait of children at play give the book its lively voice.

The Bastable stories first appeared between 1894 and 1899 in several periodicals, among them The Pall Mall Magazine and the Windsor Magazine, and were collected in book form in 1899. Their adventures continue in The Wouldbegoods (1901).
carmilla: Laura lives with her father in an isolated castle in Styria. One evening a carriage accident brings to their door a young woman of strange beauty, Carmilla, who stays with them while her mother continues her journey. The two girls become close friends, though Carmilla's languid moods, her secrecy about her past and her passionate affection trouble Laura. At the same time, young women in the surrounding countryside fall victim to a mysterious illness, and Laura herself begins to have terrifying dreams.

Le Fanu's novella is a classic of Gothic horror. Its atmosphere of dread, its unreliable sense of reality and the intense relationship between the two young women made Carmilla the model for many later female vampires.

Carmilla was serialised in the magazine The Dark Blue from December 1871 to March 1872 and then appeared in Le Fanu's collection In a Glass Darkly (1872), presented as a case from the papers of the physician Dr Martin Hesselius. It predates Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897) by twenty-five years and is often cited as an influence on it.
the-king-in-yellow: The first four stories, "The Repairer of Reputations", "The Mask", "The Court of the Dragon" and "The Yellow Sign", are linked by The King in Yellow, an imaginary play whose second act brings ruin to anyone who reads it, by the mysterious Yellow Sign and by the lost city of Carcosa. The later stories turn away from horror towards romance and the life of young American art students in Paris, where Chambers himself had studied.

The book mixes the supernatural, fantasy and sentimental fiction. Its weird tales, with their sense of creeping madness, influenced later writers of horror, among them H. P. Lovecraft. The opening story describes a future America with racist and antisemitic policies, seen through the eyes of a disturbed narrator.
The King in Yellow was published in 1895 by F. Tennyson Neely in New York and by Chatto & Windus in London.
the-canterville-ghost: Hiram B. Otis, the American minister in London, buys Canterville Chase from Lord Canterville, who warns him that the house is haunted by the ghost of Sir Simon de Canterville. The practical Otis family, his wife Lucretia, their eldest son Washington, their daughter Virginia and the mischievous twins, are not impressed: they scrub away the ancient bloodstain with Pinkerton's Champion Stain Remover and offer the ghost oil for his rattling chains. Humiliated, Sir Simon tries his most terrifying performances, with little success.

Wilde's story is a comic tale of the supernatural that gently mocks both English tradition and American practicality, before turning to a more tender theme of compassion and forgiveness through the character of Virginia.
The Canterville Ghost was first published in two parts in the magazine The Court and Society Review in February and March 1887. It was the first of Wilde's stories to be published.
major-barbara: Lady Britomart Undershaft summons her grown-up children, Stephen, Sarah and Barbara, to meet their father, Andrew Undershaft, from whom she has long been separated. Undershaft is an immensely rich manufacturer of cannons and explosives. Barbara is a Major in the Salvation Army, working among the poor of London, and she is engaged to Adolphus Cusins, a professor of Greek. Father and daughter make a bargain: he will visit her Salvation Army shelter if she will visit his munitions works.

Shaw's comedy of ideas debates religion, charity, poverty, money and power, and questions whether good can be done with wealth gained from weapons and alcohol. Its arguments, sharp dialogue and paradoxes are typical of Shaw's drama.
Major Barbara was first performed on 28 November 1905 at the Court Theatre in London, in a production by J. E. Vedrenne and Harley Granville-Barker, who also played Cusins. It was published in 1907.
the-black-arrow: In fifteenth-century England, as the houses of York and Lancaster fight for the throne, young Dick Shelton is the ward of the powerful and unscrupulous Sir Daniel Brackley. A band of outlaws known as the Black Arrow, led by Ellis Duckworth, has sworn revenge on Sir Daniel, and their messages suggest that he was responsible for the death of Dick's father. Dick also befriends a young companion named John Matcham, who is not what he seems, and becomes involved in Sir Daniel's schemes concerning the heiress Joanna Sedley.

Stevenson's historical adventure novel is full of ambushes, escapes, disguises and battles, and shows the violence and shifting loyalties of the civil war. Among its characters is the young Richard of Gloucester, the future Richard III.
The Black Arrow was first published as a serial in the weekly Young Folks from June to October 1883, under the pseudonym "Captain George North", and appeared in book form in 1888.
the-toilers-of-the-sea: Gilliatt, a solitary and mistrusted fisherman of Guernsey, loves Déruchette, the niece of the shipowner Mess Lethierry. Lethierry's pride is the Durande, one of the first steamships in the Channel Islands. When the ship is wrecked on the dangerous Douvres rocks, through the scheming of its captain Clubin, Lethierry is ruined, and Déruchette promises to marry the man who brings back the engine. Gilliatt sets out alone to the reef, where he must fight storms, hunger and a giant octopus.

Hugo's novel celebrates human labour, courage and endurance against the forces of nature, and contrasts the grandeur of the sea with the narrow judgements of island society. Its long descriptions of the ocean, the rocks and the storm are among its most famous pages.

The Toilers of the Sea was published in 1866, during Hugo's exile in Guernsey. He dedicated it to the island, "the rock of hospitality and liberty". This edition reproduces the English translation by W. Moy Thomas, as completed for the Everyman's Library edition of 1911.
lost-illusions: In Angoulême, Lucien Chardon, a handsome and gifted young poet, and his friend David Séchard, a printer who loves Lucien's sister Eve, dream of success. Lucien is taken up by the cultivated Mme de Bargeton, Louise de Negrepelisse, and follows her to Paris. There, poor and ambitious, he is drawn into the world of newspapers and theatres, alongside the journalist Lousteau and the actress Coralie. Meanwhile in Angoulême, David struggles to perfect an invention while his rivals, the Cointet brothers, and the lawyer Petit-Claud plot against him.

Balzac's novel portrays the conflict between talent and ambition, the power of money, and the corruption of the press, publishing and literary life. It contrasts the patient, honest work of David with Lucien's weakness and hunger for glory.

Lost Illusions was written and published in three parts between 1837 and 1843: Two Poets (1837), A Distinguished Provincial at Paris (1839) and Eve and David (1843). It forms part of Balzac's Human Comedy, and its story continues in Scenes from a Courtesan's Life. This edition contains all three parts in the English translation by Ellen Marriage.
phaedra: In Troezen, Phaedra, wife of the hero Theseus, is wasting away from a secret love for Hippolytus, Theseus's son by another woman. Hippolytus, for his part, loves the young princess Aricia, whom his father has forbidden to marry. When news arrives that Theseus has died, Phaedra, urged on by her nurse Oenone, confesses her passion to Hippolytus. Then Theseus returns.
Racine's tragedy, written in alexandrine verse in the original, is a concentrated study of passion, guilt and fate. Racine drew on Euripides' Hippolytus and on Seneca's Phaedra.

The play was first performed on 1 January 1677 at the Hôtel de Bourgogne in Paris, under the title Phèdre et Hippolyte; Racine adopted the shorter title Phèdre in 1687. Its premiere was overshadowed by a rival play on the same subject by Nicolas Pradon, staged two days later. This verse translation is by Robert Bruce Boswell.
volpone: In Venice, the wealthy and childless Volpone, "the Fox", pretends to be gravely ill. His clever parasite Mosca persuades three would-be heirs, the lawyer Voltore, the old miser Corbaccio and the merchant Corvino, that each will be named in the will, and they bring ever richer presents to the supposed deathbed. Their greed leads them to sacrifice everything, including Corbaccio's son Bonario and Corvino's wife Celia, while the English traveller Sir Politick Would-be and his wife add a comic sub-plot.

Jonson's comedy is a merciless satire of greed, lust and hypocrisy, in which the characters bear the names of animals: Volpone the fox, Mosca the fly, Voltore the vulture, and Corbaccio and Corvino, the big and the little raven.
Volpone was first performed by the King's Men at the Globe Theatre, probably in 1606. It was published in quarto in 1607 and included in The Workes of Benjamin Jonson in 1616.
typhoon: Captain MacWhirr commands the Nan-Shan, a British-built steamer sailing under the Siamese flag, bound for the Chinese port of Fu-chau with some two hundred Chinese labourers returning home after years of work, each with a box holding his savings in silver dollars. MacWhirr is a steady, unimaginative man who trusts facts rather than books, and when the barometer falls he refuses to change course to avoid the storm. His young first mate Jukes and the chief engineer Solomon Rout must face the typhoon with him.

Conrad's novella is a powerful description of a storm at sea and a study of courage, duty and different kinds of character under pressure. The Chinese passengers are presented largely as an anonymous mass and described in the language of the period.
Typhoon was begun in 1899 and serialised in the Pall Mall Magazine from January to March 1902. It was published in book form the same year.
the-yellow-wallpaper: A young woman spends the summer with her husband John, a physician, in a rented colonial mansion. Diagnosed with a "temporary nervous depression" after the birth of her baby, she is forbidden to work or write and is kept in a large room at the top of the house, with barred windows and a torn yellow wallpaper whose pattern disturbs her. Writing secretly in her journal, she describes how the wallpaper gradually takes over her thoughts.

Told in the first person, the story describes a woman's descent into madness and is a sharp criticism of the medical treatment of women and of a marriage in which the husband's authority leaves no room for the wife's own voice.

The Yellow Wallpaper was published in the New England Magazine in January 1892. It drew on Gilman's own experience of the "rest cure" prescribed to her in 1887 by the neurologist Silas Weir Mitchell. In her 1913 essay "Why I Wrote The Yellow Wallpaper", she explained that it was written "to save people from being driven crazy".
bartleby-the-scrivener: The narrator, an elderly and comfortable Wall Street lawyer, employs two eccentric copyists, Turkey and Nippers, and an office boy nicknamed Ginger Nut. When business grows, he hires a third scrivener, the pale and silent Bartleby, who at first copies documents tirelessly. Then one day, asked to check a copy, Bartleby calmly replies, "I would prefer not to", and his refusals gradually extend to everything.

Melville's story is at once comic and deeply sad. Its mysterious hero has been read in many ways, and the story raises questions about work, isolation, charity and the limits of understanding another person.
Bartleby, the Scrivener was first published anonymously in two parts in Putnam's Monthly Magazine in November and December 1853, and was included in Melville's collection The Piazza Tales in 1856.
looking-backward-2000-1887: Julian West, a wealthy young Bostonian who suffers from insomnia, is put into a hypnotic sleep in a sealed underground chamber in 1887. He wakes in the year 2000 in the home of Dr Leete and his daughter Edith. The city around him has been transformed: industry is owned by the nation, every citizen serves in an "industrial army", goods are shared equally, and poverty, war and the conflict between capital and labour have disappeared. Dr Leete explains the new society to him.
Bellamy's novel uses a simple romantic story to present a detailed vision of a socialist utopia, and contrasts it with the inequalities and labour conflicts of the late nineteenth century.

Looking Backward was published in 1888 and became one of the best-selling American books of its century. It inspired a political movement, with many "Nationalist" clubs formed to discuss and promote its ideas, and a wave of utopian novels. Bellamy published a sequel, Equality, in 1897.
the-pathfinder: In the mid-eighteenth century, during the war between Britain and France for North America, Mabel Dunham travels through the forest with her uncle, the old sailor Charles Cap, to join her father, Sergeant Dunham, at a British fort near Oswego on Lake Ontario. They are guided by the scout Natty Bumppo, known as Pathfinder, his Mohican friend Chingachgook, and the young freshwater sailor Jasper Western. Pathfinder falls in love with Mabel, but the garrison faces danger and treachery on an expedition to the Thousand Islands.

The novel combines frontier adventure, sailing on the "inland sea" of Lake Ontario and a story of love and self-sacrifice. Its portrayal of Native Americans, including the Tuscarora Arrowhead and the "Mingo" enemies, relies on the stereotypes and vocabulary of its time.
The Pathfinder, or The Inland Sea was published in 1840. It is one of Cooper's five Leatherstocking Tales and the only one in which Natty Bumppo falls in love.
a-little-princess: Sara Crewe, brought up in India by her adoring father Captain Crewe, is sent to Miss Minchin's Select Seminary for Young Ladies in London, where she is treated as a show pupil. Imaginative and generous, she befriends the slow Ermengarde, little Lottie and Becky, the overworked scullery maid, and tells wonderful stories. When news comes that her father has died and his fortune has been lost, Miss Minchin sends Sara to live in a cold attic and to work as a servant, while a mysterious gentleman moves into the house next door.
Burnett's story celebrates imagination, kindness and dignity in hardship. Its picture of India and of the Indian servant Ram Dass reflects the colonial outlook of its time.

The story first appeared as the novella Sara Crewe, or What Happened at Miss Minchin's, serialised in St. Nicholas Magazine from December 1887 and published as a book in 1888. After turning it into a play in 1902, Burnett expanded it into the full novel A Little Princess, published in 1905.
the-return-of-sherlock-holmes: Three years after the fatal struggle with Professor Moriarty, Dr Watson is investigating the strange murder of the Honourable Ronald Adair in London when Sherlock Holmes reappears, alive, and explains his disappearance. The two friends resume their partnership, and the following stories take them from a cipher of dancing stick figures to a blackmailer of high society, from a series of smashed busts of Napoleon to a missing rugby player and a stolen diplomatic letter.
These thirteen stories continue to combine Holmes's powers of observation and deduction with vivid portraits of Victorian and Edwardian society, seen through the eyes of the loyal Watson.

The stories were first published in The Strand Magazine in Britain and Collier's in the United States between 1903 and 1904, and were collected in book form in 1905. They include "The Empty House", "The Dancing Men", "Charles Augustus Milverton", "The Six Napoleons" and "The Second Stain".
the-duchess-of-malfi: The young Duchess of Malfi, a widow, is forbidden by her brothers, Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, and the Cardinal, to marry again. Ferdinand places Bosola, a discontented former galley-slave, in her household as a spy. Defying them, the Duchess secretly marries Antonio, her honest steward, with only her maid Cariola as witness, and has children by him. When Bosola discovers the secret, the brothers' fury sets the tragedy in motion.

Webster's play is a dark Jacobean tragedy of corruption, cruelty and madness, set in the courts of Italy. Its heroine's courage and dignity in suffering, and its intense, often violent poetry, are among its most remarked features.
The Duchess of Malfi was first performed in 1613 or 1614 by the King's Men, Shakespeare's company, at the Blackfriars Theatre and at the Globe. It was printed in quarto in 1623.
the-water-babies: Tom is a poor, ignorant chimney sweep who works for the brutal master sweep Grimes. Sent to clean the chimneys of Harthover Place, the house of Sir John, he loses his way in the flues and comes out in the bedroom of the little girl Ellie. Chased away as a thief, he flees across the moors and falls into a river, where he is transformed into a water-baby. Under the guidance of the fairies Mrs Bedonebyasyoudid and Mrs Doasyouwouldbedoneby, he must learn to become good.

Kingsley's fantasy mixes adventure, natural history, moral lessons and satire, including comments on the scientific debates that followed Darwin's On the Origin of Species and a protest against the use of young children as chimney sweeps. Some passages contain disparaging remarks about the Irish and other peoples that reflect prejudices of its time.
The Water-Babies was written as a serial for Macmillan's Magazine in 1862 and 1863, and was published as a book in 1863.
utopia: While on a diplomatic mission in Flanders, Thomas More meets his friend Peter Giles in Antwerp, who introduces him to Raphael Hythloday, a Portuguese traveller who has sailed with Amerigo Vespucci. In the first part, Hythloday criticises the injustices of England and Europe, such as the hanging of thieves driven to crime by poverty. In the second, he describes the island of Utopia, its capital Amaurot, and the customs of its people, who hold all property in common, work six hours a day, choose their magistrates and tolerate different religions.

More's dialogue is at once a serious work of political philosophy and a playful fiction; the name Utopia, from the Greek, means "no place". It raises lasting questions about property, justice, work and government, though Utopian society also includes slavery and strict control over its citizens' lives.

Utopia was written in Latin and first printed at Louvain in 1516, with the help of Erasmus and Peter Giles. It was first published in English in 1551 in the translation by Ralph Robinson. This edition reproduces the translation by Gilbert Burnet, published in 1684.
allan-quatermain: After the death of his only son, Allan Quatermain cannot bear life in England and persuades his friends Sir Henry Curtis and Captain John Good to return with him to Africa, in search of a rumoured people living beyond the unexplored mountains. They are joined by the old Zulu warrior Umslopogaas and, later, by the comic French cook Alphonse. After a battle at the mission station of Mr Mackenzie, they reach the hidden kingdom of the Zu-Vendi, ruled by two rival queens, Nyleptha and Sorais.

This sequel to King Solomon's Mines combines battles, journeys and romance. Its presentation of Africa and Africans, and its idea of a hidden white civilisation, reflect the colonial and racial attitudes of its time.
Allan Quatermain was serialised in Longman's Magazine from January to August 1887 and published as a book the same year.
the-possessed: In a provincial town, the ageing liberal idealist Stepan Trofimovitch Verhovensky lives under the protection of the wealthy Varvara Petrovna, whose son, Nikolay Stavrogin, returns home after years of scandals. Soon Stepan Trofimovitch's son, Pyotr Verhovensky, arrives and gathers a small circle of radicals, among them the engineer Kirillov, obsessed with the idea of suicide, and the former student Shatov, who wants to leave the group. As Pyotr's schemes spread disorder through the town, the conspiracy moves towards violence.

Dostoevsky's novel is at once a political satire, a tragedy and a philosophical drama about faith, nihilism, freedom and the moral consequences of revolutionary ideas. Its gallery of characters, from the enigmatic Stavrogin to the crippled Marya Timofyevna and the drunken Captain Lebyadkin, mixes grotesque comedy and horror.

The novel was published in The Russian Messenger in 1871 and 1872. Dostoevsky drew on the murder in 1869 of the student Ivan Ivanov by members of the revolutionary group of Sergey Nechayev. Also known in English as Demons, it is offered here in Constance Garnett's English translation (1916) and Victor Derély's French translation (1886).
first-love-and-other-stories: In the title story, a middle-aged man, Vladímir Petróvitch, recalls the summer when he was sixteen and his family rented a country house near Moscow. In the shabby wing next door lived the impoverished Princess Zasyékin and her daughter Zinaída, a capricious and fascinating young woman of twenty-one who amused herself with a circle of admirers. Vladímir falls hopelessly in love with her, until he begins to suspect that she loves someone else. The volume also contains the stories "A Correspondence", "The Region of Dead Calm", "It Is Enough" and "The Dog".
Turgenev's novella is a delicate study of adolescent passion, jealousy and disillusion, and of a son's complicated relationship with his father, told with restraint and melancholy.

First Love was published in March 1860. Turgenev described it as the most autobiographical of his works, drawn from his own youthful infatuation with a neighbour. The English translation is by Isabel F. Hapgood, from her edition of Turgenev's novels and stories.
beyond-good-and-evil: Subtitled "Prelude to a Philosophy of the Future", the book is divided into nine parts made up of 296 numbered sections, ending with a poem. Nietzsche begins with "the prejudices of philosophers", questioning their faith in truth and in opposite values, then turns to the "free spirit", religion, morality, the scholar, the virtues, peoples and nations, and finally to the question "What is noble?".

In short, often aphoristic passages, Nietzsche criticises dogmatism and the morality he sees in Christianity and in modern democratic ideas, and develops ideas such as the will to power and the distinction between "master" and "slave" morality. Some passages contain generalisations about women and peoples that reflect prejudices of its time.

Beyond Good and Evil was published in 1886 by C. G. Naumann in Leipzig, at the author's own expense. This edition offers the German original and the English translation by Helen Zimmern, first published in 1907.
the-robbers: Count Maximilian von Moor has two sons: Karl, generous and impetuous, who is away from home, and the younger Franz, cold and envious. Franz uses a false letter to convince their father that Karl is a criminal, and the old count disowns his elder son. In despair, Karl becomes the captain of a band of robbers, among them Spiegelberg, Schweitzer and Kosinsky, while at home Franz schemes to seize the inheritance and to win Karl's beloved, Amalia. In the English translation the brothers are called Charles and Francis, and Amalia is Amelia.
Schiller's first play is a passionate drama of rebellion, freedom and justice, a key work of the Sturm und Drang movement, contrasting the noble outlaw Karl with his calculating brother.

The Robbers was published almost anonymously in 1781 and first performed on 13 January 1782 at the National Theatre in Mannheim, where its success made the young author famous. This edition offers the German original and an anonymous English translation.
in-search-of-the-castaways: Lord Glenarvan, a Scottish laird, finds a bottle inside a shark caught by his yacht, the Duncan. Its damaged messages, in English, French and German, reveal that Captain Harry Grant and two of his sailors were shipwrecked on the 37th parallel south. Moved by Grant's children, Mary and Robert, Glenarvan and his wife Helena set out to find him, accompanied by Major McNabbs, Captain John Mangles and the absent-minded French geographer Paganel, who boards the Duncan by mistake. Their search takes them across South America, Australia and New Zealand.

Verne's adventure novel combines geography, natural history, humour and suspense. Its descriptions of the indigenous peoples of South America, Australia and New Zealand, often called "savages", reflect the colonial views of its time.

Les Enfants du capitaine Grant was published in serial form in 1867 and 1868 in Hetzel's Magasin d'éducation et de récréation, in three parts entitled South America, Australia and New Zealand. This edition offers the French original and an anonymous English translation.
phaedo: At Phlius, Phaedo of Elis tells Echecrates about the last hours of Socrates, which he spent with him in the prison at Athens in 399 BC. Surrounded by friends, Socrates explains why a philosopher should not fear death, and discusses with the Thebans Simmias and Cebes whether the soul is immortal. He offers several arguments, drawing on the idea that learning is recollection and on the theory of Forms, and answers their objections, before ending with a myth about the fate of souls.

The dialogue is one of Plato's most important works on the soul, knowledge and the philosophical life, which Socrates describes as a preparation for death. It is also a moving portrait of Socrates' serenity in his final hours.
Plato wrote the Phaedo in the fourth century BC. This English translation is by Benjamin Jowett, the Oxford scholar whose translations of Plato's dialogues were published in the nineteenth century.
leviathan: Hobbes begins with human nature: sensation, imagination, reason, the passions and the restless desire for power. Without a common power to keep them in awe, he argues, people live in a condition of war of every man against every man, in which the life of man is "solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short". To escape it, they agree to transfer their rights to a sovereign whose authority must be undivided. The book is divided into four parts: Of Man, Of Common-wealth, Of a Christian Common-wealth and Of the Kingdome of Darknesse.

Leviathan is a founding work of modern political philosophy and of social contract theory. Its account of the state of nature, natural law and absolute sovereignty, and its criticism of the political power of churches, have been debated ever since.

Leviathan, or The Matter, Forme, and Power of a Common-wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civill was printed in London for Andrew Crooke in 1651, at the end of the English Civil War. This edition keeps the spelling of the original.
the-wild-duck: Gregers Werle, the son of a wealthy merchant, returns home after years away and despises his father. He finds his old school friend Hjalmar Ekdal living contentedly as a photographer with his wife Gina, their young daughter Hedvig and his father, old Ekdal, who keeps a wild duck and other animals in the garret. Convinced that his friend's happiness rests on lies about the past, and that the truth will make him free, Gregers resolves to tell Hjalmar everything, despite the warnings of Dr Relling.
Ibsen's drama, mixing comedy and tragedy, questions the demand for absolute truth and asks whether people need illusions, the "life-lie" defended by Relling, in order to live.
The Wild Duck was published in 1884 and first performed on 9 January 1885 at Den Nationale Scene in Bergen. This English translation by Eleanor Marx Aveling was published in 1890.
kipps: Arthur Kipps, an orphan brought up by his aunt and uncle in New Romney, is apprenticed to Mr Shalford's drapery shop in Folkestone. Long hours and petty rules leave him little hope of improvement, until the eccentric actor and would-be playwright Chitterlow shows him a newspaper advertisement that leads to a large inheritance. Suddenly rich, Kipps becomes engaged to the refined Helen Walshingham, who sets out to educate him, but he is torn between his new life and his childhood sweetheart Ann Pornick.
Wells's comic novel is an affectionate and satirical study of the English class system, social snobbery and the difficulty of crossing class boundaries.
Kipps: The Story of a Simple Soul was published in 1905.
jo-s-boys: Plumfield, the school run by Jo and Professor Bhaer, has become a college. The boys who grew up there are now young men: Nat studies music in Germany, Emil is a sailor, the restless Dan seeks adventure in the West, Demi looks for his career, and Tommy, Ted and the others face love, work and their own mistakes. Jo, now a famous author besieged by admirers, follows each of them with affection and advice.

Alcott's final novel about the March family deals with growing up, choosing a vocation, temptation and women's education and independence. Its picture of Native Americans, seen through Dan's adventures in the West, reflects the attitudes and vocabulary of its time.

Jo's Boys, and How They Turned Out: A Sequel to "Little Men" was written between 1882 and 1886, while Alcott was suffering from chronic illness, and published in 1886. It is the last book of the series that began with Little Women.
the-aeneid: Aeneas, son of the goddess Venus and the Trojan Anchises, escapes from burning Troy with his father and his young son Ascanius. Pursued by the anger of Juno, he and his companions are shipwrecked on the coast of Africa, where Queen Dido of Carthage welcomes them and falls in love with him. But the gods remind Aeneas of his destiny in Italy. After a descent into the underworld, he reaches Latium, where King Latinus offers him his daughter Lavinia, and war breaks out with Turnus, leader of the Rutulians.

Virgil's epic in twelve books follows the model of Homer: the first six books tell of Aeneas's journey, the last six of the war in Italy. It celebrates duty, piety and the destiny of Rome, while giving voice to the suffering of those, like Dido and Turnus, who stand in its way.

Virgil worked on the Aeneid from about 29 BC until his death in 19 BC, and it was published after his death. This English verse translation is by John Dryden, published in 1697 in his Works of Virgil.
the-consolation-of-philosophy: Boethius, once a powerful official, lies in prison, condemned on a charge of treason and lamenting his fate. A majestic woman appears to him: Lady Philosophy. She drives away the Muses of poetry who feed his grief, and in a dialogue spread over five books she leads him to understand that fortune is by nature changeable, that true happiness lies not in wealth, power or fame but in the highest good, and that divine providence can be reconciled with human free will.

Written in alternating prose and verse, the work combines the thought of Plato, Aristotle and the Stoics. It was one of the most widely read books of the Middle Ages, translated by King Alfred and by Chaucer, among others.
Boethius wrote the Consolation around 524 while imprisoned by the Ostrogothic king Theodoric, before his execution. This English translation is by H. R. James.
the-song-of-roland: After seven years of war in Spain, Charlemagne has conquered every city except Saragossa, ruled by the Saracen king Marsile. When Marsile offers peace, Roland proposes his stepfather Ganelon (called Guenes in this translation) as envoy. Humiliated and resentful, Ganelon plots with the enemy, and as the Frankish army crosses the Pyrenees, the rearguard led by Roland, his companion Oliver and Archbishop Turpin is attacked by an enormous army at Rencesvals. Oliver urges Roland to blow his olifant to call Charlemagne back.

The oldest major work of French literature, this chanson de geste celebrates feudal loyalty, Christian faith and heroic courage, and contrasts the pride of Roland with the wisdom of Oliver. It presents the Muslim Saracens as enemies of the faith, in the spirit of the crusading era in which it was written.

The poem transforms a real event, the ambush of Charlemagne's rearguard at Roncevaux in 778. Its best-known text is the Oxford manuscript, copied in Anglo-Norman in the twelfth century, whose last line names a certain Turoldus. This translation by C. K. Scott Moncrieff, published in 1919, follows the metre of the original.
the-rivals: Lydia Languish, a young heiress who has read too many romantic novels, wants to elope with a poor soldier. To win her, Captain Jack Absolute has disguised himself as "Ensign Beverley". His plans are complicated when his father, Sir Anthony Absolute, arranges for him to marry the same young woman, and by the rival suitors Bob Acres and Sir Lucius O'Trigger. Meanwhile Lydia's aunt, Mrs Malaprop, confuses her words at every turn, and Jack's friend Faulkland torments his beloved Julia with his jealousy.
Sheridan's comedy of manners satirises sentimental romance and fashionable society. Mrs Malaprop's comic misuse of words gave the English language the word "malapropism".
The Rivals was Sheridan's first play. It opened at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, on 17 January 1775, was poorly received, and after extensive revision reopened on 28 January with great success.
the-kalevala: The fifty runes of the Kalevala tell the creation of the world and the adventures of the heroes of the land of Kalevala: the wise old singer Väinämöinen (Wainamoinen in this translation), the smith Ilmarinen, who forges the Sampo, a magic mill that brings wealth, and the reckless Lemminkäinen. Their rivalry with Louhi, the mistress of the northern land of Pohjola (Pohyola here), leads to wooing expeditions, battles and the theft of the Sampo. Among the episodes is the tragic story of Kullervo.
The poem mixes myth, magic, humour and tragedy, and reflects the folk beliefs and daily life of the Finnish people. It played a major role in the development of Finnish national identity and culture.

The physician and philologist Elias Lönnrot compiled the Kalevala from the folk poetry he collected on his journeys. A first version appeared in 1835, and the expanded edition of fifty runes in 1849. John Martin Crawford's English translation, based on Franz Anton Schiefner's German translation, was first published in 1888.
narrative-of-the-life-of-frederick-dougl: Douglass describes his birth into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland, separated from his mother as an infant and never knowing his exact age. He recounts the cruelty he witnessed on Colonel Lloyd's plantation, his years in Baltimore, where his mistress began to teach him the alphabet until her husband forbade it, and how he went on teaching himself in secret. Hired out to Edward Covey, a farmer notorious for breaking the will of enslaved people, he finally fights back. The book ends with his escape to the North and his new life in New Bedford, Massachusetts.

Written in a clear and powerful style, the Narrative is both a personal testimony and an argument against slavery, showing how it degrades both the enslaved and the enslavers and exposing the hypocrisy of slaveholding Christianity. Douglass deliberately gives no details of his escape in order to protect those who might still use the same route.

The Narrative was published in Boston in 1845 by the Anti-Slavery Office, with a preface by William Lloyd Garrison and a letter by Wendell Phillips. It sold some 5,000 copies in its first four months and became the best-known of the American slave narratives.
the-narrative-of-arthur-gordon-pym-of-na: Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, eager for adventure, is smuggled aboard the whaling brig Grampus by his friend Augustus Barnard, whose father is its captain, and hidden in the hold with his dog Tiger. A bloody mutiny breaks out, and Pym, Augustus and the sailor Dirk Peters fight to survive, then drift on the wreck, suffering terribly from hunger and thirst. Rescued by the British schooner Jane Guy, Pym sails into the Antarctic seas, towards an unknown island called Tsalal.

Poe's only completed novel mixes the sea adventure, the horror tale and the false travel narrative, presented as a true account. Its depiction of the black-skinned islanders of Tsalal and of the "half-breed" Dirk Peters reflects the racial attitudes of its time.
The novel was published by Harper & Brothers in July 1838, after a few opening instalments had appeared in the Southern Literary Messenger.
the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher: One dark autumn day, the narrator arrives at the melancholy House of Usher in answer to a letter from his boyhood friend Roderick Usher, who suffers from a nervous illness and an extreme sensitivity of the senses. Roderick's twin sister, Madeline, is wasting away from a mysterious disease. The narrator tries to distract his friend with reading, painting and music, but the atmosphere of the decaying house weighs on them all.
Poe's tale is a classic of Gothic fiction, in which the decaying house mirrors the minds and the fate of the family that lives in it. It explores fear, madness, isolation and the bond between twins.

"The Fall of the House of Usher" was first published in September 1839 in Burton's Gentleman's Magazine and, slightly revised, in Poe's collection Tales of the Grotesque and Arabesque (1840). It includes the poem "The Haunted Palace", which Poe had published separately earlier in 1839.
the-happy-prince-and-other-tales: High above a city stands the statue of the Happy Prince, covered in gold leaf and jewels. From there he sees the misery of the poor, and he asks a little Swallow, who has stayed behind on his journey to Egypt, to carry his treasures to them. The collection also contains "The Nightingale and the Rose", "The Selfish Giant", "The Devoted Friend" and "The Remarkable Rocket".
Written in the form of fairy tales for children, Wilde's stories mix wit and tenderness, and speak of generosity, sacrifice, selfishness and vanity, often with a melancholy ending.
The Happy Prince and Other Tales was published in London by David Nutt in May 1888, with illustrations by Walter Crane and Jacomb Hood.
mrs-warren-s-profession: Vivie Warren, a clever and independent young woman who has just done brilliantly in mathematics at Cambridge, is spending time in a cottage in Surrey when her mother, whom she barely knows, arrives with her friends, the artistic Mr Praed and the coarse Sir George Crofts. Vivie is also courted by Frank Gardner, the idle son of the local clergyman. Questioning her mother, she discovers the source of the money that has supported her all her life.

Shaw's play attacks the hypocrisy of a society that condemns prostitution while leaving poor women few other means of escaping poverty, and that profits from it in respectable ways. It also portrays a new kind of independent, working woman in Vivie.

Shaw completed the play in 1893, but the Lord Chamberlain refused to license it for public performance. It was published in Plays Unpleasant in 1898 and first performed privately by the Stage Society in London on 5 January 1902. This edition includes the author's apology of 1902.
up-from-slavery: Washington recalls his childhood as an enslaved boy on a Virginia plantation, and the family's move after emancipation to Malden, West Virginia, where he worked in a salt furnace and a coal mine while trying to learn to read. Determined to study, he made his way to the Hampton Institute, where General Samuel Armstrong became his mentor. In 1881 Armstrong recommended him to lead a new school for Black students at Tuskegee, Alabama, which began in a run-down shanty and a church.

The autobiography presents Washington's belief in education, hard work, practical skills and self-reliance as the path to progress for African Americans. Its full text of his 1895 Atlanta Exposition Address, which called for cooperation between the races in the South, also reflects the compromise with segregation for which he was later criticised.
Up from Slavery was published in 1901 and became Washington's best-known work.
antony-and-cleopatra: Mark Antony, one of the three rulers of the Roman world with Octavius Caesar and Lepidus, lingers in Alexandria with Cleopatra, neglecting his duties. Called back to Rome by the threat of Pompey, he makes peace with Octavius and marries his sister Octavia, but soon returns to Egypt. War breaks out between the two men. At the battle of Actium, Cleopatra's ships flee and Antony follows her, and even his loyal lieutenant Enobarbus begins to doubt him.
Shakespeare's tragedy contrasts the discipline of Rome with the splendour and pleasures of Egypt, and portrays one of his most complex heroines, whose "infinite variety" fascinates Antony to the end.

The play was probably first performed around 1607 by the King's Men. It was first printed in the First Folio of 1623, from which this English text, in its original spelling, is taken; the play draws on Thomas North's 1579 translation of Plutarch's Lives. The French translation is by François Guizot.
uncle-silas: Maud Ruthyn, a young heiress, lives with her rich and reclusive father Austin Ruthyn at Knowl. Her father's brother Silas has long been under suspicion since a man to whom he owed a large gambling debt was found dead in a locked room of his house at Bartram-Haugh. Her father engages a sinister French governess, Madame de la Rougierre, who frightens Maud. On her father's death, his will places Maud in the care of Uncle Silas, whom he wishes to clear of suspicion, and she goes to live at Bartram-Haugh with his son Dudley and his daughter Milly.
Told by Maud herself, Le Fanu's novel is a classic of Victorian Gothic suspense, combining a locked-room mystery, an isolated heroine and a growing sense of menace.

Uncle Silas was first serialised in the Dublin University Magazine in 1864 under the title Maud Ruthyn and Uncle Silas, and appeared in December 1864 as a three-volume novel published by Richard Bentley in London.
the-man-who-laughs: On a winter night on the English coast, a band of child-traffickers, the comprachicos, abandon a young boy. Wandering through a snowstorm, he rescues a baby girl whose mother has frozen to death. The two children are taken in by Ursus, a vagabond philosopher and mountebank, and his wolf Homo. Fifteen years later, the boy, Gwynplaine, whose mouth has been mutilated into a perpetual grin, is a famous performer, and he loves the blind Dea. Then the scheming Barkilphedro, the duchess Josiana and the court of Queen Anne enter his life.
Hugo's novel is a powerful attack on aristocratic privilege and social injustice, in which the deformed Gwynplaine becomes a symbol of the suffering people.

L'Homme qui rit was published in April 1869. A note at the end of the French text states that it was begun in Brussels on 21 July 1866 and finished there on 23 August 1868. This edition offers the French original and an anonymous English translation.
the-man-who-would-be-king: The narrator, a newspaper editor in India, meets two penniless adventurers, Daniel Dravot and Peachey Carnehan, who are, like him, Freemasons. They tell him that India is not big enough for them and that they intend to go to Kafiristan, a remote region of Afghanistan, armed with rifles and their military experience, to set themselves up as kings. Two years later, a broken and crippled man comes into the narrator's office at night and tells him what happened.

Kipling's story is a tale of adventure and ambition, and a parable about imperial power, pride and its fall. Its portrayal of the people of Kafiristan and of the adventurers' plans reflects the imperial outlook of its time.
"The Man Who Would Be King" was first published in 1888 in The Phantom 'Rickshaw and Other Tales.
three-men-in-a-boat: J., the narrator, and his friends George and Harris decide that they are suffering from "overwork" and need a rest. After rejecting a country stay and a sea trip, they settle on a boating holiday up the River Thames, from Kingston upon Thames to Oxford, camping on the way, accompanied by J.'s dog Montmorency. Packing, cooking, pitching the tent, towing the boat and dealing with other river users all lead to comic disasters, interrupted by anecdotes and reflections on the places they pass.

Jerome's comic travelogue mixes slapstick, gentle irony and occasional lyrical or historical passages. Its humour comes largely from the narrator's self-mocking voice and from the small frustrations of everyday life.

Three Men in a Boat (To Say Nothing of the Dog) was published in 1889. George and Harris were based on Jerome's real friends George Wingrave and Carl Hentschel; the dog Montmorency, according to Jerome, was entirely fictional.
the-man-who-was-thursday: In the London suburb of Saffron Park, the poet Gabriel Syme argues with Lucian Gregory, an anarchist poet, about whether poetry is rebellion or order. Syme is in fact a member of a secret police corps devoted to fighting anarchism. Gregory takes him to an underground meeting place, and Syme manages to have himself elected to the post of "Thursday" on the central anarchist council, whose seven members are named after the days of the week and are led by the enormous and terrifying Sunday.

Subtitled "A Nightmare", Chesterton's novel begins as a comic spy thriller and becomes a metaphysical fable about order and chaos, doubt and faith. It is prefaced by a poem addressed to his friend Edmund Clerihew Bentley.
The Man Who Was Thursday was published in 1908.
sons-and-lovers: Gertrude Coppard, a refined young woman, marries Walter Morel, a rough and lively miner, after meeting him at a Christmas dance, but the marriage soon turns bitter in the poverty of the mining village of Bestwood. Gertrude pours her affection into her sons, first William, then Paul. As Paul grows up and begins to paint, he falls into a relationship with Miriam, a farmer's daughter, and later with Clara Dawes, a woman separated from her husband Baxter, while his mother's hold over him remains strong.

Lawrence's novel explores family conflict, class, work in the mines and the emotional and sexual development of a young man, with a powerful sense of the landscape and community of the Nottinghamshire coalfield.
Sons and Lovers was published in 1913 by Duckworth in London and Mitchell Kennerley in New York. Before publication it was usually called Paul Morel.
captain-blood: In 1685 Peter Blood, an Irish physician who has once been a soldier and sailor, lives quietly in Bridgwater, Somerset, tending his geraniums. Called to treat a rebel wounded at the battle of Sedgemoor during the Monmouth Rebellion, he is arrested and condemned for treason by Judge Jeffreys at the Bloody Assizes. Transported to Barbados and sold to the brutal Colonel Bishop, he wins the friendship of Bishop's niece Arabella, then escapes with other convicts, among them the young navigator Jeremy Pitt, and becomes a buccaneer captain in the Caribbean, rival of the cruel Levasseur.

Sabatini's swashbuckling novel combines sea battles, honour and romance with real historical events. Its picture of the Caribbean plantations and of enslaved Africans reflects the language and attitudes of its time.

The adventures of Captain Blood first appeared as short stories in Premier Magazine in 1920 and 1921, which Sabatini wove into a continuous novel, Captain Blood: His Odyssey, published in 1922. The first part was inspired by the real story of Henry Pitman, a surgeon transported to Barbados after the Monmouth Rebellion.
the-garden-party-and-other-stories: In the title story, the wealthy Sheridan family prepare to give a garden party. Young Laura supervises the workmen putting up the marquee, while her mother has ordered masses of lilies. Then the news arrives that Mr Scott, a working-class neighbour, has been killed just outside their gate. Laura wants the party called off, but her mother and her sister Jose do not agree. The collection opens with "At the Bay", a portrait of a family's summer days in a seaside settlement, and also includes "The Daughters of the Late Colonel", "Life of Ma Parker", "Miss Brill" and "Her First Ball".
Mansfield's stories capture fleeting moments of feeling and perception, class differences, loneliness and the discovery of death, in a concise, poetic and modern style.

"The Garden Party" first appeared in the Westminster Gazette in February 1922, and the collection The Garden Party and Other Stories was published the same year. Several stories, including "At the Bay" and "The Garden Party", were written in Switzerland, and the title story draws on Mansfield's childhood home in Wellington.
this-side-of-paradise: Amory Blaine, raised by his eccentric mother Beatrice, believes that he is destined for greatness without knowing what form it will take. At Princeton he dabbles in literature, makes friends such as the idealistic Burne Holiday and the poet Tom D'Invilliers, and falls in and out of love with a series of young women, among them Isabelle, the debutante Rosalind and the wild Eleanor, while his mentor Monsignor Darcy advises him from afar.
Fitzgerald's first novel portrays the manners, ambitions and romances of a privileged younger generation in the 1910s, and the search of a young man for identity and meaning.

This Side of Paradise was published by Charles Scribner's Sons in March 1920, when Fitzgerald was 23. Its title comes from Rupert Brooke's poem "Tiare Tahiti". It caused a sensation and made its author a spokesman for rebellious youth.
a-portrait-of-the-artist-as-a-young-man: The novel follows Stephen Dedalus from his first memories, through his years at the Jesuit boarding school of Clongowes Wood and the family's decline into poverty, a violent quarrel over Irish politics at a Christmas dinner, adolescent guilt and a period of intense religious devotion, to his years as a student in Dublin, where he debates art and beauty with his friends Cranly, Davin and Lynch and decides to leave Ireland.

Joyce's first novel, a Künstlerroman written in a modernist style, uses a language that changes as its hero grows up, and makes extensive use of free indirect speech to follow Stephen's developing consciousness. It explores religion, Irish nationalism, family and the vocation of the artist.

Joyce reworked an earlier abandoned novel, Stephen Hero, into this five-chapter book. Thanks to Ezra Pound it was serialised in the London magazine The Egoist in 1914 and 1915, and it was published as a book in 1916 by B. W. Huebsch in New York.
the-diary-of-a-nobody: Charles Pooter, a clerk in the City firm of Perkupp's, has just moved with his wife Carrie into "The Laurels", Brickfield Terrace, Holloway. In his diary he records the events of the following fifteen months: visits from his friends Gowing and Cummings, quarrels with tradesmen, social evenings that end in embarrassment, and the troubles caused by his son Lupin, who wants to make his own way in the world and becomes engaged to Daisy Mutlar.

The humour of the book comes from Pooter's unconscious pomposity and from the way his sense of importance is constantly punctured by gaffes and minor social disasters, in a gentle satire of lower-middle-class respectability.
The Diary first appeared as an intermittent serial in Punch in 1888 and 1889, and was published as a book, with additional text and illustrations by Weedon Grossmith, in 1892.
salome: On a moonlit night, on a terrace of the palace of Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Judaea, the young Syrian captain and the page of Herodias watch the princess Salomé. From a cistern rises the voice of the prophet Jokanaan (John the Baptist), whom Herod keeps prisoner. Salomé, Herodias's daughter and Herod's stepdaughter, insists on seeing him and is fascinated by him, but he rejects her. Herod, who desires Salomé, begs her to dance for him, promising her anything she asks.
Wilde's one-act tragedy turns the biblical story into a Symbolist drama of desire, obsession and death, written in a rhythmic, incantatory language full of repeated images, above all the moon.

Wilde wrote Salomé in French in Paris in late 1891. Rehearsals with Sarah Bernhardt in London in 1892 were stopped when the Lord Chamberlain refused a licence. The French text was published in 1893 and an English translation in 1894; the English text here comes from a 1907 edition with drawings by Aubrey Beardsley. The first performance was given in Paris on 11 February 1896 by the Théâtre de l'Œuvre, while Wilde was in prison. This edition offers the French original and the English translation credited to Lord Alfred Douglas.
jacob-s-room: The novel begins on a beach in Cornwall, where the widowed Betty Flanders is writing a letter while her sons play, among them Jacob. It follows Jacob Flanders through his childhood in Scarborough, his years at Cambridge, his life in London, where he has an affair with the art student Florinda and is loved by the reserved Clara Durrant, and his travels to Italy and Greece. His friend Bonamy and the women in his life give their scattered impressions of him.

Woolf's third novel breaks with conventional storytelling: Jacob is seen almost entirely through the perceptions of others, and motifs of emptiness and absence give the book an elegiac tone. His surname evokes the generation of young men who died in the fields of Flanders.
Jacob's Room was first published on 26 October 1922.
the-innocence-of-father-brown: In "The Blue Cross", the great French detective Valentin pursues the master thief Flambeau across London, following a trail of strange incidents, while a small, clumsy priest from Essex carries a precious silver cross. That priest is Father Brown, who understands crime through his knowledge of the human soul. In the following stories, Flambeau, a reformed criminal, becomes his friend and assistant, and together they solve mysteries such as "The Secret Garden", "The Queer Feet", "The Invisible Man" and "The Hammer of God".
Chesterton's detective stories combine ingenious puzzles with paradox, humour and reflections on faith and reason.
Father Brown first appeared in "The Blue Cross" in 1910. The Innocence of Father Brown, published in 1911, is the first of the five collections of his adventures.
scaramouche: André-Louis Moreau, a young lawyer of unknown parentage, lives in the Breton village of Gavrillac with his godfather, Quentin de Kercadiou, and has grown up with Kercadiou's niece Aline. When his idealistic friend Philippe de Vilmorin is killed in a duel by the arrogant Marquis de La Tour d'Azyr, André-Louis vows revenge. On the run, he joins the travelling troupe of Binet, where he plays the character of Scaramouche and courts the actress Climène, before becoming a revolutionary orator and a master swordsman.

Sabatini's romance combines adventure, sword fights, wit and love with the events of the French Revolution. It opens with the famous line "He was born with a gift of laughter and a sense that the world was mad."
Scaramouche was published in 1921 and brought Sabatini his first great success. Its opening line is inscribed on his gravestone. In the English text the hero's name is spelled Andre-Louis.
the-winter-s-tale: Leontes, King of Sicily, is visited by his childhood friend Polixenes, King of Bohemia. When his wife Hermione persuades Polixenes to extend his stay, Leontes is seized by a violent jealousy and becomes convinced that she has been unfaithful. He orders his counsellor Camillo to poison Polixenes, imprisons Hermione and rejects her newborn daughter, whom the loyal Antigonus must abandon on a distant shore, despite the protests of the fearless Paulina.

Grouped with the comedies in the First Folio and now often called one of Shakespeare's late romances, the play moves from intense psychological drama in its first three acts to a pastoral comedy, with the rogue Autolycus and the love of Florizel and Perdita, and a happy ending.
The Winter's Tale was first published in the First Folio of 1623, from which this English text, in its original spelling, is taken. The French translation is by François Guizot.
the-analects: The Analects gather short sayings and conversations of Confucius, "the Master", with his disciples and contemporaries. They speak of humaneness, filial piety, ritual propriety, the cultivation of the self through learning, the qualities of the "superior man" and the duties of rulers and ministers, and give glimpses of Confucius's own character and life.

The Analects became a central text of Confucianism and one of the "Four Books" of Chinese education. For more than two thousand years they have been among the most widely read and studied books in China, with a lasting influence on East Asian thought and values.

According to tradition, the text was compiled by Confucius's disciples after his death in 479 BC; scholars believe large parts were written during the Warring States period (475–221 BC). This English translation by the Scottish sinologist James Legge forms part of his Chinese Classics.
the-valley-of-fear: Holmes receives a cipher message from Fred Porlock, an informer within the organisation of Professor Moriarty, warning of danger to a man named Douglas of Birlstone House. Almost at once Inspector MacDonald arrives at Baker Street with the news that Douglas has been murdered. Holmes and Watson travel to Birlstone, a manor surrounded by a moat, where Cecil Barker, a frequent guest, discovered the body. The second part of the novel moves back in time to the coal-mining Vermissa Valley in the United States, terrorised by a secret society, the Scowrers, which the newcomer McMurdo joins.
The novel combines a detective puzzle in an English country house with a long story of crime and secret societies set in America.

The Valley of Fear is the fourth and last Sherlock Holmes novel. It was first published in the Strand Magazine from September 1914 to May 1915, and as a book in New York on 27 February 1915. Its American story is loosely based on the Molly Maguires and the Pinkerton agent James McParland.
the-secret-agent: Adolf Verloc keeps a small shop in Soho and lives with his wife Winnie, her mother and her vulnerable younger brother Stevie, whom Winnie protects like a son. Verloc is also a member of a circle of anarchists, among them Comrade Ossipon, Michaelis and the sinister "Professor", and secretly an agent of a foreign embassy. Mr Vladimir, its new First Secretary, demands that he prove his usefulness by staging an outrage: the destruction of the Greenwich Observatory by a bomb.
Conrad's ironic novel explores terrorism, espionage, politics and the exploitation of the vulnerable, and contrasts the cynicism of its plotters with the tragedy of an ordinary family.
The Secret Agent: A Simple Tale was first printed in eleven instalments in Ridgway's in 1905 and 1906 and published as a book on 12 September 1907.
the-beetle: Robert Holt, a clerk who has spent the day looking in vain for work, takes shelter in an empty house and falls into the power of a strange being who controls him through mesmerism. The creature sends him to the house of Paul Lessingham, a member of the House of Commons, to steal letters from his desk. The story is then taken up by Sydney Atherton, by Marjorie Lindon and by the detective Augustus Champnell, as the menace linked to the cult of Isis closes in.

Told by four narrators, Marsh's fin-de-siècle Gothic thriller mixes horror, suspense and the supernatural. Its depiction of Egypt and of its foreign, shape-shifting villain draws on the orientalist fears and stereotypes of its time.
The Beetle was published in 1897, the same year as Bram Stoker's Dracula, and was at first more popular, outselling it several times over.
the-food-of-the-gods: Mr Bensington, a chemist, and Professor Redwood, who studies growth, develop a substance that accelerates growth, which they call Herakleophorbia IV. Their experimental farm at Hickleybrow is entrusted to the careless Skinners, and soon giant chickens, wasps, earwigs and rats terrorise the countryside, until the energetic engineer Cossar organises their destruction. But the food, popularly called "Boomfood", is also given to children, among them Redwood's son, Cossar's sons and the Skinners' grandson Caddles, who grow into giants.
Wells's novel begins as a comic scientific fantasy and becomes a fable about progress, change and the resistance of a narrow-minded society to anything larger than itself.
The Food of the Gods and How It Came to Earth was first published in 1904.
new-arabian-nights: In "The Suicide Club", Prince Florizel of Bohemia and his faithful Colonel Geraldine, roaming London in disguise, are led to a secret club where, each evening, a game of cards decides which member will die and who will kill him. "The Rajah's Diamond" follows the fortunes of a fabulous stolen jewel. The collection also contains "The Pavilion on the Links", "A Lodging for the Night", about the poet François Villon, "The Sire de Malétroit's Door" and "Providence and the Guitar".
Stevenson's stories transpose the spirit of the Thousand and One Nights to modern London and Paris, mixing adventure, mystery, irony and the macabre.
New Arabian Nights was published in 1882. Its stories had appeared in magazines between 1877 and 1880; the Florizel stories were first published in the London Magazine in 1878.
growth-of-the-soil: Isak, a strong and simple man, settles on an empty stretch of land in the north of Norway and begins to clear it for farming. He asks passing Lapps to tell women that he needs help, and one day Inger, a sturdy young woman with a harelip, arrives and stays. Together they build the farm of Sellanraa and raise their sons Eleseus and Sivert, helped by the official Geissler and troubled by the scheming Oline. In the second part, the neighbouring settler Axel and the servant Barbro have their own story, as mining, trade and the town reach the wilderness.

Hamsun's novel celebrates the patient work of the soil and the cycle of rural life, and contrasts it with the restlessness of modern society. Its depiction of the Sami, called Lapps in the text, reflects the prejudices of its time.

Growth of the Soil (Markens Grøde) was first published in 1917, and Hamsun was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1920 for this novel. This edition offers the English translation by W. W. Worster and the German translation by Pauline Klaiber.
niels-lyhne: Niels Lyhne grows up on the estate of Lönborggaard, between a romantic, poetic mother, Bartholine, and a practical father. As a boy he loses his faith in God after the death of his beloved aunt Edele, and later, in Copenhagen, he dreams of becoming a poet. He falls in love with the married Mrs Boye, then with Fennimore, the wife of his friend the painter Erik, and later marries the young Gerda, while trying to live by his convictions as an atheist.

Jacobsen's novel, written in a refined and poetic style, is a work of Scandinavian naturalism that follows a man's failures as a lover and an artist, and is at the same time a critique of atheism and of faith. The poet Rainer Maria Rilke recommended it, with the Bible, as one of the two books most worth reading.
Niels Lyhne was published in 1880. This English translation by Hanna Astrup Larsen appeared in the series Scandinavian Classics.
dona-perfecta: Don José (Pepe) Rey, a young engineer from Madrid with modern, liberal ideas, travels to the cathedral town of Orbajosa to marry his cousin Rosario, a match arranged between his father and his father's sister, Doña Perfecta. Pepe and Rosario soon fall in love, but the canon of the cathedral, Don Inocencio, and the townspeople, among them the rough Caballuco, distrust the newcomer. When Doña Perfecta learns that Pepe is not a believer, she sets herself against the marriage.

Galdós's realist novel is a powerful study of religious intolerance and fanaticism, and of the conflict between the traditional outlook of the Spanish provinces and the modern, liberal outlook of Madrid.
Doña Perfecta was published in 1876. This English translation is by Mary J. Serrano.
the-book-of-tea: In seven short chapters, Okakura traces the history of tea from a medicine in ancient China to the ritual of the Japanese tea ceremony, which he calls "Teaism". He discusses the schools of tea, Taoism and Zen, the tea room, art appreciation, flowers and the great tea masters, ending with the death of the tea master Rikiu (Sen no Rikyu).

Addressed to a Western audience and written in English, the book links the tea ceremony to Japanese aesthetics and ways of life, praising simplicity, purity and humility, and protests against Western caricatures of "the East".
The Book of Tea was published in 1906, in the wake of the Russo-Japanese War.
billy-budd-and-other-prose-pieces: Billy Budd, a handsome and good-natured young sailor, is pressed into service in 1797 from the merchant ship Rights-of-Man onto a British man-of-war, at a time when the Royal Navy has just been shaken by the mutinies at Spithead and the Nore. Admired by the crew, he arouses the envy of the master-at-arms, John Claggart, who falsely accuses him before Captain Edward Fairfax Vere of plotting mutiny. Unable to answer because of his stammer, Billy strikes his accuser.

Melville's novella is a tragedy of innocence and evil, law and conscience. The volume also contains other prose pieces by Melville, including the essay "Hawthorne and His Mosses" and stories such as "Cock-a-Doodle-Doo!" and "The Paradise of Bachelors and the Tartarus of Maids".

Billy Budd was left unfinished at Melville's death in 1891 and first published in 1924 in this edition by Raymond Weaver, as volume XIII of the Standard Edition of Melville's works. Later editions corrected Weaver's text; in this version the warship is called the Indomitable, renamed Bellipotent in later editions.
